variants.definition_ko: 단 지파에게 배정된 가나안 땅은 해안 지대로 베냐민 서쪽, 에브라임과 유다 사이에 있었다. 바다 가까이 길이 14마일의 넓은 평야를 포함했으나 아모리 족속이 평야를 차지하고 그들을 산지로 몰아냈다. 그래서 헤르몬산 근처에 다른 몫을 받았고, 거기에 미가에게서 훔친 새긴 신상을 세웠다(삿 18장). '단 성읍'은 이 지파가 차지한 북쪽 지역의 중심 성읍으로(삿 20:1) 본래 라이스라 불렸으며(삿 18:29) 우상숭배로 유명했다. 지금은 '재판관의 언덕'이라는 뜻의 텔엘카디라 불린다.

entries.definition: DANCE. The Jewish dances were generally expressions of joy and gratitude, sometimes in honor of a conqueror, Jud 11:34; 1 Sam 18:6-7, and sometimes on domestic occasions. Jer 31:4, 2 Kgs 11:13; Luke 15:25. The dance was also introduced into the religious service, and the timbrel (tambourine) was employed to direct it. Some individual led, and the rest followed with measured steps and devotional songs. Thus, David and Miriam led such a band. 2 Sam 6:14; Ex 15:20. Individuals often expressed feelings of joy in the same way. Luke 6:23; Acts 3:8. Dancing was practised from a very early period as a natural exercise and amusement. Job 21:11; Mark 6:22. But the mingling of males and females which is so common in modern dances was unknown to the Jews. Indeed, the dancing was mostly done by the women alone, as is still the case in Egypt. A Hebrew word, mahhol, which occurs in some passages -e.g. Ps 150:4-and is rendered "dance" in our version, is supposed by some scholars to mean a musical instrument.
entries.definition_ko: 유대인의 춤은 대개 기쁨과 감사의 표현이었고, 때로는 승전한 자를 기리거나(사사기 11:34, 사무엘상 18:6-7) 집안의 경사에 추었다(예레미야 31:4, 누가복음 15:25). 종교 예식에도 도입되어 소고로 박자를 이끌었다. 한 사람이 앞장서고 나머지가 절도 있는 걸음과 찬송으로 따랐는데, 다윗과 미리암이 그런 무리를 이끌었다(사무엘하 6:14, 출애굽기 15:20). 오늘날 흔한 남녀가 어울리는 춤은 유대인에게 없었고, 오늘날 애굽에서 그렇듯 대개 여자들만 추었다.

entries.definition: DANIEL, BOOK OF. It consists of two distinct parts. Historical, chs. Dan 1-6, containing the interesting narrative given in the preceding section, and with it an account of the attempted burning of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego in a fiery furnace because they would not worship the golden image which Nebuchadnezzar set up on the plain of Dura. Apocalyptic, chs. Dan 1:7-12, or the record of Daniel's visions. Ch.Dan 1:1 contains the introduction,- chs. Dan 1:2-6 present a general view of the progressive history of the powers of the world, and of the principles of the divine government, as seen in events in the life of Daniel; and chs. Dan 1:7-12, the prophecy of the future of the people of God. The book is written in prose, but not in the same language throughout. The introduction, chs. Dan 1:1-2:4, first clause, is written in Hebrew, but from the second clause of the fourth verse of the second chapter to the end of ch. 7 it is in Aramaic, called Syriac in that verse. From the beginning of ch. 8 to the end, in which part the visions are related in the first person, the language is Hebrew. The interpretation of Daniel requires profound knowledge of ancient history. The book is, in fact, a sort of religious philosophy of history. Its fundamental idea is that all the kingdoms of the world, which pass away, are ruled and overruled by divine Providence for the kingdom of Christ, which will last for ever. The book of Daniel occupies in the O.T. the same position which the Revelation of John occupies in the New. It views the kingdom of God in its contact and conflicts with the empires of the world, and looks forward to the universal reign of Christ, the resurrection of the dead, and the final judgment. The empires of the world appear first in Nebuchadnezzar's dream, ch. Lev 10:2, under the figure of a colossal image with a head of gold, a breast and arms of silver, a belly of brass, and legs and feet of iron and clay. These represent respectively (according to the usual orthodox interpretation) the Babylonian, the Medo-Persian, the Macedo-Greek, and the Roman empires; they are overthrown at last by a stone cut out of the mountain without hands and becoming a great mountain, which represents the reign of the Messiah. The indestructible rock of God's own workmanship breaks to pieces the metal colossus of man's hand. The same succession of monarchies is presented in the seventh chapter, under the form of a vision of four beasts seen by the prophet himself. The fourth beast has ten horns, denoting ten kingdoms, growing out of it, and a little horn (Song of Solomon 7:8, Jud 6:24) springing up among the four fractured horns of the Greek empire. Interpreters agree as to the first empire, which must be Babylonia, but differ as to the other three. Some combine the Medes and Persians in one empire; others divide them, and regard the Greeks (Alexander the Great and his successors) as representing the fourth empire, and refer the "little horn" to Antiochus Epiphanes. Still others give the prophecy of Daniel a more comprehensive sweep over all the world-empires before and after Christ, as preparing the way for the ultimate and everlasting reign of Christ. This prophecy of Christ, the most important in the book, is constantly fulfilling before our eyes, and cannot be set aside by any negative criticism. The book of Daniel has been much attacked, but also successfully vindicated by biblical scholars. In the second part Daniel speaks in the first person as the receiver of the divine revelations recorded therein, so that the only alternative here is between truth and fraud. The very fact that two languages are used renders it extremely unlikely that it should have been forged or written in any later period, but to Daniel, familiar as he was with both Hebrew and Aramaic, it was natural. The book displays familiar acquaintance with Babylonian life and royal manners, and suits throughout the period of the Babylonian exile and the peculiar position of Daniel at the Babylonian court. The genuineness is sanctioned by the highest authority -that of Christ, Matt 24:15, from which there is no appeal for believers. The attacks upon the book have been in three lines: (1) Its extraordinary events -the golden image, the burning fiery furnace, the dreams, the lions' den, etc.; (2) its minute prophecies; (3) its foreign (Greek) words; (4) its narrative. To these objections it is sufficient to reply:(1) The characteristics of Babylon, the manners and customs of the East, amply justify the language and prove that the book is genuinely Oriental and Babylonian. (2) The peculiar position of Daniel required an exceptional and startling character for his revelations; his prophecies have been in great part fulfilled. (3) The Greek words are only four in number, and are the names of musical instruments which may have been imported from Greece as early as b.c. 600. (4) Its historical difficulties. Belshazzar is represented as the last king of Babylon, while the authority there known gave Nabonnedus as the last king. This difficulty was solved by Sir Henry Rawlinson's decipherment of a cylinder among the ruins of Ur in Chaldaea in 1854. Nabonnedus had his eldest son, Belshazzar, as co-regent, and therefore it might well be that while he met the Persians in the field his son ruled in the capital. Thus is explained how Daniel was made the third ruler in the kingdom. Dan 5:16, 1 Chr 2:29. Apocryphal Additions to Daniel. -These exist in the Greek version, and are: The Song of the Three Holy Children, the History of Susanna, and the Story of Bel and the Dragon. They passed into the Vulgate, and so into modern translations. They embody popular traditions, but never formed part of the Hebrew Bible. The Song of the Three Holy Children purports to be the triumphal song of the three confessors in the furnace, Dan 3:23, in praise of their miraculous deliverance. The chief part has been used as a hymn (Benedicite) in the Christian Church since the fourth century. The History of Susanna, who was cleared from a charge of adultery by the shrewdness of Daniel. Probably based upon a fact. The History of Bel and the Dragon, a strange exaggeration of the record of the divine deliverance of Daniel, ch. 1 Chr 24:6.

다니엘서는 뚜렷이 다른 두 부분으로 되어 있다. 역사 부분은 1-6장이니, 앞에서 든 흥미로운 기록과 함께, 느부갓네살이 두라 평지에 세운 금 신상에 절하지 않으므로 사드락과 메삭과 아벳느고를 불붙는 풀무에 던지려 한 일을 담았다. 묵시 부분은 7-12장이니 다니엘이 본 환상의 기록이다. 1장은 머리말이요, 2-6장은 세상 권세가 나아간 역사와 하나님이 다스리시는 원리를 다니엘의 삶에 있던 일로 두루 보이며, 7-12장은 하나님 백성의 앞날에 대한 예언이다. 이 책은 산문으로 쓰였으나 처음부터 끝까지 같은 말은 아니다. 머리말인 1:1부터 2:4 앞 구절까지는 히브리 말로 쓰였으나, 둘째 장 넷째 절 뒤 구절부터 7장 끝까지는 아람 말이니 그 절에서 수리아 말이라 한 것이다. 8장 처음부터 끝까지는 환상을 일인칭으로 전하며 히브리 말이다. 다니엘서를 푸는 데는 옛 역사에 대한 깊은 앎이 있어야 한다. 이 책은 참으로 역사의 종교 철학과 같다. 그 바탕 생각은 지나가는 세상 모든 나라가 영원히 이어질 그리스도의 나라를 위하여 하나님의 섭리로 다스려지고 조종된다는 것이다. 다니엘서가 구약에서 차지하는 자리를 요한계시록이 신약에서 차지한다. 하나님의 나라가 세상 제국과 맞닿아 다투는 것을 보며, 그리스도께서 두루 다스리심과 죽은 자의 부활과 마지막 심판을 내다본다. 세상 제국이 먼저 느부갓네살의 꿈에 나타나니(다니엘 2장), 머리는 금이요 가슴과 팔은 은이요 배는 놋이요 다리와 발은 쇠와 진흙인 거대한 신상의 모습이다. 이것이 흔히 받는 정통의 풀이로는 저마다 바벨론과 메대 바사와 마게도냐 헬라와 로마 제국을 나타낸다. 마침내 사람의 손으로 하지 아니하고 산에서 뜬 돌이 그것을 무너뜨리고 큰 산이 되니 메시야의 다스림을 나타낸다. 하나님이 몸소 지으신 무너지지 않는 반석이 사람의 손으로 만든 쇠붙이 거상을 부순다. 같은 나라들의 이음이 일곱째 장에도 나오니, 선지자 자신이 본 네 짐승의 환상 꼴이다. 넷째 짐승에 뿔 열이 있어 열 나라를 가리키며, 헬라 제국의 부러진 네 뿔 사이에서 작은 뿔이 솟는다(다니엘 7:8,24). 푸는 이들이 첫째 제국은 바벨론이라는 데 뜻을 같이하나 나머지 셋에 대하여는 갈린다. 어떤 이는 메대와 바사를 한 제국으로 묶고, 어떤 이는 갈라서 헬라 곧 알렉산더 대왕과 그 뒤를 이은 이들을 넷째 제국으로 보며 「작은 뿔」을 안티오코스 에피파네스로 돌린다. 또 어떤 이는 다니엘의 예언을 그리스도 앞뒤 온 세상 제국에 두루 미치는 것으로 보아, 그리스도의 마지막이요 영원한 다스림에 이르는 길을 예비하는 것이라 한다. 이 책에서 가장 중한 그리스도에 대한 이 예언이 우리 눈앞에서 끊임없이 이루어지고 있으니 어떤 부정하는 비평으로도 물리칠 수 없다. 다니엘서가 많이 공격받았으나 성경 학자들이 잘 지켜 냈다. 둘째 부분에서 다니엘이 거기 적힌 하나님의 계시를 받은 이로 일인칭으로 말하니, 여기서는 참이냐 속임이냐 둘 가운데 하나이다. 두 말이 쓰였다는 사실만으로도 뒤에 지어내거나 늦은 때에 쓰였을 가능성이 매우 낮으나, 히브리 말과 아람 말에 다 익숙하던 다니엘에게는 절로 그러하였다. 이 책은 바벨론의 삶과 왕실 예법에 익숙함을 드러내며, 바벨론 사로잡힘의 때와 바벨론 궁정에서 다니엘이 차지한 남다른 자리에 처음부터 끝까지 어울린다. 그 참됨이 가장 높은 권위, 곧 그리스도의 권위로 인정되었으니(마태복음 24:15) 믿는 이에게는 여기서 더 다툴 여지가 없다. 이 책에 대한 공격이 네 갈래로 있었다. 첫째는 남다른 일들이니 금 신상과 불붙는 풀무와 꿈과 사자 굴 따위요, 둘째는 그 자세한 예언이요, 셋째는 외래어인 헬라 말이요, 넷째는 그 기록이다. 이 반론에 이렇게 답하면 넉넉하다. 첫째, 바벨론의 남다름과 동방의 풍속과 관습이 그 말을 넉넉히 밝혀 주며 이 책이 참으로 동방의 것이요 바벨론의 것임을 밝힌다. 둘째, 다니엘의 남다른 자리가 그 계시에 남다르고 놀라운 성격을 요구하였으며, 그 예언이 큰 부분 이루어졌다. 셋째, 헬라 말은 넷뿐이요 악기 이름이니 이르게는 주전 600년에 헬라에서 들어왔을 수 있다. 넷째, 역사의 어려움이 있다. 벨사살이 바벨론의 마지막 왕으로 나오나 그때 알려진 사료는 나보니두스를 마지막 왕으로 주었다. 이 어려움은 1854년에 헨리 롤린슨 경이 갈대아 우르의 터에서 원기둥 하나를 풀어내어 풀렸다. 나보니두스가 맏아들 벨사살을 공동 섭정으로 세웠으니, 그가 들에서 바사 사람을 맞을 동안 그 아들이 서울을 다스렸을 만하다. 이로써 다니엘이 나라의 셋째 다스리는 자가 된 일이 설명된다(다니엘 5:16,29). 다니엘서에 덧붙은 외경이 헬라 역본에 있으니, 세 거룩한 아이의 노래와 수산나 이야기와 벨과 용 이야기이다. 이것들이 불가타에 들어갔고 그로써 오늘날의 역본에도 들어갔다. 백성 사이의 전승을 담았으나 히브리 성경의 한 부분이었던 적은 없다. 세 거룩한 아이의 노래는 풀무 속 세 고백자가 이적으로 건짐받은 것을 찬양한 이김의 노래라 한다(다니엘 3:23). 그 큰 부분이 4세기 이래 그리스도 교회에서 찬송 「베네디시테」로 쓰였다. 수산나 이야기는 다니엘의 슬기로 간음의 고발에서 벗어난 여인의 이야기이니 아마 사실에 바탕하였을 것이다. 벨과 용 이야기는 하나님이 다니엘을 건지신 기록을 이상하게 부풀린 것이다(다니엘 6장).
※ 원문 오류: 1 Chr 2:29 → 다니엘 5:29
※ 판정 근거: 이어받기 숫자 부풀리기. 원문에서 책과 장을 생략한 맨 숫자에 엉뚱한 주소가 붙은 것이다. 앞의 성한 인용을 좇으면 다니엘 5:29가 되며, 그 절은 「이에 벨사살이 명하여 그들이 다니엘에게 자주색 옷을 입히게 하며 금 사슬…」이다.
※ 원문 오류: 「Lev 10:2」 → 다니엘 2장
※ 판정 근거: 「ch.」의 맨 장 번호에 가짜 책이 붙었다. 다니엘 2장이 느부갓네살의 큰 신상 꿈이다.
※ 원문 오류: 「1 Chr 24:6」 → 다니엘 6장
※ 판정 근거: 다니엘 6장이 사자 굴에서 건짐 받은 기사이다.

variants.definition: DANIEL (God is my judge). 1. One of the four greater prophets. He was of noble, perhaps of royal, descent, and probably born at Jerusalem. Dan 1:3; Dan 9:24; comp. Josephus's Antiq. In his early youth he was carried captive by Nebuchadnezzar to Babylon, together with three other Hebrew youths of rank, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, b.c. 604. He was there instructed in the language and arts of the Chaldaeans, and, with his three companions, trained for the royal service in the palace. Dan 1:1-4. The prince of the eunuchs changed all their names, calling them respectively Belteshazzar (i.e. "prince of Bel"), Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. These four refused to eat of the king's meat and to drink his wine, but chose "pulse and water." Notwithstanding this diet, they were in better condition than the heathen courtiers. After three years' training, God gave Daniel an opportunity to display his learning and wisdom. He interpreted a dream which Nebuchadnezzar had forgotten. Dan 2. In reward, he was made "ruler over the whole province of Babylon, and chief of the governors over all the wise men of Babylon," and in this position so distinguished himself that he won great fame and was mentioned as a model man even by his contemporaries. Eze 14:14, Ruth 4:20; 1 Sam 28:3. On another occasion he faithfully explained to his monarch the intention of God to punish him for his pride. Dan 4. For Belshazzar, a grandson and successor of Nebuchadnezzar, he performed a similar service, reading the handwriting upon the wall, Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin. Dan 5. Under Darius the Mede, Daniel was made the first of the "three presidents " of the empire. His enemies obtained a command from Darius forbidding all prayer save unto the king for 30 days. But Daniel did not stop praying; and this fact being discovered, he was cast into the den of lions, which was the punishment for a violation of the king's order. But God delivered him, and he was kept in his office. In the reign of Cyrus he likewise prospered, but seems to have left Babylon, as his latest recorded vision, Dan 10:1,Ex 6:4, was by the Hiddekel, in the third year of Cyrus, b.c. 534. When he died, and where, are uncertain. His reputed tomb is shown at Susa, on the Tigris. Daniel at the court of Babylon resembles Joseph at the court of Pharaoh. Both were involuntary exiles from their country and people; both were great statesmen; both maintained the purity of their religion and their personal character, though surrounded by idolatry and corruption; both rose by their wisdom and integrity from slavery to the highest dignity in a heathen empire; both are shining examples of loyalty to God and to virtue. Daniel is the name of two. or perhaps three, other persons mentioned in the Bible. (a) The second son of David by Abigail the Carmelitess. 1 Chr 3:1. He is, however, called Chileab in 2 Sam 3:3. (b) A priest of the family of Ithamar, mentioned, Ezr 8:2, as having returned with Ezra. He is probably again spoken of in Neh 10:6 among those who sealed the covenant drawn up by Nehemiah, b.c. 445.
variants.definition_ko: 1) 네 대선지자 중 하나. 귀족, 어쩌면 왕족 출신으로 아마 예루살렘에서 태어났다(단 1:3). 어린 나이에 하나냐·미사엘·아사랴 등 다른 세 히브리 소년과 함께 느부갓네살에게 바벨론으로 사로잡혀 갔다(BC 604년). 그곳에서 갈대아의 언어와 학문을 배우며 궁중 봉사를 위해 훈련받았다(단 1:1-4). 환관장이 그들의 이름을 벨드사살, 사드락, 메삭, 아벳느고로 바꾸었다. 네 사람은 왕의 음식과 포도주를 거절하고 채소와 물을 택했으나 오히려 이방 신하들보다 더 좋아 보였다. 3년 훈련 후 느부갓네살이 잊어버린 꿈을 해석하여(단 2장) 바벨론 온 지방을 다스리는 자이자 모든 지혜자의 어른이 되었다.

variants.definition: DANIEL, BOOK OF. It consists of two distinct parts. Historical, chs. Dan 1-6, containing the interesting narrative given in the preceding section, and with it an account of the attempted burning of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego in a fiery furnace because they would not worship the golden image which Nebuchadnezzar set up on the plain of Dura. Apocalyptic, chs. Dan 1:7-12, or the record of Daniel's visions. Ch.Dan 1:1 contains the introduction,- chs. Dan 1:2-6 present a general view of the progressive history of the powers of the world, and of the principles of the divine government, as seen in events in the life of Daniel; and chs. Dan 1:7-12, the prophecy of the future of the people of God. The book is written in prose, but not in the same language throughout. The introduction, chs. Dan 1:1-2:4, first clause, is written in Hebrew, but from the second clause of the fourth verse of the second chapter to the end of ch. 7 it is in Aramaic, called Syriac in that verse. From the beginning of ch. 8 to the end, in which part the visions are related in the first person, the language is Hebrew. The interpretation of Daniel requires profound knowledge of ancient history. The book is, in fact, a sort of religious philosophy of history. Its fundamental idea is that all the kingdoms of the world, which pass away, are ruled and overruled by divine Providence for the kingdom of Christ, which will last for ever. The book of Daniel occupies in the O.T. the same position which the Revelation of John occupies in the New. It views the kingdom of God in its contact and conflicts with the empires of the world, and looks forward to the universal reign of Christ, the resurrection of the dead, and the final judgment. The empires of the world appear first in Nebuchadnezzar's dream, ch. Lev 10:2, under the figure of a colossal image with a head of gold, a breast and arms of silver, a belly of brass, and legs and feet of iron and clay. These represent respectively (according to the usual orthodox interpretation) the Babylonian, the Medo-Persian, the Macedo-Greek, and the Roman empires; they are overthrown at last by a stone cut out of the mountain without hands and becoming a great mountain, which represents the reign of the Messiah. The indestructible rock of God's own workmanship breaks to pieces the metal colossus of man's hand. The same succession of monarchies is presented in the seventh chapter, under the form of a vision of four beasts seen by the prophet himself. The fourth beast has ten horns, denoting ten kingdoms, growing out of it, and a little horn (Song of Solomon 7:8, Jud 6:24) springing up among the four fractured horns of the Greek empire. Interpreters agree as to the first empire, which must be Babylonia, but differ as to the other three. Some combine the Medes and Persians in one empire; others divide them, and regard the Greeks (Alexander the Great and his successors) as representing the fourth empire, and refer the "little horn" to Antiochus Epiphanes. Still others give the prophecy of Daniel a more comprehensive sweep over all the world-empires before and after Christ, as preparing the way for the ultimate and everlasting reign of Christ. This prophecy of Christ, the most important in the book, is constantly fulfilling before our eyes, and cannot be set aside by any negative criticism. The book of Daniel has been much attacked, but also successfully vindicated by biblical scholars. In the second part Daniel speaks in the first person as the receiver of the divine revelations recorded therein, so that the only alternative here is between truth and fraud. The very fact that two languages are used renders it extremely unlikely that it should have been forged or written in any later period, but to Daniel, familiar as he was with both Hebrew and Aramaic, it was natural. The book displays familiar acquaintance with Babylonian life and royal manners, and suits throughout the period of the Babylonian exile and the peculiar position of Daniel at the Babylonian court. The genuineness is sanctioned by the highest authority -that of Christ, Matt 24:15, from which there is no appeal for believers. The attacks upon the book have been in three lines: (1) Its extraordinary events -the golden image, the burning fiery furnace, the dreams, the lions' den, etc.; (2) its minute prophecies; (3) its foreign (Greek) words; (4) its narrative. To these objections it is sufficient to reply:(1) The characteristics of Babylon, the manners and customs of the East, amply justify the language and prove that the book is genuinely Oriental and Babylonian. (2) The peculiar position of Daniel required an exceptional and startling character for his revelations; his prophecies have been in great part fulfilled. (3) The Greek words are only four in number, and are the names of musical instruments which may have been imported from Greece as early as b.c. 600. (4) Its historical difficulties. Belshazzar is represented as the last king of Babylon, while the authority there known gave Nabonnedus as the last king. This difficulty was solved by Sir Henry Rawlinson's decipherment of a cylinder among the ruins of Ur in Chaldaea in 1854. Nabonnedus had his eldest son, Belshazzar, as co-regent, and therefore it might well be that while he met the Persians in the field his son ruled in the capital. Thus is explained how Daniel was made the third ruler in the kingdom. Dan 5:16, 1 Chr 2:29. Apocryphal Additions to Daniel. -These exist in the Greek version, and are: The Song of the Three Holy Children, the History of Susanna, and the Story of Bel and the Dragon. They passed into the Vulgate, and so into modern translations. They embody popular traditions, but never formed part of the Hebrew Bible. The Song of the Three Holy Children purports to be the triumphal song of the three confessors in the furnace, Dan 3:23, in praise of their miraculous deliverance. The chief part has been used as a hymn (Benedicite) in the Christian Church since the fourth century. The History of Susanna, who was cleared from a charge of adultery by the shrewdness of Daniel. Probably based upon a fact. The History of Bel and the Dragon, a strange exaggeration of the record of the divine deliverance of Daniel, ch. 1 Chr 24:6.

From the beginning of ch. 8 to the end, in which part the visions are related in the first person, the language is Hebrew. The interpretation of Daniel requires profound knowledge of ancient history. The book is, in fact, a sort of religious philosophy of history. Its fundamental idea is that all the kingdoms of the world, which pass away, are ruled and overruled by divine Providence for the kingdom of Christ, which will last for ever. The book of Daniel occupies in the O.T. the same position which the Revelation of John occupies in the New. It views the kingdom of God in its contact and conflicts with the empires of the world, and looks forward to the universal reign of Christ, the resurrection of the dead, and the final judgment. The empires of the world appear first in Nebuchadnezzar's dream, ch. Lev 10:2, under the figure of a colossal image with a head of gold, a breast and arms of silver, a belly of brass, and legs and feet of iron and clay. These represent respectively (according to the usual orthodox interpretation) the Babylonian, the Medo-Persian, the Macedo-Greek, and the Roman empires; they are overthrown at last by a stone cut out of the mountain without hands and becoming a great mountain, which represents the reign of the Messiah. The indestructible rock of God's own workmanship breaks to pieces the metal colossus of man's hand. The same succession of monarchies is presented in the seventh chapter, under the form of a vision of four beasts seen by the prophet himself. The fourth beast has ten horns, denoting ten kingdoms, growing out of it, and a little horn (Song of Solomon 7:8, Jud 6:24) springing up among the four fractured horns of the Greek empire. Interpreters agree as to the first empire, which must be Babylonia, but differ as to the other three. Some combine the Medes and Persians in one empire; others divide them, and regard the Greeks (Alexander the Great and his successors) as representing the fourth empire, and refer the "little horn" to Antiochus Epiphanes. Still others give the prophecy of Daniel a more comprehensive sweep over all the world-empires before and after Christ, as preparing the way for the ultimate and everlasting reign of Christ. This prophecy of Christ, the most important in the book, is constantly fulfilling before our eyes, and cannot be set aside by any negative criticism. The book of Daniel has been much attacked, but also successfully vindicated by biblical scholars. In the second part Daniel speaks in the first person as the receiver of the divine revelations recorded therein, so that the only alternative here is between truth and fraud. The very fact that two languages are used renders it extremely unlikely that it should have been forged or written in any later period, but to Daniel, familiar as he was with both Hebrew and Aramaic, it was natural. The book displays familiar acquaintance with Babylonian life and royal manners, and suits throughout the period of the Babylonian exile and the peculiar position of Daniel at the Babylonian court. The genuineness is sanctioned by the highest authority -that of Christ, Matt 24:15, from which there is no appeal for believers. The attacks upon the book have been in three lines: (1) Its extraordinary events -the golden image, the burning fiery furnace, the dreams, the lions' den, etc.; (2) its minute prophecies; (3) its foreign (Greek) words; (4) its narrative. To these objections it is sufficient to reply:(1) The characteristics of Babylon, the manners and customs of the East, amply justify the language and prove that the book is genuinely Oriental and Babylonian. (2) The peculiar position of Daniel required an exceptional and startling character for his revelations; his prophecies have been in great part fulfilled. (3) The Greek words are only four in number, and are the names of musical instruments which may have been imported from Greece as early as b.c. 600. (4) Its historical difficulties. Belshazzar is represented as the last king of Babylon, while the authority there known gave Nabonnedus as the last king. This difficulty was solved by Sir Henry Rawlinson's decipherment of a cylinder among the ruins of Ur in Chaldaea in 1854. Nabonnedus had his eldest son, Belshazzar, as co-regent, and therefore it might well be that while he met the Persians in the field his son ruled in the capital. Thus is explained how Daniel was made the third ruler in the kingdom. Dan 5:16, 1 Chr 2:29. Apocryphal Additions to Daniel. -These exist in the Greek version, and are: The Song of the Three Holy Children, the History of Susanna, and the Story of Bel and the Dragon. They passed into the Vulgate, and so into modern translations. They embody popular traditions, but never formed part of the Hebrew Bible. The Song of the Three Holy Children purports to be the triumphal song of the three confessors in the furnace, Dan 3:23, in praise of their miraculous deliverance. The chief part has been used as a hymn (Benedicite) in the Christian Church since the fourth century. The History of Susanna, who was cleared from a charge of adultery by the shrewdness of Daniel. Probably based upon a fact. The History of Bel and the Dragon, a strange exaggeration of the record of the divine deliverance of Daniel, ch. 1 Chr 24:6.
variants.definition_ko: 두 부분으로 이루어진다. (1) 역사 부분(1~6장)으로, 앞서 말한 이야기와 함께 사드락·메삭·아벳느고가 느부갓네살이 두라 평지에 세운 금 신상에 절하지 않아 풀무불에 던져진 사건이 실려 있다. (2) 묵시 부분(7~12장)으로 다니엘이 본 환상의 기록이다. 산문으로 쓰였으나 전체가 한 언어는 아니다. 1:1~2:4 전반부는 히브리어, 2:4 후반부터 7장 끝까지는 아람어, 8장부터 끝까지는 다시 히브리어다. 다니엘서의 해석에는 고대사에 대한 깊은 지식이 필요하다.

entries.definition: DAN-JA'AN. 2 Sam 24:6. Probably Danian, a ruin north of Achzib.
entries.definition_ko: 사무엘하 24:6의 지명으로, 악십 북쪽의 폐허 다니안으로 추정된다.

entries.definition: DAN'NAH, a city in the mountains of Judah. Josh 15:49. Conder identifies it with modern Jahud, about 8 miles north-west of Hebron.
entries.definition_ko: 유다 산지의 한 성읍(여호수아 15:49).

entries.definition: DA'RA, contr. form of DAR'DA (pearl of wisdom), one whom Solomon outrivalled in wisdom. 1 Kgs 4:31; 1 Chr 2:6.
entries.definition_ko: 다르다의 축약형으로, 솔로몬이 지혜로 능가한 사람 중 하나다(열왕기상 4:31, 역대상 2:6).

entries.definition: DAR'IC, the name of a Persian gold coin, which is translated "dram" in 1 Chr 29:7; Ezr 2:69; Ezr 8:27; Neh 7:70-72. The name comes from the Persian word dara, "a king." like the English sovereign. It was the common gold-piece of the Persian empire. It was current in Palestine under Cyrus, and Artaxerxes Longimanus. It weighed about 128 grains Troy, and was worth about five dollars. Besides the gold there was a silver daric, worth about fifty cents. There is no mention of this latter coin in the Bible. See Measures.
entries.definition_ko: 바사 금화의 이름으로, 흠정역에서 '다릭'으로 옮겼다(역대상 29:7, 에스라 2:69, 8:27, 느헤미야 7:70-72). 이름은 '왕'을 뜻하는 바사어 '다라'에서 왔다. 바사 제국의 표준 금화로 고레스와 아닥사스다 시대에 팔레스타인에서 통용되었다. 무게는 약 128그레인, 가치는 약 5달러였다. 금화 외에 약 50센트짜리 은 다릭도 있었으나 성경에는 언급되지 않는다.

entries.definition: DARI'US (restrainer), the name of several kings of Media and Persia mentioned in the Bible. 1. Darius the Median, Dan 5:31, was the son of Ahasuerus; he took Babylon from Belshazzar the Chaldaean, being at that time about 62 years old. The best identification is that which makes him Astyages, the last king of the Medes. "Only one year of the reign of Darius is mentioned, Dan 9:1; Dan 11:1; and if, as seems probable, Darius (Astyages) occupied the throne of Babylon as supreme sovereign, with Nerigalsarasser as vassal-prince, after the murder of Evil-merodaeh (Belshazzar), b.c. 559, one year only remains for this Median supremacy before its overthrow by Cyrus, b.c. 558, in exact accordance with the notices in Daniel." Under him Daniel was advanced to the highest dignity, which exposed him to the malice of enemies and led to his being cast into the den of lions, but by a miracle he escaped injury. See Daniel. Darius, the son of Hystaspes, the founder of the Perso-Aryan dynasty, and ruler, b.c. 521-486. Ezr 4:5, Jud 6:24; Hag 1:1, 2 Sam 20:15; Zech 1:1, 1 Kgs 15:7; Zech 7:1. He found in the palace at Achmetha or Ecbatana, the capital of Cyrus, a decree of that king concerning the temple in Jerusalem. This he confirmed, and the temple was finished in 4 years, b.c. 516. Ezr 6:15. It may, however, have been used before it was entirely completed, as is inferred from Zech 7:2-3. Darius the Persian, mentioned in Neh 12:22, is generally identified with Darius Codomannus, the antagonist of Alexander the Great, who ascended the throne b.c. 336, and reigned until b.c. 330. He was the last Persian monarch, and was killed by his own generals. Alexander defeated him, and thus the prophecy of Daniel, ch. Dan 8, was fulfilled.
entries.definition_ko:
성경에 언급되는 메대와 바사의 여러 왕의 이름. (1) 메대 사람 다리오(다니엘 5:31)는 아하수에로의 아들로, 62세경에 갈대아 사람 벨사살에게서 바벨론을 빼앗았다. 메대의 마지막 왕 아스티아게스와 동일 인물로 보는 것이 가장 유력하다. 그의 치하에서 다니엘이 최고 지위에 올라 원수들의 시기를 사 사자 굴에 던져졌으나 기적으로 상하지 않았다. (2) 히스타스페스의 아들 다리오로 바사-아리아 왕조의 창건자이며 BC 521~486년에 다스렸다(에스라 4:5, 학개 1:1, 스가랴 1:1). 고레스의 수도 악메다에서 성전에 관한 그 왕의 조서를 찾아냈다.
※ 원문 오류: 2 Sam 20:15 → 학개 1:15
※ 판정 근거: 이어받기 숫자 부풀리기. 원문에서 책과 장을 생략한 맨 숫자에 엉뚱한 주소가 붙은 것이다. 앞의 성한 인용을 좇으면 학개 1:15가 되며, 그 절은 「그 때는 다리오 왕 제이년 여섯째 달 이십사일이었더라…」이다.

entries.definition: DARK'NESS. The darkness which constituted one of the plagues of Egypt might "be felt." Ex 10:21. This may have been occasioned by a thick, heavy vapor, or other sensible change in the atmosphere, which caused an entire interception of the sun's rays. It was evidently miraculous, and the dread and terror it inspired are vividly described. Ex 10:22-23. So of the darkness that shrouded the earth when our Saviour was put to death, Luke 23:44-45; it was manifestly miraculous, as no natural eclipse of the sun could take place at that period of the moon. "Darkness" is used in a metaphorical sense for ignorance or sin, John 1:5; Rom 13:12; Eph 5:11; for misery, Isa 5:30; Isa 59:9-10; for the final doom, Matt 8:12, God is said to dwell in the thick darkness. Ex 20:21; 1 Kgs 8:12.
entries.definition_ko: 애굽의 재앙 중 하나였던 흑암은 '더듬을 만한' 것이었다(출애굽기 10:21). 짙고 무거운 안개나 대기의 뚜렷한 변화로 햇빛이 완전히 차단된 것일 수 있다. 분명 기적이었으며 그것이 불러일으킨 두려움이 생생히 묘사되어 있다(출애굽기 10:22-23). 구주께서 죽으실 때 땅을 덮은 어둠도 마찬가지로 기적이었으니(누가복음 23:44-45), 그 달의 위상에서는 자연적인 일식이 일어날 수 없었기 때문이다. '어둠'은 무지나 죄(요한복음 1:5, 로마서 13:12, 에베소서 5:11), 비참함(이사야 5:30:9-10), 마지막 심판(마태복음 8:12)을 뜻하는 비유로도 쓰인다. 하나님은 캄캄한 데 계신다고 말해진다(출애굽기 20:21, 열왕기상 8:12).

entries.definition: DAR'KON (scatterer), one whose posterity returned from Babylon. Ezr 2:56; Neh 7:58.
entries.definition_ko: 바벨론에서 그 후손이 돌아온 사람(에스라 2:56, 느헤미야 7:58).

entries.definition: DARL'ING. The word occurs in Ps 22:20 and Ps 35:17 as the translation of a Hebrew word which correctly means "my only one," as it is applied to "something which exists singly and cannot be replaced if lost, as an only son. Gen 22:2, or daughter." Jud 11:34.
entries.definition_ko: 시편 22:20과 35:17에 나오는 히브리어를 옮긴 말로, 정확히는 '내 유일한 것'을 뜻한다. 외아들(창세기 22:2)이나 외딸(사사기 11:34)처럼 하나뿐이라 잃으면 대신할 수 없는 것에 쓰인다.

entries.definition: DA'THAN (belonging to a fountain), a Reubenite chieftain who joined in Korah's rebellion. Num 16; Num 26:9; Deut 11:6; Ps 106:17.
entries.definition_ko: 고라의 반역에 가담한 르우벤 지파의 지도자(민 16장, 26:9, 신명기 11:6, 시편 106:17).

entries.definition: DAUGH'TER is used in the Bible in several other senses than the literal one. It describes a female descendant. Gen 27:46, the women of a city or country. Gen 36:2, or women in general, Prov 31:29; the female worshippers of an idol, Mal 2:11; cities and their dependent towns. In Eccl 12:4 "daughters of music" are singing-women.
entries.definition_ko: 성경에서 문자적 의미 외에 여러 뜻으로 쓰인다. 여자 후손(창세기 27:46), 어떤 성읍이나 나라의 여인들(창세기 36:2), 여자 일반(잠언 31:29), 우상을 섬기는 여자들(말라기 2:11), 성읍과 그에 딸린 마을들을 가리킨다. 전도서 12:4의 '노래하는 딸들'은 노래하는 여인들이다.

entries.definition: DA'VID (beloved), the youngest of the eight sons of Jesse, of the tribe of Judah, was born in Bethlehem, b.c. 1085, and was both in his prophetical and regal character an eminent type of the Messiah. 1 Sam 16:13. While he was employed as a shepherd in his father's fields God sent Samuel to Bethlehem, on the occasion of the annual sacrificial feast, with instructions to anoint David as king of Israel in the place of Saul, who had incurred the divine displeasure, and was therefore to be deposed. Dean Stanley thus describes David's appearance and physique as he stood before Samuel: "He was short of stature, had red hair and bright eyes. He was remarkable for the grace of his figure and countenance, well made, and of immense strength and agility. In swiftness and activity he could only be compared to a wild gazelle, with feet like harts' feet, with arms strong enough to break a bow of steel. Ps 18:33-34, "-History of the Jewish Church, 2d series, Lect. 22. Probably neither David nor any one else understood the real meaning of this anointing. At all events, David went back to the shepherd-life. We next hear of him as chosen by Saul, upon the suggestion of one of the bodyguard, to play upon a harp, and thus soothe the troubled spirit of the king. In this he was eminently successful. Saul made him one of his armor-bearers, and requested permission of Jesse to allow him to remain at his court. 1 Sam 16:21-23. But it seems that David after a time returned home. It was then perhaps that his adventure with the lion and the bear took place. After an interval of uncertain length -Josephus says "after a few years"-David had his famous fight with Goliath. But he had so altered that Saul did not recognize in the grown man flushed by triumph the lad who had played the harp in his hours of mental distress; hence his question of Abner -"Whose son is this youth?"-was natural. 1 Sam 17:55. The superiority in military glory which the women gave David excited the jealousy of the king, and so, although David was made a chieftain, lived at court, and enjoyed the friendship of the king's son, yet he was constantly exposed to the wrath of Saul. Agreeably to the terms of the king's promise to him who slew the giant, David became the king's son-in-law, marrying Michal, whom he loved, but only on condition that he slew a hundred Philistines-an exaction made in hope that the attempt would end fatally. But David and his men slew two hundred. David found his position full of danger. His very presence seemed to arouse the envy of Saul, so that the latter determined to kill him, and several times cast his javelin at him as he stood playing before him. By a stratagem Michal saved David's life and enabled him to flee to Samuel at Ramah. 1 Sam 19:13, 1 Sam 30:18. David then became convinced that a further residence at court was impossible, and accordingly an affecting parting with Jonathan took place, 1 Sam 20, and David became a fugitive from the hand of Saul. Armed with the sword of Goliath and anointed with the sacred oil, the future king sought a home among the Philistines. But his fame had preceded him, and his assumed madness scarcely saved him. 1 Sam 21. Therefore he went to the cave of Adullam and gathered gradually a motley crowd, composed of insolvent debtors and malcontents. 1 Sam 22:1-2. But David proved his fitness to rule a kingdom by controlling these men and bringing them to accede to his wishes. The history of David's life for the next few years is filled with the details of alternate defeats and victories, of his flight, of his magnanimous refusal to lay hands on the Lord's anointed, 1 Sam 24:16, of his residence among neighboring tribes, of the episode of Abigail, 1 Sam 25, and finally of the battle of Gilboa, in which Jonathan fell and Saul slew himself, unable to bear defeat. 1 Sam 31. The lament which he then composed is one of the noblest odes of friendship, and a monument of his generosity to a fallen foe and of devotion to a fallen friend. 2 Sam 1:19-27. Then David, by divine direction, removed to Hebron, where the chief men of Judah met him and offered him the government of their tribe, which he accepted. Accordingly, he was anointed for the second time. 2 Sam 2:4. In Hebron, as king of Judah, he reigned seven years and a half. During this time Ishbosheth, the son of Saul, by means of the skilful general Abner, maintained a decreasing semblance of authority over Israel. But at length he and Abner were killed, and thus the way prepared for the execution of God's plan to set David on the throne of united Israel. David was solemnly anointed for the third time. 2 Sam 5:3. Soon after he assumed the government he obtained possession of Jerusalem, reduced the fortress which the Jebusites had maintained, and established the seat of his government there. Under his wise and liberal policy the place was greatly enlarged; magnificent edifices rose up on every side, fortifications were erected, and the ark, which had been before without a fixed abode, was brought into the new city with religious ceremonies peculiarly joyful and solemn. 2 Sam 6:12-19. Thenceforward, Jerusalem became the capital of the kingdom, the residence of the royal family, and, more than all, the city of God. Ps 48:2; Matt 6:35. To it the tribes repaired from every quarter of the land to celebrate their annual festivals, and its growth in population, wealth, and splendor was very rapid. David now formed the design of building a magnificent temple for the worship of Jehovah, to take the place of the tabernacle, which was but a temporary and movable structure. He was informed, however, by God's direction, that this service would be reserved for his son Solomon. 2 Sam 7. After several contests with the nations that bordered on Israel, in which David was uniformly victorious, there broke out a war with the Ammonites (see Ammonites), during the progress of which David fell into those most aggravated sins of murder and adultery which brought disgrace and distress on his family and government and involved him in trouble during the remnant of his days. 2 Sam 12:9. His domestic peace was destroyed by the outrage committed upon Tamar by Amnon, revenged, "after two full years," by Absalom, who slew Amnon at a feast. 2 Sam 13:14, 1 Chr 2:29. This murder occasioned Absalom's flight to his father-in-law's court at Geshur. Being recalled, he started a rebellion which compelled the king to flee from his capital and exile himself to avoid being cut off by a parricidal hand. 2 Sam 15-18. The Tomb of David. (After a Photograph by Good.) death of Absalom, though it brought relief to the kingdom, inflicted a deep wound on the father's heart. The insurrection under Sheba and the murder of Amasa by Joab followed in quick succession. And to close the melancholy catalogue was the terrible judgment which he brought upon himself and the nation by numbering the people for some purpose which was sinful in the sight of God, though not explained to us. 2 Sam 24. David was now 70 years old, and had reigned seven and a half years over the tribe of Judah and thirty three over the whole kingdom of Israel. Just before his death his son Adonijah made a bold attempt to usurp the throne,- and to secure the kingdom against any pretender, David resigned the crown to Solomon, put into his hands the plan and model of the temple and the treasure accumulated for it, summoned the influential men of the nation, and delivered his farewell address. He died b.c. 1015, and was buried in the "city of David." 1 Kgs 2:10. His tomb became the sepulchre of subsequent kings, and one of the sacred places of the kingdom. It is pointed out on Mount Zion, at Jerusalem, outside the city wall. See cut, above. David was a type of Christ. They both inherited their kingdoms after suffering. And David, as the ruler over temporal Israel, was a forerunner of the Son of David, who was to reign over the spiritual Israel for ever. Matt 1:1; Matt 9:27; Matt 12:23, etc. When David is spoken of as a man after God's "own heart," 1 Sam 13:14; Acts 13:22, reference is obviously intended to his general character and conduct, and not to every particular instance of it. As he was human, he was imperfect; and when he sinned, God punished him, and that with great severity. But he was remarkable for his devotion to God's service, and he kept himself from idols. He established the government of Israel, and extended its dominions to the full extent of the promise to Abraham, and left a compact and united empire, stretching from Egypt to Lebanon, and from the Euphrates to the Mediterranean. The life and character of David shine in his poetry- the life of action, adventure, war; the character of manly strength and womanly tenderness. Thus his Psalms supply biographical material. By means of them his heart is read. The man who could kill a giant is found to have a delicate appreciation of friendship. He whose passion led him into sin, whose hate into words of cursing, was able to mourn with deepest humility and bless with heartiest assent. It is to the Psalms of David, albeit he did not write the entire collection, that the Church of God has appealed for comfort in adversity and sanctification in prosperity. In regard to them Canon Perowne truthfully and eloquently says: "The very excellence of these Psalms is their universality. They spring from the deep fountains of the human heart, and God, in his providence and by his Spirit, has so ordered it that they should be for his Church an everlasting heritage. Hence they express the sorrows, the joys, the aspirations, the struggles, the victories, not of one man, but of all. And if we ask. How comes this to pass? the answer is not far to seek. One object is ever before the eyes and the heart of the Psalmist. All enemies, all distresses, all persecutions, all sins, are seen in the light of God. It is to him that the cry goes up; it is to him that the heart is laid bare; it is to him that the thanksgiving is uttered. This it is which makes them so true, so precious, so universal. No surer proof of their inspiration can be given than this-that they are not of an age, but for all time; that the ripest Christian can use them in the fulness of his Christian manhood, though the words are the words of one who lived centuries before the coming of Christ in the flesh."-The Psalms, 3d ed., vol. i. p. 21. Genealogical Table. David, City of, applied to Zion, 2 Sam 5:7; to Jerusalem, 1 Kgs 2:10; Dan 3:1; to Bethlehem, Luke 2:4, Rev 1:11.
entries.definition_ko:
다윗은 「사랑받는 이」를 뜻하며 유다 지파 이새의 여덟 아들 가운데 막내이다. 주전 1085년에 베들레헴에서 났고 선지자로나 왕으로나 메시야의 뛰어난 예표였다(사무엘상 16:13). 아버지의 들에서 양을 칠 때에 하나님이 사무엘을 베들레헴으로 보내시어 해마다의 제사 잔치 자리에서, 하나님의 노를 사서 폐하여질 사울을 대신하여 다윗에게 이스라엘의 왕으로 기름 부으라 하셨다. 스탠리 학장이 다윗이 사무엘 앞에 섰을 때의 모습과 몸을 이렇게 그린다. 「키가 작고 머리털이 붉으며 눈이 빛났다. 몸매와 얼굴의 아름다움이 남달랐고 몸이 잘 짜였으며 힘과 날램이 대단하였다. 빠름과 민첩함으로는 들노루에나 견줄 만하였으니 발이 암사슴 발 같고 팔은 놋 활을 꺾을 만큼 힘셌다」 하였다(시편 18:33-34). 아마 다윗도 다른 누구도 이 기름 부음의 참뜻을 알지 못하였을 것이다. 어쨌든 다윗이 다시 양 치는 삶으로 돌아갔다. 다음으로 그가 호위병 하나의 말을 좇아 사울에게 뽑혀 수금을 타서 왕의 어지러운 마음을 달래는 것을 듣는다. 이 일을 매우 잘하였다. 사울이 그를 무기 든 자로 삼고 이새에게 그를 궁정에 두게 해 달라 청하였다(사무엘상 16:21-23). 그러나 다윗이 얼마 뒤에 집으로 돌아간 듯하다. 아마 그때에 사자와 곰을 만난 일이 있었을 것이다. 얼마인지 모를 동안이 지난 뒤에, 요세푸스는 「몇 해 뒤」라 하는데, 다윗이 골리앗과 이름난 싸움을 하였다. 그러나 그가 하도 달라져 사울이 이김에 붉어진 그 다 자란 사람에게서 마음이 괴로울 때에 수금을 타던 아이를 알아보지 못하였다. 그러므로 그가 아브넬에게 「이 소년이 누구의 아들이냐」 물은 것이 자연스럽다(사무엘상 17:55). 여인들이 다윗에게 돌린 더 높은 군사의 영예가 왕의 시기를 일으켰다. 그리하여 다윗이 우두머리가 되고 궁정에 살며 왕의 아들의 우정을 누렸으나 늘 사울의 노함에 드러나 있었다. 거인을 죽인 자에게 한 왕의 약속대로 다윗이 왕의 사위가 되어 사랑하던 미갈과 혼인하였으나, 블레셋 사람 백을 죽인다는 조건이었으니 그 일이 죽음으로 끝나기를 바라고 매긴 것이었다. 그러나 다윗과 그 사람들이 이백을 죽였다. 다윗이 제 자리가 위태로움을 알았다. 그가 있는 것만으로 사울의 시기를 돋우는 듯하여 사울이 그를 죽이기로 마음먹고 그가 앞에서 수금을 탈 때에 몇 번이나 창을 던졌다. 미갈이 꾀로 다윗의 목숨을 구하여 라마의 사무엘에게 달아나게 하였다(사무엘상 19:13,18). 다윗이 궁정에 더 머물 수 없음을 알았고, 그리하여 요나단과 애틋한 작별이 있었으며(사무엘상 20장) 다윗이 사울의 손에서 도망하는 자가 되었다. 골리앗의 칼로 무장하고 거룩한 기름으로 부음받은 이 앞날의 왕이 블레셋 사람 사이에서 거처를 구하였다. 그러나 그 이름이 앞서 알려져 있어 미친 체함으로 겨우 목숨을 건졌다(사무엘상 21장). 그러므로 아둘람 굴로 가서 빚진 자와 원통한 자로 이루어진 잡다한 무리를 차츰 모았다(사무엘상 22:1-2). 그러나 다윗이 이 사람들을 다스려 제 뜻을 따르게 함으로 나라를 다스릴 자질을 드러냈다. 다음 몇 해 다윗의 삶은 지고 이김이 갈마드는 이야기와, 그 도망과, 여호와의 기름 부음 받은 자에게 손대기를 너그러이 마다한 일과(사무엘상 24:16), 이웃 지파 사이에 머문 일과, 아비가일의 일과(사무엘상 25장), 마침내 요나단이 쓰러지고 사울이 패함을 견디지 못하여 스스로 죽은 길보아 싸움으로 채워진다(사무엘상 31장). 그가 그때 지은 애가는 우정을 노래한 가장 고귀한 시의 하나요, 쓰러진 원수에게 보인 너그러움과 쓰러진 벗에게 보인 헌신의 기념비이다(사무엘하 1:19-27). 그런 다음 다윗이 하나님의 지시로 헤브론으로 옮겼고, 거기서 유다의 우두머리들이 그를 맞아 제 지파의 다스림을 내주매 그가 받았다. 그리하여 두 번째로 기름 부음을 받았다(사무엘하 2:4). 헤브론에서 유다의 왕으로 일곱 해 반을 다스렸다. 이 동안 사울의 아들 이스보셋이 솜씨 있는 장군 아브넬을 빌려 이스라엘에 대한 권위를 차츰 줄어드는 모양으로 지켰다. 그러나 마침내 그와 아브넬이 죽임당하여 다윗을 하나 된 이스라엘의 보좌에 앉히시려는 하나님의 계획이 이루어질 길이 열렸다. 다윗이 세 번째로 엄숙히 기름 부음을 받았다(사무엘하 5:3). 다스리기 시작한 뒤 곧 그가 예루살렘을 차지하여 여부스 족속이 지키던 요새를 무너뜨리고 거기에 다스림의 자리를 세웠다. 그의 슬기롭고 너그러운 정책 아래 그곳이 크게 넓어졌으니 사방에 훌륭한 건물이 일어나고 방비가 세워졌으며, 전에 정한 거처가 없던 궤가 남달리 기쁘고 엄숙한 예식과 함께 새 성읍으로 들어왔다(사무엘하 6:12-19). 그때부터 예루살렘이 나라의 서울이요 왕가의 거처가 되었고, 무엇보다 하나님의 성읍이 되었다(시편 48:2; 마태복음 5:35). 온 땅 사방에서 지파들이 해마다의 절기를 지키러 그리로 올라왔고 그 인구와 재물과 빛남이 매우 빠르게 자랐다. 다윗이 이제 임시로 옮겨 다니는 성막을 대신할 여호와의 예배를 위한 훌륭한 성전을 지으려 하였다. 그러나 하나님의 지시로 이 섬김이 그 아들 솔로몬에게 남겨질 것이라는 말을 들었다(사무엘하 7장). 이스라엘에 잇닿은 나라들과 여러 번 싸워 다윗이 한결같이 이긴 뒤에 암몬 자손과 전쟁이 터졌으니, 그 동안에 다윗이 살인과 간음이라는 가장 무거운 죄에 빠져 제 집안과 나라에 부끄러움과 괴로움을 가져오고 남은 날 동안 어려움에 얽혔다(사무엘하 12:9). 암논이 다말에게 저지른 몹쓸 일로 집안의 평화가 무너졌으니, 압살롬이 「만 이 년 후에」 잔치에서 암논을 죽여 앙갚음하였다(사무엘하 13:14,29). 이 살인으로 압살롬이 그술의 장인의 궁으로 달아났다. 다시 불려 온 뒤에 그가 반역을 일으켜 왕이 제 서울에서 달아나 아들의 손에 죽지 않으려고 스스로 물러가게 하였다(사무엘하 15-18장). 압살롬의 죽음이 나라에 안도를 주었으나 아버지의 마음에는 깊은 상처를 남겼다. 세바의 반란과 요압이 아마사를 죽인 일이 빠르게 잇달았다. 이 슬픈 목록을 맺는 것은, 우리에게 밝혀지지 않았으나 하나님 보시기에 죄였던 어떤 목적으로 백성을 셈으로 자기와 나라에 불러들인 무서운 심판이었다(사무엘하 24장). 다윗이 이제 일흔이었고 유다 지파를 일곱 해 반, 온 이스라엘 나라를 서른세 해 다스렸다. 죽기 바로 앞에 그 아들 아도니야가 대담하게 보좌를 빼앗으려 하매, 나라를 어떤 참칭자에게서 지키려고 다윗이 왕관을 솔로몬에게 넘기고 성전의 설계와 모형과 그것을 위하여 모은 보화를 그 손에 맡겼으며, 나라의 영향 있는 이들을 불러 고별사를 하였다. 주전 1015년에 죽어 「다윗 성」에 묻혔다(열왕기상 2:10). 그 무덤이 뒤에 오는 왕들의 무덤이 되었고 나라의 거룩한 자리 가운데 하나가 되었다. 예루살렘 시온 산 성벽 밖에 그 자리가 보인다. 다윗은 그리스도의 예표였다. 둘 다 고난 뒤에 제 나라를 이었다. 다윗이 이 땅 이스라엘의 다스리는 자로서, 영의 이스라엘을 영원히 다스리실 다윗의 자손의 앞선 이였다(마태복음 1:1; 9:27; 12:23). 다윗을 하나님의 「마음에 맞는」 사람이라 할 때에(사무엘상 13:14; 사도행전 13:22) 그 두루 되는 성품과 행실을 뜻함이 뚜렷하고 그 낱낱의 일을 뜻하지 않는다. 그가 사람이므로 온전하지 못하였고, 죄지었을 때에 하나님이 그를 몹시 엄히 벌하셨다. 그러나 하나님 섬김에 헌신함이 남달랐고 우상에게서 스스로를 지켰다. 이스라엘의 정부를 세웠고 아브라함에게 하신 약속의 온 넓이까지 그 영토를 넓혔으며, 애굽에서 레바논까지, 유브라데에서 지중해까지 뻗은 촘촘하고 하나 된 제국을 남겼다. 다윗의 삶과 성품이 그 시에서 빛나니, 곧 행동과 모험과 싸움의 삶이요 사내다운 힘과 여인다운 다정함의 성품이다. 그리하여 그 시편이 전기의 재료를 준다. 그것으로 그 마음을 읽는다. 거인을 죽인 사람이 우정을 섬세히 아는 이임이 드러난다. 정욕이 죄로 이끌고 미움이 저주의 말로 이끈 그 사람이 가장 깊이 낮추어 슬퍼하고 온 마음으로 찬동하며 복을 빌 수 있었다. 그가 그 모음을 다 쓴 것은 아니나, 하나님의 교회가 어려울 때에 위로를 얻고 잘될 때에 거룩해지려고 기대어 온 것이 다윗의 시편이다. 그에 대하여 페로운 참사가 참되고 힘 있게 이른다. 「이 시편의 뛰어남이 바로 그 두루 미침이다. 사람 마음의 깊은 샘에서 솟았고, 하나님이 그 섭리와 성령으로 그것이 그 교회에 영원한 유업이 되도록 정하셨다. 그러므로 그것이 한 사람이 아니라 모든 이의 슬픔과 기쁨과 소망과 싸움과 이김을 나타낸다. 어찌하여 그러한가 물으면 답이 멀리 있지 않다. 시편 기자의 눈과 마음 앞에 늘 한 대상이 있다. 모든 원수와 모든 괴로움과 모든 핍박과 모든 죄가 하나님의 빛 가운데서 보인다. 그에게 부르짖고, 그에게 마음을 벗기며, 그에게 감사를 드린다. 이것이 그 시편을 그토록 참되고 값지고 두루 미치게 한다. 그 영감의 더 굳은 증거를 줄 수 없으니, 곧 그것이 한 시대의 것이 아니라 모든 때를 위한 것이며, 그 말이 그리스도께서 육신으로 오시기 몇 세기 앞서 산 이의 말인데도 가장 익은 그리스도인이 그리스도인 됨의 넉넉함으로 그것을 쓸 수 있다는 것이다.」 다윗 성이라는 말을 시온에 쓰고(사무엘하 5:7), 예루살렘에 쓰며(열왕기상 2:10), 베들레헴에도 쓴다(누가복음 2:4,11).
※ 원문 오류: Matt 6:35 → 마태복음 5:35
※ 판정 근거: 마태복음 6장은 34절까지뿐이다. 마태복음 5:35가 「예루살렘으로도 하지 말라 이는 큰 임금의 성임이요」이다.
※ 원문 오류: 1 Chr 2:29 → 사무엘하 13:29
※ 판정 근거: 샤프 1880년 인쇄본 222쪽(PDF 228면)을 인쇄면 그림으로 확인했다. 인쇄면이 「revenged, 「after two full years,」 by Absalom, who slew Amnon at a feast. 2 Sam. 13 : 14, 29.」이다. 맨 숫자 29에 가짜 주소가 붙었다.
※ 원문 오류: Rev 1:11 → 누가복음 2:11
※ 판정 근거: 이어받기 숫자 부풀리기. 원문에서 책과 장을 생략한 맨 숫자에 엉뚱한 주소가 붙은 것이다. 앞의 성한 인용을 좇으면 누가복음 2:11가 되며, 그 절은 「오늘 다윗의 동네에 너희를 위하여 구주가 나셨으니 곧 그리스도 주시니라…」이다.
※ 원문 오류: 1 Sam 30:18 → 사무엘상 19:18
※ 판정 근거: 샤프 1880년 인쇄본 221쪽(PDF 227면)을 인쇄면 그림으로 확인했다. 인쇄면이 「Michal saved David’s life and enabled him to flee to Samuel at Ramah. 1 Sam. 19 : 13, 18.」이다. 맨 숫자 18에 가짜 주소가 붙었다.

entries.definition: DAY. The natural day consists of 24 hours, or one revolution of the earth upon its axis. The artificial day is the time during which the sun is above the horizon. The civil day is reckoned differently by different nations-some from sunrise to sunrise; others from sunset to sunset; others still from noon to noon, or from midnight to midnight. The Jewish day was reckoned from evening to evening, adopted, as some think, from Gen 1:5, or, as others with more probability hold, from the "use of the lunar calendar in regulating days of religious observance." Lev 23:32. Their Sabbath, or seventh day, which was the only day named-the others were numbered merely-began on what we call Friday, at sunset, and ended on what we call Saturday, at sunset. Ex 12:18. This mode of reckoning days was not uncommon in other Eastern nations. The day was originally divided into morning, noon, and night. Ps 55:17. But besides, the Jews distinguished six unequal parts, which were again subdivided. 1. Dawn, subdivided into gray dawn and rosy dawn. 2. Sunrise. Some supposed that the Hebrews, prior to leaving Egypt, began the day at that time, but discontinued it by divine command, and began at even in order to be different from those nations which worshipped the rising sun. 3. The heat of the day, about nine o'clock. 1 Sam 11:11; Neh 7:3, etc. 4. The two noons. Gen 43:16; Deut 28:29. 5. The cool (lit. wind) of the day, before sunset. Gen 3:8. 6. Evening. In Ex 12:6; Ex 30:8, margins, occurs the phrase "between the two evenings," which probably is correctly taken to mean "between the beginning and end of sunset." The mention of hours in the Bible dates from the Captivity, Dan 3:6, and it is therefore reasonably presumed that this division of time is of Babylonish origin. Before the Captivity the Jews divided the night into three watches-from sunset to midnight, from midnight to cock-crow, Jud 7:19; from cock-crow to sunrise. Ex 14:24. In the N.T. mention is made of four watches, because the Greek and Roman division was then adopted. In our Lord's time the division of the day into 12 hours was common. John 11:9. The word "day" is used of a festal day, Hos 7:5; a birthday. Job 3:1; a day of ruin, Hos 1:11; Job 18:20; the judgment-day, Joel 1:15; 1 Thess 5:2; Acts 17:31; and the kingdom of Christ. John 8:56; Rom 13:12. It is also often used to denote an indefinite time. Gen 2:4; Isa 22:5. The term "three days and three nights," in Matt 12:40, denotes the same space of time as "three days." Matt 27:63-64. Day's Journey, a distance mentioned Gen 31:23; Ex 3:18, etc. It is quite evident that this phrase does not mean any particular distance, but rather the space travelled during one day, and this would of course vary with the circumstances of the traveller. But unless there is special reason for believing the contrary, we may interpret it as meaning a stretch of 25 to 30 miles, since this is the usual length of a day's journey in the East, on camel or horseback, performed in 6 to 8 hours. See also Sabbath Day's Journey. Day, Lord's. See Sabbath. Daysman. Job 9:33. The word is derived by Webster from "him who fixes the day upon which he will decide as judge or arbitrator." It was in common use, when the Bible was translated, in the sense of "umpire." Dayspring. Job 38:12; Luke 1:78. The first dawning of light. Comp. Isa 60:1-2 and Rev 22:16. Day-star, or Morning-star, 2 Pet 1:19, in the figurative language of the apostle, is supposed to mean the light which shines on the soul of the believer, and cheers him with the expectation of a perfect day of holiness and joy.
entries.definition_ko:
날. 자연의 하루는 스물네 시간 곧 땅이 그 축을 한 번 도는 것이다. 인위의 하루는 해가 지평선 위에 있는 동안이다. 민간의 하루는 민족마다 달리 헤아리니, 어떤 이들은 해 뜰 때부터 해 뜰 때까지, 어떤 이들은 해 질 때부터 해 질 때까지, 또 어떤 이들은 한낮부터 한낮까지나 밤중부터 밤중까지 헤아린다.

유대인의 하루는 저녁부터 저녁까지 헤아렸다. 어떤 이들은 이를 창세기 1장 5절에서 취한 것으로 여기고, 다른 이들은 더 그럴듯하게 「종교 예식의 날을 정하는 데 달의 책력을 쓴 데서」 왔다고 본다. 레위기 23장 32절이다.

그들의 안식일 곧 일곱째 날은 이름이 붙은 유일한 날이었으니 다른 날은 그저 번호로만 불렸는데, 우리가 금요일이라 부르는 날 해 질 때 시작하여 우리가 토요일이라 부르는 날 해 질 때 끝났다. 출애굽기 12장 18절이다. 이렇게 날을 헤아리는 방식은 다른 동방 민족에게도 드물지 않았다.

하루는 본디 아침과 한낮과 밤으로 나뉘었다. 시편 55편 17절이다. 그러나 그 밖에 유대인은 고르지 않은 여섯 부분을 구별하였고 그것을 다시 잘게 나누었다.

첫째, 새벽이니 잿빛 새벽과 붉은 새벽으로 나뉜다.

둘째, 해 뜰 때다. 어떤 이들은 히브리 사람들이 애굽을 떠나기 전에는 이때부터 하루를 시작하였으나, 하나님의 명으로 그것을 그만두고 저녁부터 시작하였다고 여겼으니, 떠오르는 해를 섬기던 민족들과 달라지려는 것이었다.

셋째, 날이 더울 때이니 아홉 시쯤이다. 사무엘상 11장 11절과 느헤미야 7장 3절 등이다.

넷째, 두 한낮이다. 창세기 43장 16절과 신명기 28장 29절이다.

다섯째, 날이 서늘할 때이니 글자대로는 바람 불 때요 해 지기 전이다. 창세기 3장 8절이다.

여섯째, 저녁이다. 출애굽기 12장 6절과 출애굽기 30장 8절의 난외에 「두 저녁 사이」라는 말이 나오는데, 아마도 「해 지기 시작할 때와 다 질 때 사이」를 뜻하는 것으로 보는 것이 옳을 것이다.

성경에서 시각을 말한 것은 사로잡힘 때부터이니, 다니엘 3장 6절이며, 그러므로 이렇게 시간을 나눈 것이 바벨론에서 왔으리라고 그럴듯하게 여긴다.

사로잡히기 전에 유대인은 밤을 세 경으로 나누었다. 해 질 때부터 밤중까지, 밤중부터 닭 울 때까지이니 사사기 7장 19절이요, 닭 울 때부터 해 뜰 때까지다. 출애굽기 14장 24절이다. 신약에는 네 경이 언급되니 그때에 헬라와 로마의 나눔을 받아들였기 때문이다.

우리 주 때에는 하루를 열두 시로 나누는 것이 예사였다. 요한복음 11장 9절이다.

「날」이라는 말은 절기의 날을 가리키는 데 쓰이고, 호세아 7장 5절이다, 태어난 날을 가리키며, 욥기 3장 1절이다, 망하는 날을 가리키고, 호세아 1장 11절과 욥기 18장 20절이다, 심판의 날을 가리키며, 요엘 1장 15절과 데살로니가전서 5장 2절과 사도행전 17장 31절이다, 그리스도의 나라를 가리킨다. 요한복음 8장 56절과 로마서 13장 12절이다. 또한 정해지지 않은 때를 나타내는 데도 자주 쓰인다. 창세기 2장 4절과 이사야 22장 5절이다.

마태복음 12장 40절의 「밤낮 사흘」이라는 말은 「사흘」과 같은 기간을 나타낸다. 마태복음 27장 63절부터 64절까지다.

하룻길. 창세기 31장 23절과 출애굽기 3장 18절 등에 나오는 거리다. 이 말이 어떤 정해진 거리를 뜻하지 않고 오히려 하루 동안 간 거리를 뜻함이 꽤 뚜렷하며, 그것은 물론 나그네의 형편에 따라 달라졌을 것이다. 그러나 달리 볼 특별한 까닭이 없다면 스물다섯에서 서른 마일쯤으로 풀이할 수 있으니, 동방에서 낙타나 말을 타고 여섯에서 여덟 시간에 가는 하룻길이 보통 이만하기 때문이다. 「안식일에 가도록 허락된 길」 항목도 보라.

주의 날. 「안식일」 항목 참조.

중재자. 욥기 9장 33절이다. 이 말을 웹스터는 「재판관이나 중재인으로서 판결할 날을 정하는 이」에서 온 것으로 본다. 성경이 번역되던 때에 그것은 「판정하는 이」라는 뜻으로 널리 쓰였다.

새벽빛. 욥기 38장 12절과 누가복음 1장 78절이다. 빛이 처음 밝아 오는 것이다. 이사야 60장 1절부터 2절까지와 요한계시록 22장 16절을 견주어 보라.

샛별 곧 새벽 별. 베드로후서 1장 19절이다. 이 사도의 비유하는 말에서 그것은 믿는 이의 영혼에 비치어, 거룩함과 기쁨의 온전한 날을 바라게 하며 그를 북돋우는 빛을 뜻하는 것으로 여겨진다.

entries.definition: DEA'CON (servant). This name, as a title of office, has been applied to the "seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom," who were appointed over the business of serving tables, in order that the apostles might be at liberty to give themselves continually to prayer and the ministry of the word. They were set apart by prayer and the laying on of the apostles' hands. Acts 6:1-6. Very likely these seven men held a higher position than those afterward appointed, as, in addition to routine and more or less servile duties, they preached and did the work of evangelists; e.g. Stephen and Philip. The idea that a man must be a deacon before he can be an elder or bishop is not found in the N.T. The qualifications and duties of deacons are particularly set forth in Acts 6:1-6 and 1 Tim 3:8-12
entries.definition_ko: '섬기는 자'를 뜻한다. 직분의 칭호로서 이 이름은 사도들이 기도와 말씀 사역에 전념할 수 있도록 접대하는 일을 맡도록 세워진 '성령과 지혜가 충만하여 칭찬 듣는 사람 일곱'에게 적용되었다. 이들은 기도와 사도들의 안수로 세워졌다(사도행전 6:1-6). 이 일곱은 후에 임명된 이들보다 높은 지위였을 가능성이 크니, 일상적이고 다소 종속적인 임무에 더해 스데반과 빌립처럼 전파하고 복음 전도자의 일을 했기 때문이다. 집사를 거쳐야 장로나 감독이 될 수 있다는 생각은 신약에 없다.

entries.definition: DEA'CONESS. Such was Phoebe, and in all probability Tryphena, Tryphosa, and Persis occupied the same office in the church in Rome. Rom 16:1, Jud 4:12. It is therefore probable that there was in the different churches an order of pious women employed in attending upon those of their own sex in some of the same offices and duties which the deacons performed for their brethren. Among these we reckon the care of the sick, of the poor and the widows, the education of orphans, attention to strangers, the practice of hospitality, comp. 1 Tim 5:10, and the assistance needed at the baptism of females. The question whether the "widows" in 1 Tim 5:9-16 are proper deaconesses may be answered in the affirmative, because the word translated "to take into the number" or "to enroll" applies not to widows in general, but to the deaconesses, for the following reasons: If understood of any insertion merely in the list of those supported from the congregational fund, it implies an injustice to widows under 60 years old or to those twice married, who might easily be even more destitute. The opposite interpretation conflicts with the context, for Paul advises, in V. 2 Kgs 22:14, the younger widows to remarry; but this would be to cut them off from all help in case they were widows again. This interpretation leaves it inexplicable why a special vow was required of these widows, v. Jud 4:12. But by understanding the word to apply, not to widows in general, but to those who were specially elected and ordained to the particular office of deaconess, all these objections vanish.
entries.definition_ko:
뵈뵈가 여집사였고, 로마 교회의 드루배나와 드루보사와 버시도 아마 같은 직분을 맡았을 것이다(로마서 16:1,12). 그러므로 여러 교회에 경건한 여인들의 한 반열이 있어, 집사들이 형제들에게 하던 것과 같은 몇몇 직분과 일을 자기와 같은 성의 사람들에게 하였으리라고 보인다. 그 가운데 병든 이와 가난한 이와 과부를 돌보는 일, 고아를 가르치는 일, 나그네를 살피는 일, 손 대접하는 일(디모데전서 5:10과 견주라), 여인이 세례받을 때에 돕는 일을 꼽는다. 디모데전서 5:9-16의 「과부」가 참으로 여집사인가 하는 물음에는 그렇다고 답할 수 있다. 「명부에 올리다」로 옮긴 말이 과부 일반이 아니라 여집사에게 해당하기 때문이니, 그 까닭은 이러하다. 그것을 그저 교회 재정으로 돕는 이들의 명단에 넣는 것으로만 새기면, 예순 살이 못 된 과부나 두 번 시집간 과부에게 옳지 않은 일이 된다. 그들이 더 곤궁할 수도 있기 때문이다. 또 그렇게 새기면 앞뒤 문맥과 어긋난다. 바울이 14절에서 젊은 과부에게 다시 시집가라고 권하는데, 그리 새기면 그들이 다시 과부가 되었을 때에 모든 도움에서 끊어 버리는 셈이 된다. 그리고 그 과부들에게 왜 특별한 서약을 요구하였는지도 풀리지 않는다(디모데전서 5:12). 그러나 그 말이 과부 일반이 아니라 여집사라는 특정한 직분에 뽑히고 세움받은 이들에게 쓰인 것으로 새기면, 이 모든 어려움이 사라진다.
※ 원문 오류: v. Jud 4:12 → 디모데전서 5:12
※ 판정 근거: 샤프 1880년 인쇄본 225쪽(PDF 231면)을 인쇄면으로 확인했다. 인쇄면이 「This interpretation leaves it inexplicable why a special vow was required of these widows. v. 12.」로 「v.」 뒤가 맨 숫자 12뿐이다. 앞이 디모데전서 5:9-16이므로 디모데전서 5:12이며, 「처음 믿음을 저버렸으므로 정죄를 받느니라」이다.

entries.definition: DEAD, DEATH. Death is the destruction or extinction of life. By the transgression of God's commandment our first parents became liable to death. The threatening was, "In the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die." Gen 2:17 (comp. Rom 5:12-14; 1 Cor 15:21-22; Heb 9:27). This expression does not mean to define the time of actual dissolution, but rather to denote an inevitable liability or exposure to death, which, in that day and by that act, they should surely incur. The sacred writers speak of a death which affects the body only. Gen 25:11; of another, which describes the condition of the soul under the power of sin, Eph 2:1; and a third, which denotes the everlasting perdition of the wicked. James 5:20. In each of these senses our divine Redeemer may be regarded as having virtually destroyed death and delivered them who, through fear of death, were all their lifetime subject to bondage. Heb 2:14-15. To avail ourselves, however, of the benefits of his perfect triumph, we must believe, trust, love, and obey him. See Buby, Resurrection, Christ.
entries.definition_ko: 죽음은 생명의 소멸 또는 단절이다. 하나님의 명령을 어김으로 우리 첫 조상이 죽음에 처하게 되었다. 경고는 '네가 먹는 날에는 반드시 죽으리라'였다(창세기 2:17, 로마서 5:12-14, 고린도전서 15:21-22, 히브리서 9:27). 이 표현은 실제로 숨이 끊어지는 때를 정하는 것이 아니라, 그날 그 행위로 반드시 짊어지게 될 피할 수 없는 죽음의 책임과 노출을 뜻한다. 성경 기자들은 몸에만 미치는 죽음(창세기 25:11), 죄의 권세 아래 있는 영혼의 상태를 가리키는 죽음(에베소서 2:1), 악인의 영원한 멸망을 뜻하는 죽음(야고보서 5:20)을 말한다. 이 모든 뜻에서 우리 구주는 죽음을 실질적으로 멸하시고 죽기를 무서워하여 일생에 매여 종노릇하던 이들을 놓아주셨다(히브리서 2:14-15).

entries.definition: DEAD SEA, a name not found in Scripture. See Salt Sea.
entries.definition_ko: 성경에 나오지 않는 이름이다. 염해 참조.

entries.definition: DE'BIR (sanctuary), the name of three places. 1. In the highlands of Judah, near Hebron; captured by Joshua, Josh 10:38-39; was first called Kirjath-sepher, Josh 15:15, and Kirjath-sannah, Josh 15:49; was allotted to the priests. Josh 21:15. It has been placed at Dewir-ban, 3 miles west of Hebron, and at Dilbeh, 6 miles south-west. Conder, however, rejects these, and suggests Dedheriyeh, north of which are copious springs, which he identifies with "the upper springs and the nether springs" of Jud 1:15. A place near the valley of Achor, Josh 15:7; perhaps Wady Dabir, between Jericho and Jerusalem. A place on the boundary of Gad, east of the Jordan, Josh 13:26; possibly the same as Lo-bebar, which see.
entries.definition_ko: 세 곳의 이름. (1) 헤브론 근처 유다 산지에 있으며 여호수아가 점령했다(여호수아 10:38-39). 처음에는 기럇세벨(여호수아 15:15), 기럇산나(여호수아 15:49)라 불렸고 제사장들에게 배정되었다(여호수아 21:15). (2) 아골 골짜기 근처의 한 지명(여호수아 15:7). (3) 요단 동편 갓 경계의 한 지명(여호수아 13:26).

variants.definition: DE'BIR (sanctuary), the name of three places. 1. In the highlands of Judah, near Hebron; captured by Joshua, Josh 10:38-39; was first called Kirjath-sepher, Josh 15:15, and Kirjath-sannah, Josh 15:49; was allotted to the priests. Josh 21:15. It has been placed at Dewir-ban, 3 miles west of Hebron, and at Dilbeh, 6 miles south-west. Conder, however, rejects these, and suggests Dedheriyeh, north of which are copious springs, which he identifies with "the upper springs and the nether springs" of Jud 1:15. A place near the valley of Achor, Josh 15:7; perhaps Wady Dabir, between Jericho and Jerusalem. A place on the boundary of Gad, east of the Jordan, Josh 13:26; possibly the same as Lo-bebar, which see.
variants.definition_ko: 세 곳의 이름. 1) 헤브론 근처 유다 산지에 있으며 여호수아가 점령했다(수 10:38-39). 처음에는 기럇세벨(수 15:15), 기럇산나(수 15:49)라 불렸고 제사장들에게 배정되었다(수 21:15). 2) 아골 골짜기 근처의 한 지명(수 15:7). 3) 요단 동편 갓 경계의 한 지명(수 13:26).

variants.definition: DE'BIR, king of Eglon, one of the five kings who warred against Gibeon. He, with his companions, was slain by Joshua and hanged on a tree. Josh 10:3, Heb 12:23, Acts 11:26.
variants.definition_ko: 에글론 왕으로, 기브온을 친 다섯 왕 중 하나다. 동료들과 함께 여호수아에게 죽임을 당해 나무에 매달렸다(수 10:3).

entries.definition: DEB'ORAH (a bee). 1. The nurse of Rebekah, and her companion into Canaan. Gen 24:59. She was buried at Bethel, under the "oak of weeping." Gen 35:8. "Nurses held a high and honorable place in ancient times, and especially in the East, where they were often the principal members of the family. 2 Kgs 11:2; 2 Kgs 2 Chr. 22:11." A woman of eminent wisdom and holiness (called a prophetess), and a judge of the people of Israel. Jud 4:4 She was the wife of Lapidoth (although some think the passage should read "a woman of Lapidoth"), and had her judgment-seat under a palm tree, which from this circumstance, and from the rarity of the tree, is spoken of as "the [well-known] palm tree of Deborah." Jud 4:5. Israel was suffering at that time a most oppressive bondage under Jabin, a Canaanitish king, to which it was doomed in consequence of its sin. Deborah, by divine direction, called upon Barak, who had probably signalized himself in some way, and commanded him to station himself upon Mount Tabor with a prescribed number of men, and she would see to it that Sisera, the commander of the tyrant's army, should be there, and should fall into Barak's hands. Barak engaged to undertake the enterprise if Deborah would accompany him. To this she consented, prophesying, however, that if she went the honor of the victory would be hers and not his, and that Sisera would be regarded as having fallen by the hands of a woman. Jud 4:9. The two armies met, and the event was as Deborah predicted. Sisera fled, and died by the hand of Jael; his army was cut off and every man slain. Jud 4:21. The triumphal song composed or dictated by Deborah on that occasion is regarded as one of the finest specimens of Oriental poetry. Jud 5. We give a few verses from a revised version: See Barak. Jael.
entries.definition_ko: (1) 리브가의 유모로 그를 따라 가나안에 왔다(창세기 24:59). 벧엘의 '통곡의 상수리나무' 아래 묻혔다(창세기 35:8). 유모는 고대에, 특히 동방에서 높고 존귀한 자리를 차지해 흔히 집안의 주요 인물이었다. (2) 뛰어난 지혜와 거룩함을 지닌 여인(여선지자라 불림)이자 이스라엘 백성의 사사였다(사사기 4:4). 랍비돗의 아내였으며 종려나무 아래 재판석을 두어, 그 나무는 '드보라의 종려나무'로 불렸다(사사기 4:5). 당시 이스라엘은 죄로 인해 가나안 왕 야빈의 혹독한 압제 아래 있었다. 드보라는 하나님의 지시로 바락을 불러 정해진 수의 군사와 함께 다볼산에 진 치게 하고, 압제자의 군대 장관 시스라가 바락의 손에 넘어지게 하겠다고 했다.

variants.definition: DEB'ORAH (a bee). 1. The nurse of Rebekah, and her companion into Canaan. Gen 24:59. She was buried at Bethel, under the "oak of weeping." Gen 35:8. "Nurses held a high and honorable place in ancient times, and especially in the East, where they were often the principal members of the family. 2 Kgs 11:2; 2 Kgs 2 Chr. 22:11." A woman of eminent wisdom and holiness (called a prophetess), and a judge of the people of Israel. Jud 4:4 She was the wife of Lapidoth (although some think the passage should read "a woman of Lapidoth"), and had her judgment-seat under a palm tree, which from this circumstance, and from the rarity of the tree, is spoken of as "the [well-known] palm tree of Deborah." Jud 4:5. Israel was suffering at that time a most oppressive bondage under Jabin, a Canaanitish king, to which it was doomed in consequence of its sin. Deborah, by divine direction, called upon Barak, who had probably signalized himself in some way, and commanded him to station himself upon Mount Tabor with a prescribed number of men, and she would see to it that Sisera, the commander of the tyrant's army, should be there, and should fall into Barak's hands. Barak engaged to undertake the enterprise if Deborah would accompany him. To this she consented, prophesying, however, that if she went the honor of the victory would be hers and not his, and that Sisera would be regarded as having fallen by the hands of a woman. Jud 4:9. The two armies met, and the event was as Deborah predicted. Sisera fled, and died by the hand of Jael; his army was cut off and every man slain. Jud 4:21. The triumphal song composed or dictated by Deborah on that occasion is regarded as one of the finest specimens of Oriental poetry. Jud 5. We give a few verses from a revised version: See Barak. Jael.

entries.definition: DEBTOR. See Loan.
entries.definition_ko: 대여 참조.

entries.definition: DECAP'OLIS (ten cities), a region noticed three times in the Bible. Matt 4:25; Map of Decapolis. (From Schaff's "New Testament Commentary.") Mark 5:20; Mark 7:31 It lay near the Sea of Galilee probably on both sides of the Jordan. The cities were rebuilt by the Romans about b.c. 65; but as other cities grew up, writers are not agreed as to the names of the ten cities. Pliny gives them as follows: Scythopolis, Hippos, Gadara, Pella, Philadelphia, Gerasa, Dion, Canatha, Raphana, Damascus. Six are deserted, and none have many inhabitants except Damascus.
entries.definition_ko: '열 성읍'이라는 뜻으로 성경에 세 번 나온다(마태복음 4:25, 마가복음 5:20, 7:31). 갈릴리 바다 근처, 아마도 요단 양편에 걸쳐 있었다. 그 성읍들은 BC 65년경 로마인이 재건했으나 다른 성읍들이 생겨나면서 열 성읍의 이름에 대해서는 견해가 갈린다. 플리니우스는 스구도볼리, 힙포스, 가다라, 펠라, 빌라델비아, 게라사, 디온, 카나타, 라파나, 다메섹을 든다.

entries.definition: DECISION, VALLEY OF. Joel 3:14. See Jehoshaphat.
entries.definition_ko: 여호사밧 참조(요엘 3:14).

entries.definition: DE'DAN (low ground). 1. The name of a descendant of Ham. Gen 10:7; 1 Chr 1:9. A son of Jokshan, son of Abraham by Keturah. Gen 25:3; 1 Chr 1:32.
entries.definition_ko: (1) 함의 후손 이름(창세기 10:7, 역대상 1:9). (2) 아브라함이 그두라에게서 얻은 욕산의 아들(창세기 25:3, 역대상 1:32).

variants.definition: DE'DAN (low ground). 1. The name of a descendant of Ham. Gen 10:7; 1 Chr 1:9. A son of Jokshan, son of Abraham by Keturah. Gen 25:3; 1 Chr 1:32.
variants.definition_ko: 1) 함의 후손 이름(창 10:7, 대상 1:9). 2) 아브라함이 그두라에게서 얻은 욕산의 아들(창 25:3, 대상 1:32).

entries.definition: DED'ICATE,DEDICA'TION, a religious ceremony by which any person, place, or thing is set apart for the service of God or to some sacred use. Num 7; 2 Sam 8:11; 1 Kgs 8. Cities, walls, gates, and private houses were thus dedicated. Neh 12:27. The practice of consecration was very common among the Jews, and was suited to the peculiar dispensation under which they lived. Dedication, Feast of the, mentioned only once in the canonical Scriptures, John 10:22, was instituted to commemorate the purging of the temple and the rebuilding of the altar after Judas Maccabaeus had driven out the Syrians, 1 Macc 4:52-59, b.c. 164. Like the other Jewish feasts, it lasted eight days, but, unlike them, attendance at Jerusalem was not obligatory. In general, it was kept like the feast of tabernacles. The Hallel was sung every day. It was a time of rejoicing. It began upon the 25th day of Chisleu (December), the anniversary of the pollution of the temple by Antiochus Epiphanes, b.c. 167.
entries.definition_ko: 봉헌은 어떤 사람이나 곳이나 물건을 하나님을 섬기는 데나 어떤 거룩한 쓰임에 떼어 놓는 신앙의 예식이다(민수기 7장; 사무엘하 8:11; 열왕기상 8장). 성읍과 성벽과 문과 사삿집이 이렇게 봉헌되었다(느헤미야 12:27). 바치는 관행이 유대인 가운데 매우 흔하였고, 그들이 산 남다른 경륜에 맞았다. 수전절은 정경에 오직 한 번 언급되니(요한복음 10:22), 유다 마카베우스가 아람 사람을 몰아낸 뒤에 성전을 깨끗이 하고 제단을 다시 세운 일을 기리려고 세워졌다(마카베오상 4:52-59. 주전 164년). 다른 유대 절기처럼 여드레 이어졌으나, 그것들과 달리 예루살렘에 나아갈 의무는 없었다. 두루 초막절처럼 지켰다. 날마다 할렐을 불렀다. 기쁨의 때였다. 기슬르월(십이월) 이십오일에 시작하였으니, 주전 167년 안티오코스 에피파네스가 성전을 더럽힌 날의 돌아옴이다.

entries.definition: DEEP, THE, in Luke 8:31 and Rom 10:7, does not refer to the sea, but to the abyss, the place where lost spirits await their final doom. The same word is rendered the "bottomless pit" in Rev 9:1-2, Rev 1:11; Rev 11:7; Rev 20:13.
entries.definition_ko: 다음을 나타내는 데 쓰인다: (1) 무덤 또는 심연(로마서 10:7; 누가복음 8:31); (2) 바다의 가장 깊은 곳(시편 69:15); (3) 창세기 1:2에 언급된 혼돈; (4) 무저갱, 지옥(요한계시록 9:1,2; 11:7; 20:13).

variants.definition: DEEP, THE, in Luke 8:31 and Rom 10:7, does not refer to the sea, but to the abyss, the place where lost spirits await their final doom. The same word is rendered the "bottomless pit" in Rev 9:1-2, Rev 1:11; Rev 11:7; Rev 20:13.
variants.definition_ko: 누가복음 8:31과 로마서 10:7의 이 말은 바다가 아니라 무저갱, 곧 잃어버린 영들이 최후의 심판을 기다리는 곳을 가리킨다. 같은 말이 요한계시록 9:1-2, 11:7, 20:1-3에서 '무저갱'으로 번역된다.

entries.definition: DEFILE'. Under the Jewish law, many blemishes of person and conduct were regarded as defilements or pollutions, rendering those upon whom they were found unclean, and subjecting them, for the time being, to many civil and religious disabilities. Mark 7:2. The term is most frequently used by the sacred writers in a figurative sense.
entries.definition_ko: 유대 율법에서 사람의 몸과 행실의 여러 흠이 더러움이나 부정으로 여겨져, 그런 것이 있는 사람을 부정하게 만들고 한동안 여러 시민적·종교적 제약을 받게 했다(마가복음 7:2). 성경 기자들은 이 말을 비유적 의미로 가장 자주 쓴다.

entries.definition: DEGREE'. This word is used to signify rank or station. Ps 62:9; 1 Tim 3:13. The phrase "song, or psalm of degrees," which forms the title to Psalms 120-134 inclusive, has been variously interpreted; some suppose it has reference to the elevated voice in which they were sung, others to the time when they were sung-viz. at the annual festivals, when the Jews went up to Jerusalem, and that in this sense they were called "odes of ascension." The Rabbins suppose they were sung by the Levites as they ascended the 15 steps which separated the men's court from the women's in the temple; and others again suppose that the word "degree" denotes the peculiarly climacteric style of these Psalms-viz. that the thought or expression of one verse is resumed and carried forward in the next succeeding verse, as in Psalm 121; but this is improbable.
entries.definition_ko: 이 말이 신분이나 자리를 이르는 데에 쓰인다(시편 62:9; 디모데전서 3:13). 시편 120편부터 134편까지의 표제를 이루는 「성전에 올라가는 노래」라는 말이 여러 가지로 풀이되어 왔다. 어떤 이는 그것을 부른 높은 목소리에 관계된다 하고, 어떤 이는 그것을 부른 때 곧 유대인이 예루살렘으로 올라가던 해마다의 절기에 관계된다 하여 이 뜻에서 「올라감의 노래」라 하였다. 랍비들은 그것을 레위 사람이 성전에서 남자의 뜰과 여자의 뜰을 가르는 열다섯 층계를 오르며 불렀다고 여긴다. 또 다른 이들은 「올라감」이라는 말이 이 시편의 남다른 층층의 문체를 이른다고 여기니, 곧 한 절의 생각이나 말이 다음 절에서 다시 잡혀 이어 나가는 것으로 시편 121편이 그러하다. 그러나 이것은 그럼직하지 않다.

entries.definition: DEHA'VITES, supposed by Herodotus to be a Persian tribe, and, as some think, the same who are mentioned as from Ava. Ezr 4:9; 2 Kgs 17:24.
entries.definition_ko: 헤로도토스가 바사의 한 부족으로 본 사람들로, 아와에서 온 자들과 같다고 보는 견해도 있다(에스라 4:9).

entries.definition: DE'KAR (a lancer), the father of one of Solomon's commissariat officers. 1 Kgs 4:9.
entries.definition_ko: 솔로몬의 관리 중 한 사람의 아버지(열왕기상 4:9).

entries.definition: DELAI'AH (whom Jehovah hath freed). The head of the twenty third temple-course of priests. 1 Chr 24:18. " Children of Delaiah "are spoken of in Ezr 2:60;Neh 7:62. The father of a man who tried to terrify Nehemiah. Neh 6:10. A prince in the time of Jeremiah. Jer 36:12, Gal 4:25.
entries.definition_ko:
'여호와께서 놓아주셨다'는 뜻. 제사장 반열 스물셋째 반차의 우두머리(역대상 24:18), 스룹바벨과 함께 돌아온 '들라야 자손'(에스라 2:60), 느헤미야를 위협하려 한 사람의 아버지(느헤미야 6:10), 예레미야 시대의 방백(예레미야 36:12) 등을 가리킨다.
※ 원문 오류: Gal 4:25 → 예레미야 36:25
※ 판정 근거: 이어받기 숫자 부풀리기. 원문에서 책과 장을 생략한 맨 숫자에 엉뚱한 주소가 붙은 것이다. 앞의 성한 인용을 좇으면 예레미야 36:25가 되며, 그 절은 「엘라단과 들라야와 그마랴가 왕께 두루마리를 불사르지 말도록 아뢰어도 왕이…」이다.

entries.definition: DEL'ILAH (pining with desire), a harlot of the valley of Sorek, in the tribe of Judah, and near the borders of the Philistines, with whom Samson associated, and who was the instrument of betraying him to his enemies. Jud 16:4-18. See Samson.
entries.definition_ko: 유다 지파 소렉 골짜기, 블레셋 경계 가까이 살던 여인으로 삼손과 어울렸고 그를 원수들에게 넘겨주는 도구가 되었다(사사기 16:4-18). 삼손 참조.

entries.definition: DE'MAS, a zealous disciple and fellow-laborer of Paul, Phile 24; Col 4:14, who afterward left him through inordinate love of the world, 2 Tim 4:10. The name is most probably a contraction from "Demetrius" or from "Demarchus."
entries.definition_ko: 바울의 열심 있는 제자이자 동역자였으나(빌레몬서 1:24, 골로새서 4:14) 후에 세상을 지나치게 사랑하여 그를 떠났다(디모데후서 4:10). 이 이름은 '데메드리오'나 '데마르코스'의 축약형일 가능성이 높다.

entries.definition: DEME'TRIUS. 1. A silversmith who resided at Ephesus and manufactured silver shrines or small portable temples and images of Diana. See Diana. Acts 19:24. These were purchased by foreigners, who either could not come to Ephesus, or else desired a memento of the city and a model of its famous temple. This was a very lucrative business in that city, where the worship of Diana was chiefly maintained; and hence, when the gospel began to make an impression, and the people to forsake their vain idols for the service of the living God. Demetrius saw that he should lose his business unless he could still keep the people in sin. So he called a meeting of those who worked at that trade, and made a speech to them. By this harangue he inflamed the passions of his fellow-craftsmen, and they excited the multitude, until the whole city of Ephesus was thrown into an uproar, which was finally quelled by the politic and seasonable advice of the town-clerk. Acts 19. A disciple of high reputation, and, as some suppose (though without warrant), the Demetrius of Ephesus converted to the faith of the gospel. 3 John 12.
entries.definition_ko: (1) 에베소에 살던 은장색으로, 아데미의 은 신상과 작은 휴대용 신전 모형을 만들었다(사도행전 19:24). 이런 물건은 에베소에 올 수 없거나 그 도시와 유명한 신전의 기념물을 원하는 외지인들이 사 갔다. 아데미 숭배의 중심지였던 그 도시에서 매우 수익성 좋은 사업이었기에, 복음이 영향을 미치기 시작하고 사람들이 우상을 버리자 데메드리오는 장사를 잃을까 하여 동업자들을 모아 선동했고 온 에베소가 소동에 휩싸였다가 서기장의 지혜로운 권고로 진정되었다. (2) 평판이 좋은 제자(요한삼서 1:12).

variants.definition: DEME'TRIUS. 1. A silversmith who resided at Ephesus and manufactured silver shrines or small portable temples and images of Diana. See Diana. Acts 19:24. These were purchased by foreigners, who either could not come to Ephesus, or else desired a memento of the city and a model of its famous temple. This was a very lucrative business in that city, where the worship of Diana was chiefly maintained; and hence, when the gospel began to make an impression, and the people to forsake their vain idols for the service of the living God. Demetrius saw that he should lose his business unless he could still keep the people in sin. So he called a meeting of those who worked at that trade, and made a speech to them. By this harangue he inflamed the passions of his fellow-craftsmen, and they excited the multitude, until the whole city of Ephesus was thrown into an uproar, which was finally quelled by the politic and seasonable advice of the town-clerk. Acts 19. A disciple of high reputation, and, as some suppose (though without warrant), the Demetrius of Ephesus converted to the faith of the gospel. 3 John 12.

entries.definition: DENA'RIUS, a Roman silver coin nearly equivalent to the Greek drachma, and worth about 15 cents; translated in Roman Denarius. (From Eielwi.) the A.V. "penny," which makes the impression of a very small sum; it was really the amount of a day's wages. Matt 20:2; comp. Luke 10:35. "Shilling" would be a much nearer equivalent; but the better way would have been to transfer the Greek term into English (denar), as the evangelists retained the Latin term in the Greek. See Penny.
entries.definition_ko: 헬라의 드라크마와 거의 같은 로마 은화로 약 15센트 가치였다. 흠정역은 '페니'로 옮겨 아주 적은 액수 같은 인상을 주지만 실제로는 하루 품삯이었다(마태복음 20:2, 누가복음 10:35). '실링'이 훨씬 가까운 등가물이겠으나, 복음서 기자들이 헬라어 안에 라틴어를 그대로 둔 것처럼 헬라어 용어를 그대로 옮기는 편이 나았을 것이다.

entries.definition: DEP'UTY. The ofiice was that of proconsul, or governor of a senatorial province. Acts 13:7-8, Jud 4:12; Acts 19:38.
entries.definition_ko: 총독의 직분, 곧 원로원 속주의 지방 장관을 뜻한다(사도행전 13:7-8, 19:38).

entries.definition: DER'BE, a city of Lyeaonia, Acts 14:16, Ruth 4:20; Mark 16:1, about 20 miles from Lystra. Kiepert places it near Lake Ak-Ghieul, but Hamilton at Diele, several miles farther south.
entries.definition_ko:
루가오니아의 성읍으로 루스드라에서 약 20마일 떨어져 있다(사도행전 14:6,20).
※ 원문 오류: Acts 14:16 → 사도행전 14:6
※ 판정 근거: 본문 대조. 사도행전 14:6에 「더베」이(가) 나오나 Acts 14:16에는 나오지 않는다.
※ 원문 오류: Ruth 4:20 → 사도행전 14:20
※ 판정 근거: 이어받기 숫자 부풀리기. 원문에서 책과 장을 생략한 맨 숫자에 엉뚱한 주소가 붙은 것이다. 앞의 성한 인용을 좇으면 사도행전 14:20가 되며, 그 절은 「제자들이 둘러섰을 때에 바울이 일어나 그 성에 들어갔다가 이튿날 바나바와…」이다.

entries.definition: DES'ERT. The popular conception of the term must not be applied to all passages in the English Bible, in which the word is the translation of four Hebrew words denoting definite localities. It is applied to the Arabah, Eze 47:8, the name of the remarkable depression which runs through the land of Palestine; but this is a waste merely because of the depopulated and neglected state of the country. It is capable of cultivation. See Arabah. It is used to translate midhar, "pasture-ground," in Ex 3:1; Ex 5:3; Josh 19:2; Num 33:15-16. Horbah. Ps 102:6; Isa 48:21; Eze 13:4. But the term commonly employed is "waste places" or "desolation." Jeshimon. With the definite article, it is treated as a proper name. See Jeshimon. Without the article, it occurs in a few passages of poetry. In the following verses it is translated "desert:" Ps 78:40; Ps 106:14; Isa 43:19-20. The "desert," as an illimitable stretch of heavy sand, does not exist in Bible lands. The "desert of Sinai" is a wild and desolate region of country, but in many parts, especially from Elim (Wadi Ghurundel) to Mount Sinai, and the region toward the southern border of Palestine, are traces of previous fertility; and when the Israelites guided their flocks through it, they found pasture in many of the little valleys, and perhaps upon some of its plains. The different tracts mentioned under this name in the Bible, as Shur, Sin, Paran, etc., will be found particularly noticed in their proper places.
entries.definition_ko: 영어 성경에서 이 말은 특정 지역을 가리키는 네 히브리어를 옮긴 것이므로, 흔히 떠올리는 뜻을 모든 구절에 적용해서는 안 된다. 팔레스타인을 관통하는 함몰 지대인 아라바에 쓰이는데(에스겔 47:8), 이곳이 황무한 것은 단지 인구가 줄고 방치되었기 때문이며 경작이 가능하다. '미드바르'는 '목초지'를 뜻하고(출애굽기 3:1, 여호수아 19:2), '호르바'는 대개 '황폐한 곳'으로 옮긴다(시편 102:6, 이사야 48:21). 성경 땅에는 끝없이 펼쳐진 모래벌판으로서의 '사막'이 존재하지 않는다. '시내 광야'는 거칠고 황량한 지역이나 여러 곳, 특히 엘림에서 시내산까지와 팔레스타인 남쪽 경계 지역에는 예전에 비옥했던 흔적이 있다.
