entries.definition_ko:
달. 옛 히브리 사람들은 달을 숫자로 불렀으니 첫째 달과 둘째 달과 셋째 달 따위다. 다만 그러면서도 달마다 따로 이름을 붙여 썼다.

그러나 이렇게 두 가지로 부른 것은, 유대인이 애굽을 떠난 뒤에 쓴 두 가지 달의 흐름과는 아무 상관이 없다. 그 하나는 민간의 해를 이루고 다른 하나는 거룩한 해를 이룬다.

앞엣것은 시월의 첫 초승달에서 시작하였고 민간의 일과 농사에만 쓰였다. 뒤엣것은 사월의 첫 초승달에서 시작하였으니, 그들이 그달 열닷샛날에 애굽을 떠났기 때문이며 절기의 때를 정하는 데 쓰였다. 선지자들이 이 셈을 쓴다.

「모세 율법이 세워진 때부터 죽 달은 달의 운행을 따른 것으로 보인다. 유월절로 시작하는 종교 절기의 주기는 달의 순서만이 아니라 달 자체에 달려 있었고, 초하루 자체가 정기 절기의 때였다.」 민수기 10장 10절과 민수기 28장 11절부터 14절까지다.

한 달의 길이는 달이 차고 기우는 것으로 정해졌다. 그런데 달의 운행을 따른 열두 달이 삼백쉰나흘 여섯 시간밖에 되지 않으므로, 유대인의 한 해가 참된 해의 운행보다 열이틀 짧았다.

이 차이를 메우려고 유대인은 세 해마다 열셋째 달을 끼워 넣었으니 그것을 베아달 곧 둘째 아달이라 불렀다. 그리하여 달의 운행을 따른 그들의 해가 해의 운행을 따른 해와 같아졌다.

달이 차고 기우는 것을 꼼꼼히 살폈고, 초승달이 나타나면 나팔을 불고 봉화를 올려 정식으로 알렸다. 민수기 10장 10절과 시편 81편 3절이다.

이 관측이 유대 역사 내내 이어졌다. 다만 유대인이 달의 운행을 미리 헤아릴 수 있는 계산법을 지니고 있었음이 뚜렷하다. 사무엘상 20장 5절과 사무엘상 20장 24절과 사무엘상 20장 27절이다.

히브리 달의 이름은 다음과 같다.

「※ 원문 결함: 이 항목의 영문은 「히브리 달의 이름은 다음과 같다:」로 끝나고 그 목록이 하나도 없다. 쌍점까지 찍어 놓고 뒤가 비어 있으므로 달 이름 열둘 또는 열셋의 목록이 통째로 떨어져 나간 것이다. 이 사전에서 「도량형」과 「홍수」와 「진영」에 이어 뒷부분이 잘려 나간 네 번째 사례다. 영문에 있는 데까지만 옮겼다.」

「※ 원문 결함: 영문 원문에서 달을 숫자로 부른 예를 드는 자리와 민간의 해를 설명하는 자리에, 줄표가 있어야 할 곳에 붙임표가 쓰여 있다. 디지털화 과정에서 생긴 흠이다.」

entries.definition: MOON, Deut 33:14, or LES'SER LIGHT. Gen 1:16. The Hebrew year was a lunar year, and the new moon regulated many of the feasts and sacred services of the Jews. It was always the beginning of the month, and this day they called Neomenin, new-moon day or new month, and celebrated it with special sacrifices. Num 28:11-15. The heathens have generally worshipped the moon, under the names of "Queen of Heaven," "Venus," "Urania," "Succoth-benoth," "Ashtaroth," "Diana," "Hecate," or perhaps "Meni," etc. Deut 4:19; Deut 17:3; Job 31:26-27. The Jews were warned against this kind of idolatry, Deut 4:19; Deut 17:3, but they nevertheless burnt incense to the moon, 2 Kgs 23:5; Jer 8:2, and their women worshipped her as the queen of heaven and offered cakes of honey to her. Isa 7:18; Jer 44:17-19, Jer 44:25.
entries.definition_ko: 달이니(신명기 33:14) 작은 광명체라고도 한다(창세기 1:16). 히브리의 해는 달의 해였고, 초승달이 유대인의 여러 절기와 거룩한 섬김을 다스렸다. 그것이 언제나 달의 시작이었고, 이날을 네오메니아 곧 초하루라 하여 남다른 제사로 기렸다(민수기 28:11-15). 이방인이 두루 달을 섬겼으니 「하늘의 여왕」과 「비너스」와 「우라니아」와 「숙곳브놋」과 「아스다롯」과 「디아나」와 「헤카테」와 아마 「므니」 따위의 이름으로 그러하였다(신명기 4:19; 신명기 17:3; 욥기 31:26,27). 유대인이 이런 우상 숭배를 경계하라는 말을 들었으나(신명기 4:19; 신명기 17:3) 그러면서도 달에게 분향하였고(열왕기하 23:5; 예레미야 8:2), 그 여인들이 그를 하늘의 여왕으로 섬겨 꿀 과자를 드렸다(예레미야 44:17-19,25).

entries.definition: MO'RASTHITE, the designation of the prophet Micah, as a native of Moresheth-gath. Jer 26:18; Mic 1:1.
entries.definition_ko: 모레셋가드 출신이라는 뜻으로 선지자 미가에게 붙은 칭호다(예레미야 26:18, 미가 1:1).

entries.definition: MOR'DECAI (little man, or worshipper of Mars), a captive Jew of the family of Saul, resident at the court of Ahasuerus. An uncle of his died, leaving an orphan daughter named Hadassah, whom Mordecai adopted, and who afterward became the queen of Persia. Mordecai fell under the displeasure of Haman, one of the king's principal officers of state, and to be revenged on the despised Jew he laid a plan for the extermination of the whole body of Jews in the empire. His purpose was, however, defeated by the interposition of the queen, Haman lost his life and Mordecai was elevated to wealth and power.
entries.definition_ko:
모르드개. 「작은 사람」 또는 「마르스를 섬기는 이」라는 뜻이며 사울의 집안에 든 사로잡힌 유대 사람으로 아하수에로의 궁정에 살았다.

그의 삼촌 하나가 죽으면서 하닷사라는 고아 딸을 남겼는데, 모르드개가 그를 데려다 길렀고 그가 뒤에 바사의 왕후가 되었다.

모르드개가 왕의 으뜸가는 관리 가운데 하나인 하만의 미움을 샀다. 하만은 이 업신여기는 유대 사람에게 앙갚음하려고 그 제국 안의 유대 사람을 통째로 없앨 계략을 꾸몄다.

그러나 왕후가 나섬으로 그 뜻이 꺾였고, 하만은 제 목숨을 잃었으며 모르드개는 재물과 권세에 오르게 되었다.

entries.definition: MO'REH. The Plain, Plains, or Oaks of Moreh. It is twice noticed in Scripture; first as the halting-place of Abram after his entrance into the land of Canaan. Gen 12:6. It was near Shechem, Gen 12:6, and the mountains Ebal and Gerizim. Deut 11:30. The Hill of Moreh, where the Midianites and Amalekites were encamped before Gideon's attack upon them. Jud 7:1. It lay in the valley of Jezreel, on the north side. It is identified with Ain Jalood, the spring of Harod, and Gideon's position was on the northeast slope of Jebel Fukua (Mount Gilboa), between the village of Nuris and the spring. Little Hermon is 1815 feet above the Mediterranean. On the south is Gilboa. and on the north Tabor.
entries.definition_ko: '모레의 상수리나무'는 성경에 두 번 언급된다. 먼저 아브람이 가나안 땅에 들어온 후 머문 곳이며(창세기 12:6) 세겜과 에발산·그리심산 근처에 있었다(신명기 11:30). 또한 '모레 산'은 기드온이 치기 전 미디안과 아말렉이 진 쳤던 곳이다(사사기 7:1). 이스르엘 골짜기 북쪽에 있었다. 하롯 샘인 아인 잘루드로 확인되며, 기드온의 진지는 누리스 마을과 그 샘 사이 제벨 푸쿠아(길보아산) 북동쪽 비탈이었다. 작은 헤르몬은 해발 1,815피트다.

entries.definition: MOR'ESHETH-GATH (possession of wine-press), a town near Eleutherropolis, the birthplace of Micah, Mic 1:14; hence he is called the "Morasthite." Mic 1:1; Jer 26:18.
entries.definition_ko: 선지자 미가가 언급한 지명으로 미가의 고향 모레셋과 연관된 곳이다(미가 1:14).

entries.definition: MORI'AH (chosen of Jehovah?). The land where Abraham was directed to go and offer Isaac as a sacrifice. Gen 22:2. A mount on which Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem. 2 Chr 3:1. It was in the eastern part of the city, overlooking the valley of the Kedron, and where was the threshing-floor of Araunah, 2 Sam 24:24; 1 Chr 21:24. It lay north-east of Zion, from which it was separated by the Tyropoeon valley. Solomon erected the temple upon the levelled summit of the rock, and then immense walls were erected from its base on the four sides, and the interval between them and the sides filled in with earth or built up with vaults, so as to form on the top a large area on a level with the temple. Most authorities agree in regarding this as the place whither Abraham went to offer Isaac, and therefore identical with No. 1, above. Samaritan tradition, however, claims that the place of Abraham's altar was on Mount Gerizim, and Stanley and Grove are inclined to accept the Samaritan claim: but the arguments in favor of this view are far from satisfactory. For a description of Moriah of Jerusalem, upon which now stands the Mohammedan mosque of Omar, see IV. Topography, under Jerusalem.
entries.definition_ko:
모리아. 「여호와께서 택하신 곳」이라는 뜻인 듯하다.

아브라함이 가서 이삭을 제물로 드리라는 분부를 받은 땅이다. 창세기 22장 2절이다.

솔로몬이 예루살렘에 성전을 지은 산이다. 역대하 3장 1절이다. 성의 동쪽 편에 있어 기드론 골짜기를 굽어보았고, 아라우나의 타작마당이 있던 곳이다. 사무엘하 24장 24절과 역대상 21장 24절이다. 시온에서 북동쪽에 놓였고 그 사이를 티로포이온 골짜기가 갈랐다.

솔로몬이 바위 꼭대기를 고른 뒤에 그 위에 성전을 세웠고, 그다음에 네 면으로 그 밑동에서부터 거대한 담을 쌓아 올렸으며, 담과 비탈 사이를 흙으로 메우거나 궁륭을 틀어 올려 꼭대기에 성전과 같은 높이의 넓은 터를 이루게 하였다.

대다수 권위자는 이곳을 아브라함이 이삭을 드리러 간 곳으로 여기는 데에 뜻을 같이하니, 그러므로 위에 든 첫째 것과 같은 곳이다. 그러나 사마리아 사람이 전하는 말은 아브라함의 제단 자리가 그리심 산에 있었다고 주장하며, 스탠리와 그로브가 이 사마리아 사람의 주장을 받아들이는 쪽으로 기운다. 그러나 이 견해를 뒷받침하는 논거는 흡족한 것과는 거리가 멀다.

오늘 이슬람의 오마르 사원이 서 있는 예루살렘의 모리아를 적어 놓은 것을 보려면 예루살렘 항목 아래 넷째 지형 부분을 보라.

「※ 원문 오류: 이 항목은 모리아를 둘로 나누어 들면서 항목 번호를 하나도 붙이지 않았다. 그러면서도 뒤에서 「위에 든 No. 1」이라 하여 번호를 가리키고 있으니, 본디 번호가 매겨져 있었는데 파서가 이를 흘린 것임을 항목 스스로 증명한다. 한글은 문단을 나누고 「위에 든 첫째 것」으로 옮겼다.」

entries.definition: MORN'ING. See Day, Watch. Morning Watch. See Watch. Morning Star. See Stars.
entries.definition_ko: 낮, 경(파수) 참조. 새벽 경은 '경' 참조, 샛별은 '별' 참조.

entries.definition: MOR'TAR. See Lime.
entries.definition_ko: 석회 항목 참조.

entries.definition: MOSE'RA, and MOSE'ROTH (bond, bonds), a station in the journey of the Israelites through the wilderness, and near Mount Hor. Deut 10:6; Num 33:30-31.
entries.definition_ko: '묶임'이라는 뜻으로, 호르산 기슭, 이스라엘 백성이 광야를 유랑하며 머문 진지 중 하나(신명기 10:6; 민수기 33:30,38 참조). 호르산 오르막으로 이어지는 고갯길 아래의 작은 샘 엘타이예베와 동일시된다.

entries.definition: MOS'ES (Heb. Mosheh, *drawn out - i.e. of the water; Coptic Mo-use, watersaved), the leader and creator of the Jewish nation. This table shows the pedigree of Moses: His life falls naturally into three divisions, of forty years each, according to the account preserved in Stephen's speech. Acts 7:23, 1 Kgs 20:30, Eze 23:36. Moses was born in the dark hour of Hebrew story when a son was an object of the murderous search of the Egyptian spies. His father was Amram, his mother Jochebed, his tribe was Levi, and this fact may have determined the choice of Levi for the priesthood. Moses was the youngest child of the family; Miriam was the oldest, and Aaron came between. For three months his parents hid the babe, but at last it was no longer possible, and Jochebed, with a trembling heart, but it may be with a dim consciousness that God had great things in store for him, laid him in the little basket of papyrus she had deftly woven, pitched with bitumen within and without, and, carrying it down to the brink of one of the canals of the Nile, she hid it among the flags. The child was tenderly watched "afar off" by Miriam, who, less open to suspicion than the mother would be, stood to see what would be done to him. The daughter of the Pharaoh, the oppressor, came to the sacred river to bathe, attended by her maidens, who, surprised to find the basket, which had providentially floated down to the princess' bathing-place - or had Jochebed purposely put it there? - call the attention of their mistress to the discovery. The basket is fetched by one of them, and when opened a little babe, evidently one of the Hebrews' children, but exceedingly fair, is revealed to view. The woman-heart of the princess, who was a childless wife according to tradition, yearned over the little one. Her yearning was of God. Then Miriam drew near, gathered from the conversation that the child's life was to be spared, proposed to get a nurse for him among the Hebrew women, and thus it came to pass that Jochebed again had her child at her breast, but this time as his hired nurse. The biblical history of this period closes with the child Moses in the palace under tutors and governors, and increasing in wisdom and in stature, and in the favor of God and of man. There is a break in this history, as in that of the greater than Moses, between the infancy and the manhood. The second division of Moses' life was totally different in its character from the first. Moses, at the age of forty, is learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. The adopted grandson of the Pharaoh, initiated in the secrets of the priests, to whose order he belonged, he had a brilliant and useful worldly career before him. Had he remained in his advantageous surroundings, he would have been one of the great Egyptian sages - probably the greatest of them all. But God intended him to occupy a much more exalted position. There was needed by him a period of meditation. He must be cut off from books, and by direct contact with Nature in all her moods learn what books cannot give. The providential occasion of this violent change was Moses' slaying of an Egyptian taskmaster who had ill-treated a Hebrew. This was no secret, as he hoped it would be. The news, indeed, had been carried to Pharaoh, and so Moses was compelled to flee. It is probable that the murder was intended to impress upon the Hebrews his desire to help them - that he, the king's son, would be their deliverer; for it seems impossible to resist the conclusion that the pious teachings of his mother had not been forgotten, and that many prayers had been put up by him as he determined to be his brethren's saviour. But we see now that it was no wonder that this attempt at an insurrection proved abortive, and likewise that Moses had much to learn before he could properly lead the great Exodus. Moses fled from the prominence, the refinement, and the luxury of the court to the obscurity, the roughness, and the poverty of the wilderness. He became the shepherd of Jethro and the husband of his daughter Zipporah. Ex 2. This second period lasted forty years, and again a wondrous transformation took place. The transition was made at Horeb when one day he saw a "bush" - probably an acacia tree - which was said to be on fire and yet was unconsumed. He drew near to examine the wondrous sight, and the Angel of the Lord appeared to him and gave him his prophetic call. But now the would-be leader of forty years agone was full of excuses, deprecated his abilities, and disparaged his appearance. Accordingly, God appointed Aaron as his spokesman and brought about their meeting. Ex 3-4. Thus informed of the divine name, Ex 3:14, promised divine aid, and strengthened by miracles, Ex 4:1-7, Moses, at the age of eighty, now both a scholar and a practical man of affairs, starts out upon the deliverance of his people. On his way to Egypt his son Gershom was smitten by a mysterious illness, Zipporah thought because circumcision had not been performed. Accordingly, although loath to do it, she herself circumcised Gershom. Ex 4:24-26. The child recovered. Arrived at Goshen, Moses and Aaron at once began the discharge of their commission. But their primary efforts only increased the subject people's burdens, and the two brothers were well nigh in despair. Then began the series of miraculous visitations recounted in Ex 7-12. The last of the plagues so stunned the Egyptians that they precipitately drove the Israelites out. See Plagues, Exodus. The Israelites were prepared and went ready for the journey, which, instead of being one of three days into the desert, Ex 5:3, was one of forty years. Through all this time the Israelites were miraculously protected, fed, and led. Moses went in and out before them to the divine satisfaction, although his conduct by no means pleased every one. Nor had Moses always the proper control over himself. He flung down the God-engraven tables of the Law, enraged at the idolatry of the frivolous people while he was for forty days in the Mount with God. Ex 32:19. But the most damaging act of this nature was at Kadesh-meribah. The people murmured for water. Moses was commanded to speak to the rock; instead, he struck the rock twice with his rod. It was because on this occasion God was not honored that Moses and Aaron were forbidden to enter the Promised Land. Num 20:11-12. But to counterbalance this evil trait there were many good ones. He makes mention of one of these - viz., his meekness. Num 12:3. Besides, he was characterized by disinterestedness, impartiality, faithfulness, and courage. When he had risen superior to the fears which daunted him when he received the divine call, he was unwavering. The people might murmur or break out into rebellion, he was ready to plead with God for them; yea, when they had so grievously sinned that God declared he would destroy them, Moses asked that his name might be blotted out of the book of God rather than behold their destruction. Ex 32:32. In addition must be mentioned his eminent services as lawgiver. It is indeed a vexed question how much credit should be given to him as the publisher of a code marked throughout by "Thus saith the Lord." We are safe in saying that the Law, as we have it recorded in the Scriptures, was divinely inspired, and that Moses made the record as directed of the Lord. The Decalogue is a moral miracle in ancient legislation, and retains its power to this day in all Christian lands. See Law. As an historian Moses also is to be honored. The five books commonly called the Pentateuch, which he wrote, contain the only reliable history of the creation of man and the beginning of the human as well as of the Jewish race. See Pentateuch. But there are also other compositions attributed to him - namely, Ps 90 and the book of Job. In regard to these there is no certainty, but the ninetieth Psalm seems to fit in well with the circumstances of the Wandering, and the book of Job is perhaps his in its first draft; the Talmud makes him the author, and several commentators have adopted this view. See Job. We know Moses to have had the poetic gift, for in the Pentateuch there are several exhibitions of it: "The song which Moses and the children of Israel sung" (after the passage of the Red Sea, Ex 15:1-19). A fragment of a war-song against Amalek, Ex 17:16: A fragment of a lyrical burst of indignation, Ex 32:18: The song of Moses, composed on the east side of Jordan. Deut 32:1-43. The prophetic blessing of Moses upon the tribes. Deut 33:1-29. As a leader and as a prophet Moses comes before us. As the former "his life," says Dean Stanley in Smith's Dictionary of the Bible, "divides itself into the three epochs of the march to Sinai, the march from Sinai to Kadesh, and the conquest of the Transjordanic kingdoms. Of his natural gifts in this capacity we have but few means of judging. The two main difficulties which he encountered were the reluctance of the people to submit to his guidance and the impracticable nature of the country which they had to traverse. The incidents with which his name was specially connected, both in the sacred narrative and in the Jewish, Arabian, and heathen traditions, were those of supplying water when most wanted. In the Pentateuch these supplies of water take place at Marah, at Horeb, at Kadesh, and in the land of Moab. Of the first three of these incidents, traditional sites bearing his name are shown in the desert at the present day, though most of them are rejected by modern travellers. The route through the wilderness is described as having been made under his guidance. The particular spot of the encampment is fixed by the cloudy pillar. But the direction of the people, first to the Red Sea and then to Mount Sinai, is communicated through Moses or given by him. On approaching Palestine the office of the leader becomes blended with that of the general or the conqueror. By Moses the spies were sent to explore the country. Against his advice took place the first disastrous battle at Hormah. To his guidance is ascribed the circuitous route by which the nation approached Palestine from the east, and to his generalship the two successful campaigns in which Sihon and Og were defeated. The narrative is told so shortly that we are in danger of forgetting that at this last stage of his life Moses must have been as much a conqueror and victorious soldier as Joshua." But as a prophet Moses is evidently the revealer of the will of God, and preeminent because with him the divine revelations were made "mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches," and he beheld "the similitude of Jehovah." Num 12:8. He saw the flame in the bush; for two periods of forty days each he was in the thick darkness with God, Ex 24:18; Ex 34:28; and above all was he favored with the vision of the trailing garments of the Almighty, and he heard a voice which "proclaimed the two immutable attributes of God, justice and love," in words which became part of the religious creed of Israel and of the world. Ex 34:6-7. But perhaps the most remarkable fact is yet to be mentioned. Moses frequently met God in the tent of the congregation, which he removed outside the camp.Ex 33:9. No wonder that the subject of so many and so familiar interviews with God should be regarded with peculiar veneration by the Hebrews, the Mohammedans, and the Christians. When Moses was one hundred and twenty years old his eye was not dim nor his natural force abated. Deut 34:7. He was able, on the day of his death, to stand on Nebo, a height of the Pisgah range, and thence look across the Jordan and up and down the Promised Land. Bitter was his disappointment at not being allowed to enter, but meekly he submitted to the will of God. He had been so much with God that to die was simply to be always with Him whose voice he had heard and whose glory he had seen. But since his death would make a great change to his people, he prepared the way for it. He addressed the people and warned them against apostasy. He then gave a public charge to Joshua, his successor. He then uttered the song, Deut 32, and blessed the people. Deut 33. Quietly, it would appear, unattended, perhaps secretly, the aged yet strong man climbed the Pisgah range, stood on the height of Nebo, and viewed the extensive prospect. "As he gazed upon it the words fell upon his ears, 'This is the land which I sware unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob, saying, I will give it unto thy seed; I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes;' and then, not in sternness or in anger, but in utmost love, like a mother lifting her boy into her arms, the Lord added, 'But thou shalt not go over thither,' and in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, the soul of Moses had passed within the veil and was at home with God." - Rev. W. M. Taylor, D.D., Moses the Lawgiver, N.Y., 1879, p. 439. "And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Beth-peor; but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day." Deut 34:6. In the words of the Rabbins, "Jehovah kissed him to death" (or rather into life eternal). His remains were removed from all reach of idolatry - the sin of sins, forbidden in the first commandment. As Thomas Fuller quaintly says, "God buried also his grave." Vainly have men sought to find it. The familiar lines of Mrs. C. F. Alexander's ode, "The Death of Moses," may be appropriately quoted here: Centuries passed on. The land had witnessed many changes; the promised One stood upon the Promised Land when once more Moses is seen by mortal sight. Upon the slopes of Hermon he appeared in company with Elijah to talk with Jesus of the decease Jesus should accomplish at Jerusalem. Luke 9:31. Thus was the type brought face to face with the Pattern. And this resurrection leads to the conclusion which some hold - that Moses, like Christ, was raised from the dead after a brief sleep in the grave. Moses was of God's special preparation, the resultant of many forces. Wrought upon by inspiration, he was able to be legislator, statesman, leader, poet, saint, because he was so variedly trained. An exceptional man in original gifts, he was equally exceptional in his opportunities. To be of Hebrew extraction, and therefore by descent to share in the glorious hopes of his race, was to have a grand start Godward. To be the adopted child of Pharaoh's daughter, to breathe "the atmosphere of courts," to be acquainted as an equal with the nobility of the land, was to gain an intimate knowledge of statecraft from the best exponents of it. To be trained for the priesthood, initiated into the holy mysteries, learned in all the learning of the Egyptians, was to be thoroughly furnished unto religious service. To be exiled and compelled through many years to eat "the bread of carefulness," to be a keeper of sheep and a dweller in tents amid the sublimity of Sinaitic scenery, was to have time for reflection and for communion with God. Thus, when at eighty he returned to Egypt, he was able to debate with scholars and to sympathize with slaves. He towered above all his brethren. He was alone in the loneliness of genius. He was accessible in his feeling for the oppressed. But Moses was unique in other ways. He alone has held friendly converse with Jehovah. What though he was slow of speech? He was lofty of thought. What though he was timid? He had the promise of divine strength. And the good qualities he showed during the Wandering are such as come from fellowship with the Highest, while his bad qualities - his occasional infirmity of temper, for example - are mere spots upon the sun or temporary obscurations of the light, the times he forgot God. But when he fell all observed it, just as all notice the fallen monarch of the forest; when he stood firm few marked it, as few remark the upright tree. The above article is a mere sketch. To write fully the life of Moses would be to write the history of Israel during the Exodus. The reader will refer to the separate articles incidentally mentioned. We close by a brief study of the character of Moses, following the Rev. Dr. W.M. Taylor in his book above quoted. Three qualities give him immortal interest and prominence. 1st. Faith. By faith he esteemed "the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt." Heb 11:26. "Never more alluring prospects opened up before any man than those which the world held out to him. The throne of the greatest monarchy of his age was within his reach. All that wealth could procure, or pleasure bestow, or the greatest earthly power command, was easily at his call. But the glory of these things paled in his view before the more excellent character of those invisible honors which God set before him. This faith sustained him in the solitudes of Midian and animated him amidst all the conflicts attendant on the Exodus and all the difficulties that confronted him in the wilderness. This faith gave him courage in the hour of danger and calmness in the time of trial." (pp. 459, 460.) 2d. Prayerfnlness. "In every time of emergency his immediate resort was to Jehovah. He was not speaking to a stranger, but was like a son making application to his father; and so he never pleaded in vain." (p. 461.) His was the prayer of faith. 3d. Humility. "He coveted no distinction and sought no prominence; his greatness came to him, he did not go after it. And his humility was allied with or flowed naturally out into two other qualities, disinterestedness and meekness. (See Num 11:29 and 1 Chr 12:3 for striking illustrations.) He gave up his own ease and comfort to secure the emancipation of his people; and while laboring night and day for them, he had no thought whatever of his own interests. His office brought him no emolument." In this he was like Nehemiah. He was free from all charge of nepotism. His meekness was shown in silently listening to complaints against himself. He appealed unto God. (pp. 462-3.) The only blot upon this beautiful character is a lack of patience or self-control, but this was more evident in the earlier portion of his life, nor was it prominent enough to belie his eulogy. Moses was a type of Christ. The parallel is readily traced. "As Moses, in the early part of his career, refused the Egyptian monarchy because it could be gained to him only by disloyalty to, God, so Jesus turned away from the kingdoms of the world because they were offered on condition that he would worship Satan; as Moses became the emancipator of his people, so was Jesus; as Moses, penetrating to the soul of the symbolism of idolatry, introduced a new dispensation wherein symbolism was allied to spirituality of worship, so Jesus, seizing the spirituality of the Mosaic system, freed it from its national restrictions, and ushered in the day when the true worshipper would worship the Father anywhere; as Moses was pre-eminently a lawgiver, so Jesus, in his Sermon on the Mount, laid down a code which not only expounds but fulfils the Decalogue; as Moses was a prophet, so Jesus is the great Prophet of his Church; as Moses was a mediator, so Jesus is the Mediator of the new covenant, standing between God and man, and bridging, by his atonement and intercession, the gulf between the two. We cannot wonder, therefore, that in the vision of the Apocalypse they who have gotten the victory over the beast and his image are represented as singing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb. Rev 15:3." (p. 466.) God buried Moses. It was fitting, therefore, that he too should write his epitaph. Here it is given by his inspiration, and, though written only in a book, having a permanence as great as if it had been graven with an iron pen in the rock for ever: "And there arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face, in all the signs and the wonders which the Lord sent him to do in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh, and to all his servants, and to all his land, and in all that mighty land, and in all the great terror which Moses showed in the sight of all Israel." Deut 34:10-12. (p. 468.) Moses, Song of. This wonderful ode celebrates more fitly the miraculous deliverance of the children of Israel from Egyptian bondage. It is the national anthem, the Te Deum of the Hebrews. It sounds through the psalms of Israel, through the thanksgiving hymns of the Christian Church, through the touching songs of liberated slaves, and it will swell the harmony of the saints in heaven. Allusion to it is made in Rev 15:2-3; "They stand on the sea of glass mingled with fire . . . and sing the song of Moses the servant of God."
entries.definition_ko:
모세는 히브리어로 모셰이며 「물에서 건져 냄」을 뜻한다. 곧 물에서 건져 냈다는 말이다. 콥트어로는 모우세니 「물에서 구원받은 이」라는 뜻이다. 그는 유대 민족의 지도자요 그 민족을 세운 이다.

그의 생애는 스데반의 설교에 남아 있는 기록을 따라 저마다 마흔 해씩 세 도막으로 자연스럽게 나뉜다. 사도행전 7장 23절과 30절과 36절이다.

모세는 히브리 사람의 이야기가 어두웠던 때에 태어났으니, 그때에는 사내아이가 애굽 첩자들의 살기 어린 수색의 표적이었다. 그의 아버지는 아므람이요 어머니는 요게벳이며 그의 지파는 레위였는데, 이 사실이 제사장 직분에 레위를 고른 까닭이 되었을지도 모른다. 모세는 집안의 막내였다. 미리암이 맏이였고 아론이 그 사이에 있었다.

그의 부모는 석 달 동안 아기를 숨겼으나 마침내 더는 그럴 수 없게 되었다. 요게벳은 떨리는 마음으로, 그러나 어쩌면 하나님이 그에게 큰일을 마련해 두셨다는 어렴풋한 깨달음으로, 자기가 솜씨 있게 엮어 안팎에 역청을 칠한 작은 갈대 상자에 아기를 뉘었다. 그리고 그것을 나일 강의 어느 물길 가로 가지고 내려가 갈대 사이에 숨겼다. 미리암은 「멀찍이 서서」 아기를 애틋하게 지켜보았으니, 어머니보다 의심을 덜 살 만하였기에 그 아기가 어찌 되는지 보려고 서 있었다.

압제자 바로의 딸이 시녀들을 거느리고 그 거룩한 강에 목욕하러 왔다. 시녀들은 섭리로 공주가 목욕하는 자리까지 떠내려온 그 상자를 보고 놀라 주인에게 그 발견을 알렸다. 아니면 요게벳이 일부러 거기에 두었던 것일까. 시녀 하나가 상자를 가져와 열자, 보아하니 히브리 사람의 아이지만 유난히 잘생긴 어린아이가 드러났다. 전해 오는 말로는 자식이 없는 아내였다는 공주의 여인다운 마음이 그 어린것에게 끌렸다. 그 끌림은 하나님에게서 온 것이었다. 그때 미리암이 가까이 나아가 그 아이의 목숨을 살려 주려 한다는 것을 이야기에서 알아채고, 히브리 여인 가운데서 유모를 구해 오겠다고 하였다. 이리하여 요게벳은 다시 제 아이를 품에 안게 되었으나, 이번에는 삯을 받는 유모로서였다.

이 시기의 성경 역사는 어린 모세가 왕궁에서 스승과 보모의 손에 있으면서 지혜와 키가 자라 가고 하나님과 사람 앞에서 은혜를 더해 가는 것으로 끝난다. 모세보다 크신 이의 이야기가 그러하듯이, 이 이야기에도 어린 시절과 장년 사이에 끊긴 데가 있다.

모세의 생애 둘째 도막은 그 성격이 첫째와 아주 달랐다. 마흔 살의 모세는 애굽 사람의 모든 지혜를 배운 사람이다. 바로의 양손자로서 자기가 속한 제사장 계급의 비밀을 전수받았으니, 그 앞에는 빛나고 쓸모 있는 세상의 앞길이 놓여 있었다. 그가 그 유리한 자리에 머물렀더라면 애굽의 위대한 현자 가운데 하나가, 아마도 그들 모두 가운데 으뜸이 되었을 것이다. 그러나 하나님은 그가 훨씬 더 높은 자리에 서게 하려 하셨다. 그에게는 묵상의 기간이 있어야 했다. 그는 책에서 끊어져야 하였고, 온갖 얼굴을 지닌 자연과 곧바로 부딪혀 책이 줄 수 없는 것을 배워야 하였다.

이 거센 바뀜을 이룬 섭리의 계기는 모세가 히브리 사람을 학대하던 애굽 감독을 죽인 일이었다. 이 일은 그가 바라던 대로 비밀이 되지 못하였다. 소식은 이미 바로에게 이르렀고 그리하여 모세는 달아나야 했다. 아마도 그 죽임은 자기가 그들을 돕고자 한다는 것을, 곧 왕의 아들인 자기가 그들의 구원자가 되리라는 것을 히브리 사람들에게 새겨 주려는 뜻이었을 것이다. 어머니의 경건한 가르침이 잊히지 않았고 형제들의 구원자가 되기로 마음먹으면서 그가 많은 기도를 올렸으리라는 결론을 물리치기는 어려워 보이기 때문이다. 그러나 우리는 이제 이 봉기의 시도가 헛되이 끝난 것도, 또 모세가 저 위대한 출애굽을 제대로 이끌기까지 배울 것이 많았던 것도 이상한 일이 아님을 안다.

모세는 궁정의 두드러짐과 세련됨과 사치를 떠나 광야의 이름 없음과 거칢과 가난으로 달아났다. 그는 이드로의 목자가 되었고 그의 딸 십보라의 남편이 되었다. 출애굽기 2장이다. 이 둘째 시기가 마흔 해 이어졌고, 다시 놀라운 탈바꿈이 일어났다.

그 넘어감은 호렙에서 이루어졌다. 어느 날 그는 「떨기나무」를 보았는데 아마도 아카시아 나무였을 것이며, 불이 붙었는데도 타서 없어지지 않았다고 한다. 그가 그 놀라운 광경을 살피러 가까이 나아가자 여호와의 사자가 그에게 나타나 선지자로 부르셨다. 그러나 마흔 해 전에 지도자가 되려 하던 그 사람이 이제는 핑계로 가득 차서 제 능력을 낮추어 말하고 제 모습을 깎아내렸다. 그리하여 하나님은 아론을 그의 대변자로 세우시고 두 사람이 만나게 하셨다. 출애굽기 3장부터 4장까지다. 이렇게 하나님의 이름을 알고, 출애굽기 3장 14절이다, 하나님의 도우심을 약속받고, 기적으로 힘을 얻어, 출애굽기 4장 1절부터 7절까지다, 여든 살의 모세는 이제 학자이면서 실무에 밝은 사람이 되어 자기 백성을 건져 내는 일에 나선다.

애굽으로 가는 길에 그의 아들 게르솜이 알 수 없는 병에 걸렸다. 십보라는 할례를 행하지 않은 탓이라고 여겼다. 그리하여 내키지 않았으나 그가 손수 게르솜에게 할례를 행하였다. 출애굽기 4장 24절부터 26절까지다. 아이는 나았다.

고센에 이르자 모세와 아론은 곧바로 맡은 사명을 행하기 시작하였다. 그러나 그들의 첫 애씀은 종살이하던 백성의 짐을 더 무겁게 했을 뿐이었고 두 형제는 거의 절망할 지경이었다. 그때 출애굽기 7장부터 12장까지에 적힌 이적의 재앙이 잇달아 시작되었다. 마지막 재앙이 애굽 사람들을 어찌나 얼떨떨하게 만들었던지 그들은 이스라엘 사람들을 서둘러 내쫓았다. 「재앙」 항목과 「출애굽」 항목 참조.

이스라엘 사람들은 채비를 갖추고 길을 떠날 준비가 되어 있었다. 그러나 그 길은 광야로 사흘 걸리는 길이 아니라, 출애굽기 5장 3절이다, 마흔 해의 길이었다. 이 오랜 세월 내내 이스라엘 사람들은 이적으로 지켜지고 먹여지고 인도되었다. 모세는 하나님이 흡족해하시도록 그들 앞에서 드나들었으나 그의 행실이 모든 사람을 기쁘게 한 것은 결코 아니었다.

모세가 늘 자기를 제대로 다스린 것도 아니다. 그가 마흔 날 동안 산에서 하나님과 함께 있는 사이에 경박한 백성이 우상을 섬긴 일에 노하여, 하나님이 손수 새기신 율법의 돌판을 내던졌다. 출애굽기 32장 19절이다. 그러나 이런 종류의 일 가운데 가장 해로웠던 것은 가데스 므리바에서였다. 백성이 물을 달라고 원망하였다. 모세는 반석에게 말하라는 명을 받았으나, 그러지 않고 지팡이로 반석을 두 번 쳤다. 이때에 하나님이 영광을 받지 못하셨기에 모세와 아론은 약속의 땅에 들어가는 것이 금지되었다. 민수기 20장 11절부터 12절까지다.

그러나 이 나쁜 성품을 맞받아 좋은 성품이 많았다. 그 가운데 하나를 그가 몸소 말하고 있으니 곧 그의 온유함이다. 민수기 12장 3절이다. 그 밖에도 그는 사심 없음과 공평함과 신실함과 담대함으로 특징지어진다. 하나님의 부르심을 받을 때 그를 주눅 들게 하던 두려움을 이겨 낸 뒤로 그는 흔들리지 않았다. 백성이 원망하거나 반역으로 터져 나와도 그는 그들을 위하여 하나님께 간구할 준비가 되어 있었다. 그뿐 아니라 그들이 너무나 무겁게 죄를 지어 하나님이 그들을 멸하시겠다고 하셨을 때, 모세는 그들이 멸망하는 것을 보느니 차라리 자기 이름을 하나님의 책에서 지워 달라고 아뢰었다. 출애굽기 32장 32절이다.

여기에 율법을 준 이로서 그가 남긴 뛰어난 공로를 덧붙여야 한다. 처음부터 끝까지 「여호와께서 이같이 말씀하시니라」로 새겨진 법전을 펴낸 이로서 그에게 얼마나 공을 돌려야 하는지는 참으로 골치 아픈 문제다. 다만 우리는 성경에 적힌 그대로의 율법이 하나님의 영감으로 되었으며, 모세가 여호와의 지시를 따라 그것을 적었다고 말하여도 안전하다. 십계명은 옛 입법 가운데 도덕의 기적이며, 오늘까지 모든 기독교 나라에서 그 힘을 지니고 있다. 「율법」 항목 참조.

역사가로서도 모세는 높임을 받아 마땅하다. 그가 쓴 오경이라 흔히 불리는 다섯 책은 사람이 창조된 일과 인류가 시작된 일, 그리고 유대 민족이 시작된 일에 대한 오직 하나뿐인 믿을 만한 역사를 담고 있다. 「오경」 항목 참조.

그러나 그에게 돌려지는 다른 글도 있으니 곧 시편 90편과 욥기다. 이에 대하여는 확실한 것이 없으나, 시편 90편은 광야 유랑의 형편에 잘 들어맞아 보이고, 욥기는 그 첫 초고가 어쩌면 그의 것일지도 모른다. 탈무드는 그를 저자로 삼으며 여러 주석가가 이 견해를 받아들였다. 「욥기」 항목 참조.

모세가 시를 짓는 재능을 지녔음을 우리는 안다. 오경 안에 그것이 여러 번 드러나기 때문이다. 홍해를 건넌 뒤에 「모세와 이스라엘 자손이 부른 노래」가 있으니 출애굽기 15장 1절부터 19절까지다. 아말렉을 치는 전쟁 노래의 한 조각이 출애굽기 17장 16절에 있다. 분노가 서정으로 터져 나온 한 조각이 출애굽기 32장 18절에 있다. 요단 동편에서 지은 모세의 노래가 신명기 32장 1절부터 43절까지에 있다. 여러 지파에게 준 모세의 예언적인 축복이 신명기 33장 1절부터 29절까지에 있다.

모세는 지도자로서 또 선지자로서 우리 앞에 나온다. 앞엣것에 대하여 스탠리 수석 사제는 스미스의 「성경 사전」에서 이렇게 말한다. 「그의 생애는 시내 산으로 나아간 행군과, 시내 산에서 가데스까지의 행군과, 요단 동편 왕국들을 정복한 일이라는 세 시기로 나뉜다. 이 자격에서 그가 타고난 재능을 헤아릴 길은 얼마 되지 않는다. 그가 부딪힌 두 가지 큰 어려움은 백성이 그의 인도에 따르기를 꺼린 것과…

그들이 지나가야 할 땅의 지나기 어려운 성질이었다. 성경 기록에서나 유대와 아라비아와 이방의 전승에서나 그의 이름과 특별히 얽힌 일들은 가장 아쉬울 때에 물을 얻게 한 일이었다. 오경에서 이렇게 물을 얻은 일은 마라와 호렙과 가데스와 모압 땅에서 일어난다. 이 가운데 앞의 셋에 대하여는 그의 이름을 딴 자리가 오늘도 광야에 전해져 보여지지만, 대부분은 오늘의 여행자들이 인정하지 않는다. 광야를 지나는 길은 그의 인도 아래 정해진 것으로 적혀 있다. 진 칠 자리를 정하는 것은 구름 기둥이다. 그러나 백성을 처음에는 홍해로, 그다음에는 시내 산으로 이끄는 지시는 모세를 통하여 전해지거나 그가 내린다. 팔레스타인에 가까워지면서 지도자의 직분은 장군 곧 정복자의 직분과 하나로 섞인다. 모세가 정탐꾼을 보내어 그 땅을 살피게 하였다. 호르마에서의 첫 참패한 싸움은 그의 뜻을 거슬러 일어났다. 이 민족이 동쪽에서 팔레스타인에 다가가도록 에움길로 이끈 것도 그의 인도로 여겨지며, 시혼과 옥을 무찌른 두 번의 성공한 싸움도 그의 장수다움으로 여겨진다. 이야기가 너무 짧게 전해지는 탓에 우리는 그의 생애 이 마지막 대목에서 모세가 여호수아 못지않은 정복자요 이긴 군인이었음을 잊을 위험이 있다.」

그러나 선지자로서 모세는 뚜렷이 하나님의 뜻을 드러내는 이다. 그가 으뜸가는 것은 하나님의 계시가 그에게 「대면하여 명백히 말하고 은밀한 말로 하지 아니하며」 이루어졌고 그가 「여호와의 형상을」 보았기 때문이다. 민수기 12장 8절이다. 그는 떨기나무의 불꽃을 보았다. 저마다 마흔 날씩 두 차례 그는 하나님과 함께 짙은 어둠 속에 있었으니 출애굽기 24장 18절과 출애굽기 34장 28절이다. 무엇보다 그는 전능하신 이의 드리운 옷자락을 보는 환상을 입었고, 「하나님의 변치 않는 두 성품 곧 공의와 사랑을 선포하는」 음성을 들었으니, 그 말씀은 이스라엘과 온 세상의 신앙 고백의 한 부분이 되었다. 출애굽기 34장 6절부터 7절까지다.

그러나 어쩌면 가장 놀라운 사실은 아직 말하지 않았다. 모세는 진 밖으로 옮겨 놓은 회막에서 자주 하나님을 만났다. 출애굽기 33장 9절이다. 하나님과 이토록 여러 번, 이토록 가깝게 마주한 이가 히브리 사람과 이슬람교도와 그리스도인에게 남다른 존경을 받는 것은 이상한 일이 아니다.

모세가 백스무 살이 되었을 때에도 그의 눈이 흐리지 아니하였고 기력이 쇠하지 아니하였다. 신명기 34장 7절이다. 그는 죽는 날에도 비스가 산줄기의 한 봉우리인 느보에 설 수 있었고, 거기서 요단 건너편을 바라보며 약속의 땅을 위아래로 볼 수 있었다. 들어가지 못하게 된 것이 그에게 쓰라린 실망이었으나 그는 온유하게 하나님의 뜻에 순복하였다. 그는 하나님과 너무나 오래 함께 있었기에, 죽는다는 것은 그저 그 음성을 듣고 그 영광을 본 그분과 언제나 함께 있게 되는 일일 뿐이었다.

그러나 그의 죽음이 자기 백성에게 큰 변화를 가져올 것이므로 그는 그 길을 미리 닦았다. 그는 백성에게 말하며 배교하지 말라고 경고하였다. 그런 뒤에 자기 뒤를 이을 여호수아에게 공개로 명하였다. 그런 뒤에 노래를 읊었으니 신명기 32장이요, 백성을 축복하였으니 신명기 33장이다. 조용히, 보아하니 아무도 따르지 않은 채, 어쩌면 남몰래, 늙었으나 여전히 튼튼한 그 사람이 비스가 산줄기를 올라 느보 봉우리에 서서 너른 경치를 바라보았다.

「그가 그것을 바라볼 때에 이런 말씀이 그의 귀에 떨어졌다. '이는 내가 아브라함과 이삭과 야곱에게 맹세하여 그의 후손에게 주리라 한 땅이라 내가 네 눈으로 보게 하였거니와.' 그런 뒤에 엄하게도 노여워하지도 않으시고, 어머니가 아들을 두 팔로 들어 올리듯 지극한 사랑으로 여호와께서 덧붙이셨다. '너는 그리로 건너가지 못하리라.' 그리고 한순간에, 눈 깜짝할 사이에 모세의 영혼은 휘장 안으로 들어가 하나님과 함께 본향에 있었다.」 — 테일러 목사, 「율법을 준 이 모세」, 1879년 뉴욕, 439쪽.

「벳브올 맞은편 모압 땅에 있는 골짜기에 장사되었고 오늘까지 그의 묻힌 곳을 아는 자가 없느니라.」 신명기 34장 6절이다. 랍비들의 말로는 「여호와께서 그에게 입 맞추어 죽게 하셨다.」 아니 오히려 영원한 생명 속으로 들어가게 하셨다. 그의 주검은 우상 숭배가 미칠 수 없는 곳으로 옮겨졌으니, 우상 숭배는 첫째 계명이 금한 죄 중의 죄다. 토머스 풀러가 재치 있게 말한 대로 「하나님은 그의 무덤까지 묻으셨다.」 사람들이 그것을 찾으려 하였으나 헛되었다. 알렉산더 부인의 송가 「모세의 죽음」에 나오는 잘 알려진 시구를 여기에 옮기는 것이 알맞을 것이다.

여러 세기가 흘렀다. 그 땅은 많은 변화를 겪었다. 약속된 이가 약속의 땅에 서 계실 때에 다시 한번 모세가 사람의 눈에 보였다. 그는 헤르몬 산 비탈에서 엘리야와 함께 나타나, 예수께서 예루살렘에서 이루실 별세에 대하여 예수와 이야기하였다. 누가복음 9장 31절이다. 이렇게 예표가 본체와 얼굴을 마주하였다. 그리고 이 다시 살아남은 어떤 이들이 붙드는 결론으로 이끄니, 곧 모세도 그리스도처럼 무덤에서 잠깐 잠든 뒤에 죽은 자 가운데서 일으켜졌다는 것이다.

모세는 하나님이 특별히 준비하신 사람이었고 여러 힘이 어우러진 열매였다. 영감의 감화를 받아 그는 입법자요 정치가요 지도자요 시인이요 성도가 될 수 있었으니, 그토록 다채롭게 훈련받았기 때문이다. 타고난 재능에서 남다른 사람이었던 그는 그 기회에서도 똑같이 남달랐다. 히브리 혈통으로 나서 혈통에 따라 제 민족의 영광스러운 소망에 함께하게 된 것은 하나님을 향하여 훌륭한 출발을 한 것이었다. 바로의 딸의 양자가 되어 「궁정의 공기」를 숨 쉬고 그 나라 귀족들과 대등하게 사귄 것은 나라를 다스리는 기술을 그것을 가장 잘 아는 이들에게서 속속들이 배운 것이었다. 제사장이 되도록 훈련받아 거룩한 비밀을 전수받고 애굽 사람의 모든 학문을 배운 것은 종교의 섬김을 위하여 온전히 갖추어진 것이었다. 쫓겨나 여러 해 동안 「근심의 떡」을 먹어야 하였고, 시내 산 언저리의 웅장한 경치 가운데서 양을 치며 장막에 사는 이가 된 것은 깊이 생각하고 하나님과 사귈 시간을 얻은 것이었다.

그리하여 여든 살에 애굽으로 돌아왔을 때 그는 학자들과 논할 수도 있었고 종들과 마음을 함께할 수도 있었다. 그는 모든 형제 위에 우뚝 솟았다. 그는 천재의 외로움 속에 홀로 있었다. 그러면서도 눌린 자를 향한 마음에서는 다가가기 쉬운 사람이었다.

그러나 모세는 다른 면에서도 견줄 데가 없었다. 그만이 여호와와 벗처럼 이야기를 나누었다. 그가 말이 어눌하였던들 어떠하랴. 그의 생각은 드높았다. 그가 겁이 많았던들 어떠하랴. 그에게는 하나님이 힘 주시겠다는 약속이 있었다. 광야 유랑 동안 그가 보인 좋은 성품은 지극히 높으신 이와 사귀는 데서 오는 것이요, 그의 나쁜 성품은 이를테면 이따금 성을 다스리지 못한 것인데 해에 앉은 티끌이나 잠깐 빛이 가리는 것에 지나지 않으니 곧 그가 하나님을 잊은 때다. 그러나 그가 넘어지면 모두가 그것을 보았으니, 숲의 왕이 쓰러지면 누구나 알아보는 것과 같다. 그가 굳게 서 있을 때에는 알아보는 이가 적었으니, 곧게 선 나무를 눈여겨보는 이가 적은 것과 같다.

위의 글은 그저 밑그림일 뿐이다. 모세의 생애를 온전히 쓰려면 출애굽 동안의 이스라엘 역사를 써야 할 것이다. 읽는 이는 지나가며 말한 낱낱의 항목을 찾아보기 바란다. 앞에서 인용한 책에 실린 테일러 박사를 따라 모세의 성품을 짧게 살피며 마친다. 세 가지 성품이 그에게 길이 남을 흥미와 두드러짐을 준다.

첫째는 믿음이다. 믿음으로 그는 「그리스도를 위하여 받는 수모를 애굽의 모든 보화보다 더 큰 재물로」 여겼다. 히브리서 11장 26절이다. 「세상이 그에게 내민 것보다 더 매혹적인 앞길이 어떤 사람 앞에도 열린 적이 없다. 그 시대 가장 큰 왕국의 왕좌가 그의 손이 닿는 데 있었다. 재물이 살 수 있는 것, 쾌락이 줄 수 있는 것, 이 땅의 가장 큰 권력이 부릴 수 있는 것이 모두 손쉽게 그의 부름에 닿아 있었다. 그러나 그의 눈에는 이런 것들의 영광이, 하나님이 그 앞에 두신 보이지 않는 영예의 더 뛰어난 성질 앞에서 빛을 잃었다. 이 믿음이 미디안의 외로움 가운데 그를 붙들었고, 출애굽에 따르는 모든 다툼과 광야에서 마주한 모든 어려움 가운데 그를 북돋웠다. 이 믿음이 위험한 때에 그에게 용기를 주었고 시련의 때에 평온을 주었다.」 459쪽부터 460쪽까지다.

둘째는 기도에 힘씀이다. 「위급할 때마다 그가 곧바로 찾은 곳은 여호와였다. 그는 낯선 이에게 말하는 것이 아니라 아들이 아버지께 아뢰는 것과 같았다. 그리하여 그의 간구는 결코 헛되지 않았다.」 461쪽이다. 그의 기도는 믿음의 기도였다.

셋째는 겸손이다. 「그는 어떤 영예도 탐하지 않았고 어떤 두드러짐도 구하지 않았다. 그의 위대함이 그에게 온 것이지 그가 그것을 좇아간 것이 아니다. 그리고 그의 겸손은 다른 두 성품과 이어졌으니 곧 사심 없음과 온유함으로 자연스럽게 흘러나왔다. 두드러진 보기로 민수기 11장 29절과 12장 3절을 보라. 그는 제 백성이 놓여나게 하려고 제 편안함과 안락을 버렸다. 그리고 밤낮으로 그들을 위하여 애쓰면서도 제 이익은 조금도 생각하지 않았다. 그의 직분은 그에게 아무 삯도 가져다주지 않았다.」 이 점에서 그는 느헤미야와 같았다. 그는 친족을 끌어들였다는 어떤 나무람에서도 자유로웠다. 그의 온유함은 자기를 향한 원망을 잠잠히 듣는 데서 드러났다. 그는 하나님께 아뢰었다. 462쪽부터 463쪽까지다.

이 아름다운 성품에 남은 오직 하나의 흠은 참을성 곧 자기를 다스리는 힘이 모자란 것이나, 이는 그의 생애 앞부분에서 더 뚜렷하였고 그를 기리는 말을 뒤집을 만큼 두드러지지도 않았다.

모세는 그리스도의 예표였다. 그 견줌은 쉽게 짚어진다. 「모세가 그 생애 앞부분에서 애굽의 왕권을 물리쳤으니 그것이 하나님께 신실하지 않아야만 얻을 수 있는 것이었기 때문이다. 그처럼 예수께서도 세상 나라들에서 돌아서셨으니 그것이 사탄에게 절해야 한다는 조건으로 주어졌기 때문이다. 모세가 제 백성을 놓여나게 한 이가 되었듯이 예수께서도 그러하셨다. 모세가 우상 숭배의 상징이 지닌 속뜻을 꿰뚫어 보고 상징이 예배의 영성과 이어지는 새 경륜을 들여왔듯이, 예수께서도 모세 체계의 영성을 붙잡아 그것을 한 민족의 울타리에서 풀어내시고, 참으로 예배하는 자가 어디서든 아버지께 예배할 날을 여셨다. 모세가 무엇보다 율법을 준 이였듯이 예수께서도 산상 설교에서 십계명을 풀이할 뿐 아니라 이루는 법전을 내놓으셨다. 모세가 선지자였듯이 예수께서도 그 교회의 위대한 선지자시다. 모세가 중보자였듯이 예수께서도 새 언약의 중보자로서 하나님과 사람 사이에 서시고 그 속죄와 중보로 둘 사이의 구렁을 이으신다. 그러므로 요한계시록의 환상에서 짐승과 그 우상을 이긴 자들이 하나님의 종 모세의 노래와 어린양의 노래를 부르는 것으로 그려지는 것이 이상하지 않다. 요한계시록 15장 3절이다.」 466쪽이다.

하나님이 모세를 묻으셨다. 그러므로 그의 묘비명도 하나님이 쓰시는 것이 마땅하였다. 여기 그의 영감으로 주어진 것이 있으니, 책에만 쓰였을 뿐이나 쇠 철필로 바위에 영원히 새긴 것과 같은 든든함을 지녔다. 「그 후에는 이스라엘에 모세와 같은 선지자가 일어나지 못하였나니 모세는 여호와께서 대면하여 아시던 자요 여호와께서 그를 애굽 땅에 보내사 바로와 그의 모든 신하와 그의 온 땅에 모든 이적과 기사와 모든 큰 권능과 위엄을 행하게 하시매 온 이스라엘의 목전에서 그것을 행한 자이더라.」 신명기 34장 10절부터 12절까지다. 468쪽이다.

모세의 노래. 이 놀라운 송가는 이스라엘 자손이 애굽의 종살이에서 이적으로 건짐받은 일을 더없이 알맞게 기린다. 그것은 히브리 사람의 나라 노래요 찬미의 노래다. 그것은 이스라엘의 시편을 통하여, 기독교 교회의 감사 찬송을 통하여, 놓여난 종들의 가슴 저미는 노래를 통하여 울려 퍼지며, 하늘에서 성도들의 화음을 드높일 것이다. 이를 요한계시록 15장 2절부터 3절까지에서 넌지시 가리킨다. 「불이 섞인 유리 바다 위에 서서 …… 하나님의 종 모세의 노래를 부른다.」

「※ 원문 오류: 스데반의 설교를 가리키는 영문 인용이 「Acts 7:23, 1 Kgs 20:30, Eze 23:36」으로 되어 있으나, 본디 「사도행전 7장 23절, 30절, 36절」이다. 마흔 해씩 세 도막을 말하는 대목이므로 세 절이 모두 사도행전 7장에 있어야 하며, 열왕기상과 에스겔은 CCEL 디지털화 과정에서 벌거벗은 숫자에 가짜 주소가 붙은 것이다. 한글은 바로잡아 옮겼다.」

「※ 원문 오류: 온유함의 보기로 든 영문 인용이 「Num 11:29 and 1 Chr 12:3」으로 되어 있으나, 본디 「민수기 11장 29절과 12장 3절」이다. 온유함의 근거 구절은 민수기 12장 3절이며, 역대상 12장 3절은 다윗의 용사 명단이어서 문맥과 맞지 않는다. 앞의 인용에서 이어지는 장 번호에 가짜 책 이름이 붙은 것이다. 한글은 바로잡아 옮겼다.」

「※ 원문 결함: 알렉산더 부인의 송가 「모세의 죽음」을 여기에 옮긴다고 해 놓고 정작 그 시구가 영문 원문에 빠져 있다. 디지털화 과정에서 인용된 시가 통째로 떨어져 나간 것으로 보인다.」

variants.definition: MOS'ES (Heb. Mosheh, *drawn out - i.e. of the water; Coptic Mo-use, watersaved), the leader and creator of the Jewish nation. This table shows the pedigree of Moses: His life falls naturally into three divisions, of forty years each, according to the account preserved in Stephen's speech. Acts 7:23, 1 Kgs 20:30, Eze 23:36. Moses was born in the dark hour of Hebrew story when a son was an object of the murderous search of the Egyptian spies. His father was Amram, his mother Jochebed, his tribe was Levi, and this fact may have determined the choice of Levi for the priesthood. Moses was the youngest child of the family; Miriam was the oldest, and Aaron came between. For three months his parents hid the babe, but at last it was no longer possible, and Jochebed, with a trembling heart, but it may be with a dim consciousness that God had great things in store for him, laid him in the little basket of papyrus she had deftly woven, pitched with bitumen within and without, and, carrying it down to the brink of one of the canals of the Nile, she hid it among the flags. The child was tenderly watched "afar off" by Miriam, who, less open to suspicion than the mother would be, stood to see what would be done to him. The daughter of the Pharaoh, the oppressor, came to the sacred river to bathe, attended by her maidens, who, surprised to find the basket, which had providentially floated down to the princess' bathing-place - or had Jochebed purposely put it there? - call the attention of their mistress to the discovery. The basket is fetched by one of them, and when opened a little babe, evidently one of the Hebrews' children, but exceedingly fair, is revealed to view. The woman-heart of the princess, who was a childless wife according to tradition, yearned over the little one. Her yearning was of God. Then Miriam drew near, gathered from the conversation that the child's life was to be spared, proposed to get a nurse for him among the Hebrew women, and thus it came to pass that Jochebed again had her child at her breast, but this time as his hired nurse. The biblical history of this period closes with the child Moses in the palace under tutors and governors, and increasing in wisdom and in stature, and in the favor of God and of man. There is a break in this history, as in that of the greater than Moses, between the infancy and the manhood. The second division of Moses' life was totally different in its character from the first. Moses, at the age of forty, is learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. The adopted grandson of the Pharaoh, initiated in the secrets of the priests, to whose order he belonged, he had a brilliant and useful worldly career before him. Had he remained in his advantageous surroundings, he would have been one of the great Egyptian sages - probably the greatest of them all. But God intended him to occupy a much more exalted position. There was needed by him a period of meditation. He must be cut off from books, and by direct contact with Nature in all her moods learn what books cannot give. The providential occasion of this violent change was Moses' slaying of an Egyptian taskmaster who had ill-treated a Hebrew. This was no secret, as he hoped it would be. The news, indeed, had been carried to Pharaoh, and so Moses was compelled to flee. It is probable that the murder was intended to impress upon the Hebrews his desire to help them - that he, the king's son, would be their deliverer; for it seems impossible to resist the conclusion that the pious teachings of his mother had not been forgotten, and that many prayers had been put up by him as he determined to be his brethren's saviour. But we see now that it was no wonder that this attempt at an insurrection proved abortive, and likewise that Moses had much to learn before he could properly lead the great Exodus. Moses fled from the prominence, the refinement, and the luxury of the court to the obscurity, the roughness, and the poverty of the wilderness. He became the shepherd of Jethro and the husband of his daughter Zipporah. Ex 2. This second period lasted forty years, and again a wondrous transformation took place. The transition was made at Horeb when one day he saw a "bush" - probably an acacia tree - which was said to be on fire and yet was unconsumed. He drew near to examine the wondrous sight, and the Angel of the Lord appeared to him and gave him his prophetic call. But now the would-be leader of forty years agone was full of excuses, deprecated his abilities, and disparaged his appearance. Accordingly, God appointed Aaron as his spokesman and brought about their meeting. Ex 3-4. Thus informed of the divine name, Ex 3:14, promised divine aid, and strengthened by miracles, Ex 4:1-7, Moses, at the age of eighty, now both a scholar and a practical man of affairs, starts out upon the deliverance of his people. On his way to Egypt his son Gershom was smitten by a mysterious illness, Zipporah thought because circumcision had not been performed. Accordingly, although loath to do it, she herself circumcised Gershom. Ex 4:24-26. The child recovered. Arrived at Goshen, Moses and Aaron at once began the discharge of their commission. But their primary efforts only increased the subject people's burdens, and the two brothers were well nigh in despair. Then began the series of miraculous visitations recounted in Ex 7-12. The last of the plagues so stunned the Egyptians that they precipitately drove the Israelites out. See Plagues, Exodus. The Israelites were prepared and went ready for the journey, which, instead of being one of three days into the desert, Ex 5:3, was one of forty years. Through all this time the Israelites were miraculously protected, fed, and led. Moses went in and out before them to the divine satisfaction, although his conduct by no means pleased every one. Nor had Moses always the proper control over himself. He flung down the God-engraven tables of the Law, enraged at the idolatry of the frivolous people while he was for forty days in the Mount with God. Ex 32:19. But the most damaging act of this nature was at Kadesh-meribah. The people murmured for water. Moses was commanded to speak to the rock; instead, he struck the rock twice with his rod. It was because on this occasion God was not honored that Moses and Aaron were forbidden to enter the Promised Land. Num 20:11-12. But to counterbalance this evil trait there were many good ones. He makes mention of one of these - viz., his meekness. Num 12:3. Besides, he was characterized by disinterestedness, impartiality, faithfulness, and courage. When he had risen superior to the fears which daunted him when he received the divine call, he was unwavering. The people might murmur or break out into rebellion, he was ready to plead with God for them; yea, when they had so grievously sinned that God declared he would destroy them, Moses asked that his name might be blotted out of the book of God rather than behold their destruction. Ex 32:32. In addition must be mentioned his eminent services as lawgiver. It is indeed a vexed question how much credit should be given to him as the publisher of a code marked throughout by "Thus saith the Lord." We are safe in saying that the Law, as we have it recorded in the Scriptures, was divinely inspired, and that Moses made the record as directed of the Lord. The Decalogue is a moral miracle in ancient legislation, and retains its power to this day in all Christian lands. See Law. As an historian Moses also is to be honored. The five books commonly called the Pentateuch, which he wrote, contain the only reliable history of the creation of man and the beginning of the human as well as of the Jewish race. See Pentateuch. But there are also other compositions attributed to him - namely, Ps 90 and the book of Job. In regard to these there is no certainty, but the ninetieth Psalm seems to fit in well with the circumstances of the Wandering, and the book of Job is perhaps his in its first draft; the Talmud makes him the author, and several commentators have adopted this view. See Job. We know Moses to have had the poetic gift, for in the Pentateuch there are several exhibitions of it: "The song which Moses and the children of Israel sung" (after the passage of the Red Sea, Ex 15:1-19). A fragment of a war-song against Amalek, Ex 17:16: A fragment of a lyrical burst of indignation, Ex 32:18: The song of Moses, composed on the east side of Jordan. Deut 32:1-43. The prophetic blessing of Moses upon the tribes. Deut 33:1-29. As a leader and as a prophet Moses comes before us. As the former "his life," says Dean Stanley in Smith's Dictionary of the Bible, "divides itself into the three epochs of the march to Sinai, the march from Sinai to Kadesh, and the conquest of the Transjordanic kingdoms. Of his natural gifts in this capacity we have but few means of judging. The two main difficulties which he encountered were the reluctance of the people to submit to his guidance and the impracticable nature of the country which they had to traverse. The incidents with which his name was specially connected, both in the sacred narrative and in the Jewish, Arabian, and heathen traditions, were those of supplying water when most wanted. In the Pentateuch these supplies of water take place at Marah, at Horeb, at Kadesh, and in the land of Moab. Of the first three of these incidents, traditional sites bearing his name are shown in the desert at the present day, though most of them are rejected by modern travellers. The route through the wilderness is described as having been made under his guidance. The particular spot of the encampment is fixed by the cloudy pillar. But the direction of the people, first to the Red Sea and then to Mount Sinai, is communicated through Moses or given by him. On approaching Palestine the office of the leader becomes blended with that of the general or the conqueror. By Moses the spies were sent to explore the country. Against his advice took place the first disastrous battle at Hormah. To his guidance is ascribed the circuitous route by which the nation approached Palestine from the east, and to his generalship the two successful campaigns in which Sihon and Og were defeated. The narrative is told so shortly that we are in danger of forgetting that at this last stage of his life Moses must have been as much a conqueror and victorious soldier as Joshua." But as a prophet Moses is evidently the revealer of the will of God, and preeminent because with him the divine revelations were made "mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches," and he beheld "the similitude of Jehovah." Num 12:8. He saw the flame in the bush; for two periods of forty days each he was in the thick darkness with God, Ex 24:18; Ex 34:28; and above all was he favored with the vision of the trailing garments of the Almighty, and he heard a voice which "proclaimed the two immutable attributes of God, justice and love," in words which became part of the religious creed of Israel and of the world. Ex 34:6-7. But perhaps the most remarkable fact is yet to be mentioned. Moses frequently met God in the tent of the congregation, which he removed outside the camp.Ex 33:9. No wonder that the subject of so many and so familiar interviews with God should be regarded with peculiar veneration by the Hebrews, the Mohammedans, and the Christians. When Moses was one hundred and twenty years old his eye was not dim nor his natural force abated. Deut 34:7. He was able, on the day of his death, to stand on Nebo, a height of the Pisgah range, and thence look across the Jordan and up and down the Promised Land. Bitter was his disappointment at not being allowed to enter, but meekly he submitted to the will of God. He had been so much with God that to die was simply to be always with Him whose voice he had heard and whose glory he had seen. But since his death would make a great change to his people, he prepared the way for it. He addressed the people and warned them against apostasy. He then gave a public charge to Joshua, his successor. He then uttered the song, Deut 32, and blessed the people. Deut 33. Quietly, it would appear, unattended, perhaps secretly, the aged yet strong man climbed the Pisgah range, stood on the height of Nebo, and viewed the extensive prospect. "As he gazed upon it the words fell upon his ears, 'This is the land which I sware unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob, saying, I will give it unto thy seed; I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes;' and then, not in sternness or in anger, but in utmost love, like a mother lifting her boy into her arms, the Lord added, 'But thou shalt not go over thither,' and in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, the soul of Moses had passed within the veil and was at home with God." - Rev. W. M. Taylor, D.D., Moses the Lawgiver, N.Y., 1879, p. 439. "And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Beth-peor; but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day." Deut 34:6. In the words of the Rabbins, "Jehovah kissed him to death" (or rather into life eternal). His remains were removed from all reach of idolatry - the sin of sins, forbidden in the first commandment. As Thomas Fuller quaintly says, "God buried also his grave." Vainly have men sought to find it. The familiar lines of Mrs. C. F. Alexander's ode, "The Death of Moses," may be appropriately quoted here: Centuries passed on. The land had witnessed many changes; the promised One stood upon the Promised Land when once more Moses is seen by mortal sight. Upon the slopes of Hermon he appeared in company with Elijah to talk with Jesus of the decease Jesus should accomplish at Jerusalem. Luke 9:31. Thus was the type brought face to face with the Pattern. And this resurrection leads to the conclusion which some hold - that Moses, like Christ, was raised from the dead after a brief sleep in the grave. Moses was of God's special preparation, the resultant of many forces. Wrought upon by inspiration, he was able to be legislator, statesman, leader, poet, saint, because he was so variedly trained. An exceptional man in original gifts, he was equally exceptional in his opportunities. To be of Hebrew extraction, and therefore by descent to share in the glorious hopes of his race, was to have a grand start Godward. To be the adopted child of Pharaoh's daughter, to breathe "the atmosphere of courts," to be acquainted as an equal with the nobility of the land, was to gain an intimate knowledge of statecraft from the best exponents of it. To be trained for the priesthood, initiated into the holy mysteries, learned in all the learning of the Egyptians, was to be thoroughly furnished unto religious service. To be exiled and compelled through many years to eat "the bread of carefulness," to be a keeper of sheep and a dweller in tents amid the sublimity of Sinaitic scenery, was to have time for reflection and for communion with God. Thus, when at eighty he returned to Egypt, he was able to debate with scholars and to sympathize with slaves. He towered above all his brethren. He was alone in the loneliness of genius. He was accessible in his feeling for the oppressed. But Moses was unique in other ways. He alone has held friendly converse with Jehovah. What though he was slow of speech? He was lofty of thought. What though he was timid? He had the promise of divine strength. And the good qualities he showed during the Wandering are such as come from fellowship with the Highest, while his bad qualities - his occasional infirmity of temper, for example - are mere spots upon the sun or temporary obscurations of the light, the times he forgot God. But when he fell all observed it, just as all notice the fallen monarch of the forest; when he stood firm few marked it, as few remark the upright tree. The above article is a mere sketch. To write fully the life of Moses would be to write the history of Israel during the Exodus. The reader will refer to the separate articles incidentally mentioned. We close by a brief study of the character of Moses, following the Rev. Dr. W.M. Taylor in his book above quoted. Three qualities give him immortal interest and prominence. 1st. Faith. By faith he esteemed "the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt." Heb 11:26. "Never more alluring prospects opened up before any man than those which the world held out to him. The throne of the greatest monarchy of his age was within his reach. All that wealth could procure, or pleasure bestow, or the greatest earthly power command, was easily at his call. But the glory of these things paled in his view before the more excellent character of those invisible honors which God set before him. This faith sustained him in the solitudes of Midian and animated him amidst all the conflicts attendant on the Exodus and all the difficulties that confronted him in the wilderness. This faith gave him courage in the hour of danger and calmness in the time of trial." (pp. 459, 460.) 2d. Prayerfnlness. "In every time of emergency his immediate resort was to Jehovah. He was not speaking to a stranger, but was like a son making application to his father; and so he never pleaded in vain." (p. 461.) His was the prayer of faith. 3d. Humility. "He coveted no distinction and sought no prominence; his greatness came to him, he did not go after it. And his humility was allied with or flowed naturally out into two other qualities, disinterestedness and meekness. (See Num 11:29 and 1 Chr 12:3 for striking illustrations.) He gave up his own ease and comfort to secure the emancipation of his people; and while laboring night and day for them, he had no thought whatever of his own interests. His office brought him no emolument." In this he was like Nehemiah. He was free from all charge of nepotism. His meekness was shown in silently listening to complaints against himself. He appealed unto God. (pp. 462-3.) The only blot upon this beautiful character is a lack of patience or self-control, but this was more evident in the earlier portion of his life, nor was it prominent enough to belie his eulogy. Moses was a type of Christ. The parallel is readily traced. "As Moses, in the early part of his career, refused the Egyptian monarchy because it could be gained to him only by disloyalty to, God, so Jesus turned away from the kingdoms of the world because they were offered on condition that he would worship Satan; as Moses became the emancipator of his people, so was Jesus; as Moses, penetrating to the soul of the symbolism of idolatry, introduced a new dispensation wherein symbolism was allied to spirituality of worship, so Jesus, seizing the spirituality of the Mosaic system, freed it from its national restrictions, and ushered in the day when the true worshipper would worship the Father anywhere; as Moses was pre-eminently a lawgiver, so Jesus, in his Sermon on the Mount, laid down a code which not only expounds but fulfils the Decalogue; as Moses was a prophet, so Jesus is the great Prophet of his Church; as Moses was a mediator, so Jesus is the Mediator of the new covenant, standing between God and man, and bridging, by his atonement and intercession, the gulf between the two. We cannot wonder, therefore, that in the vision of the Apocalypse they who have gotten the victory over the beast and his image are represented as singing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb. Rev 15:3." (p. 466.) God buried Moses. It was fitting, therefore, that he too should write his epitaph. Here it is given by his inspiration, and, though written only in a book, having a permanence as great as if it had been graven with an iron pen in the rock for ever: "And there arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face, in all the signs and the wonders which the Lord sent him to do in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh, and to all his servants, and to all his land, and in all that mighty land, and in all the great terror which Moses showed in the sight of all Israel." Deut 34:10-12. (p. 468.) Moses, Song of. This wonderful ode celebrates more fitly the miraculous deliverance of the children of Israel from Egyptian bondage. It is the national anthem, the Te Deum of the Hebrews. It sounds through the psalms of Israel, through the thanksgiving hymns of the Christian Church, through the touching songs of liberated slaves, and it will swell the harmony of the saints in heaven. Allusion to it is made in Rev 15:2-3; "They stand on the sea of glass mingled with fire . . . and sing the song of Moses the servant of God."

variants.definition: MOS'ES (Heb. Mosheh, *drawn out - i.e. of the water; Coptic Mo-use, watersaved), the leader and creator of the Jewish nation. This table shows the pedigree of Moses: His life falls naturally into three divisions, of forty years each, according to the account preserved in Stephen's speech. Acts 7:23, 1 Kgs 20:30, Eze 23:36. Moses was born in the dark hour of Hebrew story when a son was an object of the murderous search of the Egyptian spies. His father was Amram, his mother Jochebed, his tribe was Levi, and this fact may have determined the choice of Levi for the priesthood. Moses was the youngest child of the family; Miriam was the oldest, and Aaron came between. For three months his parents hid the babe, but at last it was no longer possible, and Jochebed, with a trembling heart, but it may be with a dim consciousness that God had great things in store for him, laid him in the little basket of papyrus she had deftly woven, pitched with bitumen within and without, and, carrying it down to the brink of one of the canals of the Nile, she hid it among the flags. The child was tenderly watched "afar off" by Miriam, who, less open to suspicion than the mother would be, stood to see what would be done to him. The daughter of the Pharaoh, the oppressor, came to the sacred river to bathe, attended by her maidens, who, surprised to find the basket, which had providentially floated down to the princess' bathing-place - or had Jochebed purposely put it there? - call the attention of their mistress to the discovery. The basket is fetched by one of them, and when opened a little babe, evidently one of the Hebrews' children, but exceedingly fair, is revealed to view. The woman-heart of the princess, who was a childless wife according to tradition, yearned over the little one. Her yearning was of God. Then Miriam drew near, gathered from the conversation that the child's life was to be spared, proposed to get a nurse for him among the Hebrew women, and thus it came to pass that Jochebed again had her child at her breast, but this time as his hired nurse. The biblical history of this period closes with the child Moses in the palace under tutors and governors, and increasing in wisdom and in stature, and in the favor of God and of man. There is a break in this history, as in that of the greater than Moses, between the infancy and the manhood. The second division of Moses' life was totally different in its character from the first. Moses, at the age of forty, is learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. The adopted grandson of the Pharaoh, initiated in the secrets of the priests, to whose order he belonged, he had a brilliant and useful worldly career before him. Had he remained in his advantageous surroundings, he would have been one of the great Egyptian sages - probably the greatest of them all. But God intended him to occupy a much more exalted position. There was needed by him a period of meditation. He must be cut off from books, and by direct contact with Nature in all her moods learn what books cannot give. The providential occasion of this violent change was Moses' slaying of an Egyptian taskmaster who had ill-treated a Hebrew. This was no secret, as he hoped it would be. The news, indeed, had been carried to Pharaoh, and so Moses was compelled to flee. It is probable that the murder was intended to impress upon the Hebrews his desire to help them - that he, the king's son, would be their deliverer; for it seems impossible to resist the conclusion that the pious teachings of his mother had not been forgotten, and that many prayers had been put up by him as he determined to be his brethren's saviour. But we see now that it was no wonder that this attempt at an insurrection proved abortive, and likewise that Moses had much to learn before he could properly lead the great Exodus. Moses fled from the prominence, the refinement, and the luxury of the court to the obscurity, the roughness, and the poverty of the wilderness. He became the shepherd of Jethro and the husband of his daughter Zipporah. Ex 2. This second period lasted forty years, and again a wondrous transformation took place. The transition was made at Horeb when one day he saw a "bush" - probably an acacia tree - which was said to be on fire and yet was unconsumed. He drew near to examine the wondrous sight, and the Angel of the Lord appeared to him and gave him his prophetic call. But now the would-be leader of forty years agone was full of excuses, deprecated his abilities, and disparaged his appearance. Accordingly, God appointed Aaron as his spokesman and brought about their meeting. Ex 3-4. Thus informed of the divine name, Ex 3:14, promised divine aid, and strengthened by miracles, Ex 4:1-7, Moses, at the age of eighty, now both a scholar and a practical man of affairs, starts out upon the deliverance of his people. On his way to Egypt his son Gershom was smitten by a mysterious illness, Zipporah thought because circumcision had not been performed. Accordingly, although loath to do it, she herself circumcised Gershom. Ex 4:24-26. The child recovered. But to counterbalance this evil trait there were many good ones. He makes mention of one of these - viz., his meekness. Num 12:3. Besides, he was characterized by disinterestedness, impartiality, faithfulness, and courage. When he had risen superior to the fears which daunted him when he received the divine call, he was unwavering. The people might murmur or break out into rebellion, he was ready to plead with God for them; yea, when they had so grievously sinned that God declared he would destroy them, Moses asked that his name might be blotted out of the book of God rather than behold their destruction. Ex 32:32. In addition must be mentioned his eminent services as lawgiver. It is indeed a vexed question how much credit should be given to him as the publisher of a code marked throughout by "Thus saith the Lord." We are safe in saying that the Law, as we have it recorded in the Scriptures, was divinely inspired, and that Moses made the record as directed of the Lord. The Decalogue is a moral miracle in ancient legislation, and retains its power to this day in all Christian lands. See Law. As an historian Moses also is to be honored. The five books commonly called the Pentateuch, which he wrote, contain the only reliable history of the creation of man and the beginning of the human as well as of the Jewish race. See Pentateuch. But there are also other compositions attributed to him - namely, Ps 90 and the book of Job. In regard to these there is no certainty, but the ninetieth Psalm seems to fit in well with the circumstances of the Wandering, and the book of Job is perhaps his in its first draft; the Talmud makes him the author, and several commentators have adopted this view. See Job. We know Moses to have had the poetic gift, for in the Pentateuch there are several exhibitions of it: "The song which Moses and the children of Israel sung" (after the passage of the Red Sea, Ex 15:1-19). A fragment of a war-song against Amalek, Ex 17:16: The song of Moses, composed on the east side of Jordan. Deut 32:1-43. The prophetic blessing of Moses upon the tribes. Deut 33:1-29. As a leader and as a prophet Moses comes before us. As the former "his life," says Dean Stanley in Smith's Dictionary of the Bible, "divides itself into the three epochs of the march to Sinai, the march from Sinai to Kadesh, and the conquest of the Transjordanic kingdoms. Of his natural gifts in this capacity we have but few means of judging. The two main difficulties which he encountered were the reluctance of the people to submit to his guidance and the impracticable nature of the country which they had to traverse. The incidents with which his name was specially connected, both in the sacred narrative and in the Jewish, Arabian, and heathen traditions, were those of supplying water when most wanted. In the Pentateuch these supplies of water take place at Marah, at Horeb, at Kadesh, and in the land of Moab. Of the first three of these incidents, traditional sites bearing his name are shown in the desert at the present day, though most of them are rejected by modern travellers. The route through the wilderness is described as having been made under his guidance. The particular spot of the encampment is fixed by the cloudy pillar. But the direction of the people, first to the Red Sea and then to Mount Sinai, is communicated through Moses or given by him. On approaching Palestine the office of the leader becomes blended with that of the general or the conqueror. By Moses the spies were sent to explore the country. Against his advice took place the first disastrous battle at Hormah. To his guidance is ascribed the circuitous route by which the nation approached Palestine from the east, and to his generalship the two successful campaigns in which Sihon and Og were defeated. The narrative is told so shortly that we are in danger of forgetting that at this last stage of his life Moses must have been as much a conqueror and victorious soldier as Joshua." But as a prophet Moses is evidently the revealer of the will of God, and preeminent because with him the divine revelations were made "mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches," and he beheld "the similitude of Jehovah." Num 12:8. He saw the flame in the bush; for two periods of forty days each he was in the thick darkness with God, Ex 24:18; Ex 34:28; and above all was he favored with the vision of the trailing garments of the Almighty, and he heard a voice which "proclaimed the two immutable attributes of God, justice and love," in words which became part of the religious creed of Israel and of the world. Ex 34:6-7. But perhaps the most remarkable fact is yet to be mentioned. Moses frequently met God in the tent of the congregation, which he removed outside the camp.Ex 33:9. No wonder that the subject of so many and so familiar interviews with God should be regarded with peculiar veneration by the Hebrews, the Mohammedans, and the Christians. When Moses was one hundred and twenty years old his eye was not dim nor his natural force abated. Deut 34:7. He was able, on the day of his death, to stand on Nebo, a height of the Pisgah range, and thence look across the Jordan and up and down the Promised Land. Bitter was his disappointment at not being allowed to enter, but meekly he submitted to the will of God. He had been so much with God that to die was simply to be always with Him whose voice he had heard and whose glory he had seen. But since his death would make a great change to his people, he prepared the way for it. He addressed the people and warned them against apostasy. He then gave a public charge to Joshua, his successor. He then uttered the song, Deut 32, and blessed the people. Deut 33. Quietly, it would appear, unattended, perhaps secretly, the aged yet strong man climbed the Pisgah range, stood on the height of Nebo, and viewed the extensive prospect. "As he gazed upon it the words fell upon his ears, 'This is the land which I sware unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob, saying, I will give it unto thy seed; I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes;' and then, not in sternness or in anger, but in utmost love, like a mother lifting her boy into her arms, the Lord added, 'But thou shalt not go over thither,' and in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, the soul of Moses had passed within the veil and was at home with God." - Rev. W. M. Taylor, D.D., Moses the Lawgiver, N.Y., 1879, p. 439. "And he buried him in a valley in the land of Moab, over against Beth-peor; but no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day." Deut 34:6. In the words of the Rabbins, "Jehovah kissed him to death" (or rather into life eternal). His remains were removed from all reach of idolatry - the sin of sins, forbidden in the first commandment. As Thomas Fuller quaintly says, "God buried also his grave." Vainly have men sought to find it. The familiar lines of Mrs. C. F. Alexander's ode, "The Death of Moses," may be appropriately quoted here: Centuries passed on. The land had witnessed many changes; the promised One stood upon the Promised Land when once more Moses is seen by mortal sight. Upon the slopes of Hermon he appeared in company with Elijah to talk with Jesus of the decease Jesus should accomplish at Jerusalem. Luke 9:31. Thus was the type brought face to face with the Pattern. And this resurrection leads to the conclusion which some hold - that Moses, like Christ, was raised from the dead after a brief sleep in the grave. Moses was of God's special preparation, the resultant of many forces. Wrought upon by inspiration, he was able to be legislator, statesman, leader, poet, saint, because he was so variedly trained. An exceptional man in original gifts, he was equally exceptional in his opportunities. To be of Hebrew extraction, and therefore by descent to share in the glorious hopes of his race, was to have a grand start Godward. To be the adopted child of Pharaoh's daughter, to breathe "the atmosphere of courts," to be acquainted as an equal with the nobility of the land, was to gain an intimate knowledge of statecraft from the best exponents of it. To be trained for the priesthood, initiated into the holy mysteries, learned in all the learning of the Egyptians, was to be thoroughly furnished unto religious service. To be exiled and compelled through many years to eat "the bread of carefulness," to be a keeper of sheep and a dweller in tents amid the sublimity of Sinaitic scenery, was to have time for reflection and for communion with God. Thus, when at eighty he returned to Egypt, he was able to debate with scholars and to sympathize with slaves. He towered above all his brethren. He was alone in the loneliness of genius. He was accessible in his feeling for the oppressed. But Moses was unique in other ways. He alone has held friendly converse with Jehovah. What though he was slow of speech? He was lofty of thought. What though he was timid? He had the promise of divine strength. And the good qualities he showed during the Wandering are such as come from fellowship with the Highest, while his bad qualities - his occasional infirmity of temper, for example - are mere spots upon the sun or temporary obscurations of the light, the times he forgot God. But when he fell all observed it, just as all notice the fallen monarch of the forest; when he stood firm few marked it, as few remark the upright tree. The above article is a mere sketch. To write fully the life of Moses would be to write the history of Israel during the Exodus. The reader will refer to the separate articles incidentally mentioned. We close by a brief study of the character of Moses, following the Rev. Dr. W.M. Taylor in his book above quoted. Three qualities give him immortal interest and prominence. 1st. Faith. By faith he esteemed "the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt." Heb 11:26. "Never more alluring prospects opened up before any man than those which the world held out to him. The throne of the greatest monarchy of his age was within his reach. All that wealth could procure, or pleasure bestow, or the greatest earthly power command, was easily at his call. But the glory of these things paled in his view before the more excellent character of those invisible honors which God set before him. This faith sustained him in the solitudes of Midian and animated him amidst all the conflicts attendant on the Exodus and all the difficulties that confronted him in the wilderness. This faith gave him courage in the hour of danger and calmness in the time of trial." (pp. 459, 460.) 2d. Prayerfnlness. "In every time of emergency his immediate resort was to Jehovah. He was not speaking to a stranger, but was like a son making application to his father; and so he never pleaded in vain." (p. 461.) His was the prayer of faith. 3d. Humility. "He coveted no distinction and sought no prominence; his greatness came to him, he did not go after it. And his humility was allied with or flowed naturally out into two other qualities, disinterestedness and meekness. (See Num 11:29 and 1 Chr 12:3 for striking illustrations.) He gave up his own ease and comfort to secure the emancipation of his people; and while laboring night and day for them, he had no thought whatever of his own interests. His office brought him no emolument." In this he was like Nehemiah. He was free from all charge of nepotism. His meekness was shown in silently listening to complaints against himself. He appealed unto God. (pp. 462-3.) The only blot upon this beautiful character is a lack of patience or self-control, but this was more evident in the earlier portion of his life, nor was it prominent enough to belie his eulogy. Moses was a type of Christ. The parallel is readily traced. "As Moses, in the early part of his career, refused the Egyptian monarchy because it could be gained to him only by disloyalty to, God, so Jesus turned away from the kingdoms of the world because they were offered on condition that he would worship Satan; as Moses became the emancipator of his people, so was Jesus; as Moses, penetrating to the soul of the symbolism of idolatry, introduced a new dispensation wherein symbolism was allied to spirituality of worship, so Jesus, seizing the spirituality of the Mosaic system, freed it from its national restrictions, and ushered in the day when the true worshipper would worship the Father anywhere; as Moses was pre-eminently a lawgiver, so Jesus, in his Sermon on the Mount, laid down a code which not only expounds but fulfils the Decalogue; as Moses was a prophet, so Jesus is the great Prophet of his Church; as Moses was a mediator, so Jesus is the Mediator of the new covenant, standing between God and man, and bridging, by his atonement and intercession, the gulf between the two. We cannot wonder, therefore, that in the vision of the Apocalypse they who have gotten the victory over the beast and his image are represented as singing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb. Rev 15:3." (p. 466.) God buried Moses. It was fitting, therefore, that he too should write his epitaph. Here it is given by his inspiration, and, though written only in a book, having a permanence as great as if it had been graven with an iron pen in the rock for ever: "And there arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses, whom the Lord knew face to face, in all the signs and the wonders which the Lord sent him to do in the land of Egypt, to Pharaoh, and to all his servants, and to all his land, and in all that mighty land, and in all the great terror which Moses showed in the sight of all Israel." Deut 34:10-12. (p. 468.) Moses, Song of. This wonderful ode celebrates more fitly the miraculous deliverance of the children of Israel from Egyptian bondage. It is the national anthem, the Te Deum of the Hebrews. It sounds through the psalms of Israel, through the thanksgiving hymns of the Christian Church, through the touching songs of liberated slaves, and it will swell the harmony of the saints in heaven. Allusion to it is made in Rev 15:2-3; "They stand on the sea of glass mingled with fire . . . and sing the song of Moses the servant of God."
