시내는 아마 「불붙는 떨기나무」를 뜻할 것이며 한 반도와 한 산 곧 산줄기의 이름이다. 시내 반도는 홍해의 두 팔 사이에 놓인 세모꼴 지방이다. 서쪽으로 수에즈 만을 따라 190마일쯤 뻗고 동쪽으로 아카바 만을 따라 130마일쯤 뻗으며, 수에즈에서 아카바 북쪽 끝으로 그은 세모의 밑변이 150마일이다. 넓이가 만 천오백 제곱마일쯤이니 매사추세츠와 코네티컷을 합한 것보다 조금 작다. 이 지방이 크게는 메마른 산줄기로 이루어졌고 와디 곧 물길 있는 골짜기가 그것을 파 놓았으니 비 온 뒤에야 조금 찬다. 북쪽에서 쐐기처럼 파고드는 것이 티 광야 곧 「떠돎의 광야」이며 석회암층이다. 티 고원의 언덕 남쪽에 넓은 사암 띠가 있어 수에즈에서 아카바까지 거의 뻗는다. 그 남쪽에 큰 화강암 산 무리가 있으니 하도 험하고 뒤엉킨 혼돈이라 갈래 짓기 어려우며, 가장 높은 봉우리가 8,000피트에서 9,000피트 사이에 이른다. 산 사이에 깊이 팬 골짜기가 있어 큰 무리가 그리로 산지의 한복판까지 행진할 수 있다. 산줄기가 수에즈 동쪽과 아카바 서쪽을 따라 내려가 반도 남쪽에서 두 줄기가 각을 이루며 만나니, 거기서 산이 가장 가파르고 높으며 흔히 기이한 모양을 띠고 화려한 빛깔을 낸다. 이 거대한 줄기는 편마암과 화강암, 더 정확히는 빛깔 없는 석영과 장석과 초록 각섬석과 검은 점판암으로 되었고 석회암이 꽤 드러난다. 철과 구리와 터키석이 넉넉하여 애굽 사람이 그것을 「구리의 땅」이라 하였다. 옛 애굽 사람을 비롯한 이들이 한때 이 지방에서 광을 널리 캤으나 오래 버려져 있다. 가장 중한 것은 아마 마가라의 광이었을 것이니, 가파른 산비탈 골짜기 바닥에서 145피트쯤 되는 데 있다. 입구가 넓으나 낮고 굴이 바위를 꽤 깊이 뚫었으며 지붕을 받치려고 기둥을 여럿 남겼다. 거기서 아름다운 초록빛 터키석을 캤고 구리가 공작석 무리와 함께 나왔다. 광부는 정죄받은 죄인과 전쟁 포로였다. 이 지방은 애굽 자체와 거의 같은 때에 알려지고 사람이 살았다. 첫 바로가 산지 지파를 정복하고 그 광을 찾아냈다고 주장하였다. 이 지방이 힉소스 왕들의 때까지 바로에게 딸렸고, 그들이 쫓겨난 뒤에 다시 애굽에 굴복하였다. 그러나 그 으뜸가는 관심은 이스라엘 자손의 여정에서 오니, 그들이 가나안에 들어가기 전 사십 년을 여기서 떠돌았다. 그리스도교가 매우 이르게 여기에 심겼으니 아마 바울이 심었을 것이다. 이 반도가 주후 105년에 로마 제국에 딸렸다. 4세기에 은수자와 여러 수도사 무리가 여기 살았으니 그 으뜸 자리가 세르발 산과 와디 페이란이었다. 주후 373년에서 411년까지 사라센 사람에게 무서운 학살을 당하였다. 유스티니아누스의 다스림 때에 시내 산에 동정녀 교회가 세워졌다. 뒤에 회교도가 이 반도를 휩쓸었고, 그 외로운 골짜기를 메카 순례자의 무리가 지나갔고 지금도 지나간다. 이 반도의 여러 골짜기, 더욱이 「글씨 쓴」 골짜기인 와디 무카테브에서 새김글이 많이 발견되었다. 에버스가 백이 넘는 새김글을 세었으니 주로 무리 지어 있고 몇 시간 가는 동안에도 꽤 자주 나온다. 거의 다 골짜기 서쪽에 있다. 한때 매우 신비롭게 여겨져 어떤 이는 이스라엘 자손이 새겼으리라 여겼다. 새김글은 대개 나바테아 글자이나 얼마는 헬라 글자요 몇은 콥트와 아라비아 글자이다. 바위에 거칠게 새겼으니 그것을 위하여 바위를 다듬는 일이 드물었고, 작은 그림이 흔히 몹시 거칠고 서투르다. 무장한 사람과 나그네와 군사와 낙타와 탄 이가 있거나 없는 말과 염소와 별과 십자가와 배를 나타낸다. 팔을 든 제사장과 말 타는 재주꾼도 눈여겨볼 만한 그림에 든다. 이제 그리스도 앞 2세기보다 오래되지 않았다고 여기며, 얼마는 그리스도교 4세기보다 오래되지 않았다. 반도에서 가장 높은 봉우리 가운데 「산」을 뜻하는 아라비아 말 예벨을 붙여, 예벨 세르발이 6,734피트요, 예벨 무사가 7,363피트요, 예벨 움 쇼메르가 8,449피트요, 예벨 카타리나가 8,536피트요, 예벨 제비르가 8,551피트이다. 「시내」는 또한 이스라엘 자손이 율법을 받은 산줄기를 이르는 데도 쓰인다. 이 넓은 줄기의 수많은 봉우리 가운데 어느 것이 참된 율법의 산인지 가리려는 시도가 길고 뜨거운 논의의 샘이 되어 왔다. 어느 봉우리와 같은지 정하려면 몇 가지 조건을 채워야 한다. 첫째, 그 산 앞에 꼭대기에서 보이는 트인 자리가 있어 적어도 이백만 사람을 담을 만큼 넓어야 한다(출애굽기 19:11; 20:18). 둘째, 평지에서 가파르게 솟아야 하니 백성이 「나아와서 산 아래에 서니」 하였고(신명기 4:11), 「만질 만한」 산이라 하였으며(히브리서 12:18), 모세가 「사면으로 지경을 정하고」 하라는 명을 받았기 때문이다(출애굽기 19:12). 셋째, 이스라엘 자손이 그 둘레에 한 해를 머물렀으므로 물과 풀밭이 넉넉하였어야 한다. 적어도 산 다섯이 여러 때에 율법의 산과 같다고 여겨졌으나, 그 가운데 예벨 엘 에지메와 예벨 움 알라위는 조건에 전혀 맞지 않아 물려야 한다. 요세푸스는 시내 산이 그 지방에서 가장 높다고 하며, 이 때문에 8,536피트인 예벨 카타리나와 그 쌍둥이 봉우리 8,551피트인 예벨 제비르와 같다고 보게 되었다. 그러나 이 봉우리를 두른 산이 하도 에워싸 큰 무리가 모일 만한 어느 가까운 자리에서도 보이지 않는다. 그리하여 물음이 예벨 세르발과 예벨 무사와 라스 수프사페로 좁혀졌다. 윌슨이 예벨 세르발을 「아마 반도에서 가장 눈에 띄는 산」이라 그린다. 「그 기슭 골짜기보다 4,000피트 넘게 가파르게 솟고 해면보다 6,734피트이며, 그 꼭대기는 길이 3마일쯤 되는 날카로운 등성이인데 여러 봉우리로 갈려 높이는 거의 같으나 그 윤곽의 아름다움과 웅장함이 서로 겨룬다」 하였다. 「열이나 열둘쯤 되는 봉우리가 높이가 하도 비슷하여 낮은 데서나 멀리서 보면 가장 높은 것을 눈으로 가리지 못한다」 한다. 참된 시내를 그런 어지러움에서 찾을 것이 아님이 뚜렷하다. 또 그 가까이에 큰 무리가 진 칠 자리도 없다. 홀랜드가 그 기슭 골짜기를 「바위와 급류 바닥의 광야」라 그리고 골짜기 사이의 자리를 「험한 산의 혼돈」이라 그린다. 영국 측량대의 사람들이 한마음으로 참된 시내가 예벨 무사에서 찾아진다는 결론에 이르렀으니, 그 봉우리 라스 수프사페를 아우르며 시내 산 무리 한가운데서 조금 서북쪽에 있고 예벨 세르발에서 동쪽으로 조금 남쪽 20마일쯤이다. 「예벨 무사」는 동북에서 서남으로 길이 2마일에 너비 1마일 뻗은 산덩이를 두루 이르는 이름이다. 그 남쪽 끝에 7,363피트 되는 봉우리가 있으니 여러 세월 「예벨 무사」 곧 「모세의 산」이라는 이름이 붙어 왔다. 이것이 전해 오는 율법의 산이다. 전에 따로 된 산으로 여겨지던 라스 수프사페가 이제 이 예벨 무사 덩이의 북쪽 봉우리일 뿐임이 알려졌다. 6,937피트인 이 북쪽 봉우리가 이제 율법을 실제로 주신 자리로 여겨진다. 「예벨 무사」라는 이름을 두 가지로 쓰는 데서 오는 어지러움을 피하려고 윌슨이 온 산을 「무사 수프사페」라 하고 「예벨 무사」라는 이름을 남쪽 봉우리에 한정하자고 제안한다. 큰 독일 지리학자 리터를 비롯한 여러 저술가가 이 남쪽 봉우리를 율법 주신 자리로 여기고 그 남쪽에 매우 넓은 평지가 있으리라 여겼다. 그러나 스탠리 학장은 그 골짜기를 「거칠고 고르지 않고 좁다」고 그리며, 측량대는 이스라엘의 무리를 담을 만한 평지를 찾지 못하였다. 그러나 산의 북쪽 끝 라스 수프사페 봉우리에서는 모든 조건이 채워진다. 이 온 덩이가 깊은 골짜기로 둘레 산에서 외따로 있으니 그 둘레에 온전히 지경을 정할 수 있었을 것이다(출애굽기 19:12,23). 라스 수프사페 북쪽으로 그 기슭까지 뻗은 것이 에르 라하 평지이니 길이 2마일에 너비 반 마일이요 산 바로 앞에 사백 에이커의 설 자리를 아우른다. 이 평지가 그 갈래와 함께 사백이십구만 삼천 제곱야드를 담고 산이 온전히 보이니, 이스라엘 이백만이 설 자리로 넉넉하고도 남는다. 여기서 그들이 「산 기슭에」 섰을 만하며(출애굽기 19:17), 산이 평지에서 하도 가파르게 솟아 「만질 만한 산」이라는 그림에 맞는다(히브리서 12:18). 이것이 성경 기록의 모든 조건을 채우니, 이 위엄 있고 두렵게 보이는 외딴 덩이 라스 수프사페가 「여호와께서 시내 산 곧 그 산 꼭대기에 강림하시고」 하신 바로 그 산이요(출애굽기 19:20) 「하나님이 이 모든 말씀으로 말씀하여」 십계명을 주신 자리라는 결론이 나온다(출애굽기 20:1-17). 남쪽 봉우리인 예벨 무사는 평지에서 아주 가려져 있으니, 파머는 여호와께서 모세를 산 꼭대기로 부르셨을 때에 그가 이 외진 자리로 갔을 수 있다고 한다(출애굽기 19:20). 아마 거기서 그가 「사십 일 사십 야를 여호와와 함께」 있었을 것이다(출애굽기 34:28). 라스 수프사페 기슭 가까이에 하룬 곧 「금송아지의 언덕」이 있다. 동쪽 비탈에 성 카타리나 수도원이 있으니 유스티니아누스 황제가 주후 527년에 세웠고, 거기서 티셴도르프가 이름난 시내 사본을 찾아냈으니 지금 있는 신약 사본 가운데 가장 오래되고 좋은 것의 하나이다. 가까이에 흐르는 시내가 넷 있으며, 온 반도에서 예벨 무사 둘레만큼 물이 넉넉한 데가 없다. 게다가 반도에서 예벨 무사 둘레만큼 좋은 풀밭을 내는 지방도 없다. 오늘날 나그네의 증언을 더한다. 로빈슨 박사가 1838년에 찾아가 라스 수프사페에 처음 올라 그것을 참된 율법 주신 자리로 가리켰다. 그 기록에서 이렇게 말한다. 「오르기가 몹시 어렵고 위태롭기까지 하였으나 이제 우리 앞에 열린 경치가 그것을 넉넉히 갚았다. 에르 라하 온 평지가 그에 잇닿은 와디와 산과 함께 우리 발아래 펼쳐졌다. 오른쪽의 와디 에시 셰이크와 왼쪽의 우묵한 데가 둘 다 에르 라하와 이어져 넓게 열려 그 평지의 넓이를 거의 갑절로 하는 자리를 이루었다. 여기나 잇닿은 벼랑 어디가 여호와께서 「불 가운데서 강림하심이라」 하시고 율법을 선포하신 자리라는 우리 확신이 굳어졌다. 여기 온 회중이 모일 만한 평지가 있었고, 금하지 않았다면 다가가 만질 수 있는 산이 있었으며, 여호와께서 「온 백성의 목전에 시내 산에 강림하실」 때에 번개와 빽빽한 구름이 보이고 우레와 나팔 소리가 들릴 만한 오직 하나의 산마루가 여기 있었다. 우리가 그 두려운 광경의 인상에 스스로를 맡기고, 그 큰 히브리 법 주는 이가 적은 원어 그대로 그 일의 웅장한 기록과 거기서 선포된 계명을 결코 잊지 못할 느낌으로 읽었다」 하였다(출애굽기 19:9-25; 20:1-21). 1877년에 시내 산을 찾은 샤프 박사가 이렇게 그린다. 「그런 다음 우리는 화강암 덩이를 넘어 어렵게, 얼마쯤 위태롭게 라스 수프사페의 아찔한 높이로 오른다. 여기 튀어나온 바위 위에서 한 시간 쉬며 에르 라하 넓은 평지와 잇닿은 와디 에시 셰이크와 레자를 내려다보고, 그것을 두른 산의 원형극장 너머를 바라보며 지난 일을 되새기니, 그것이 여기서 압도하는 지금의 실제가 된다. 자연의 무서운 웅장함의 파노라마와, 십계명이 알려지고 읽히는 온 세상에서 오늘까지 느껴지는 그 역사의 일의 헤아릴 수 없는 뜻에 우리가 놀라 넋을 잃는다. 더 엄숙하고 감동을 주는 광경을 그리기 어렵다. 그런 다음 우리는 모세의 자취를 따른다고 여기며 어지러이 쌓인 바위를 넘어 가파른 골짜기를 내려가 에르 라하 골짜기에 이르고 수도원 가까운 우리 진으로 돌아온다(출애굽기 32:17,19). 내가 기억하는 산행 가운데 가장 고되고 가장 흥미로운 하루 일이었다. 라스 수프사페가 율법이 선포된 단이라고 내 마음이 온전히 흡족하였다. 여기에 성경 기록이 요구하는 모든 조건이 어우러진다. 모세가 더 높은 예벨 무사에서 율법을 받았을 수 있으나, 백성에게 선포된 곳은 아래 평지 어디서나 보이는 라스 수프사페였음이 틀림없다. 에르 라하가 둘레 산이 지키는 매끄럽고 거대한 진터이며, 실제로 재어 본 바로 이백만 제곱야드를 담으니, 온 이스라엘 백성이 넉넉히 자리를 얻고 위의 바위 강단에 선 하나님의 사람을 뚜렷이 보고 들을 수 있었다. 스탠리 학장이 전하기를 「라스 수프사페의 가장 높은 데서 낮은 봉우리까지 60피트쯤 되는 거리에서 책의 한 쪽을 또렷하되 크지 않게 읽는 소리가 온전히 들렸고, 여러 나그네 무리의 말이 그 바로 위에 있는 이들에게 맑게 올라왔다」 하였다. 그 산에서 두 봉우리 사이 골짜기로 내려가며 모세와 여호수아가 백성이 금송아지 둘레에서 춤추는 것을 보기 전에 그 소리를 먼저 들었을 만하다(출애굽기 32:17,19). 한마디로 이 자리가 모세가 그린 시내 산 율법 주심의 모든 정황에 더없이 온전히 들어맞는다. 전승은 예벨 무사를 편들고 성경은 라스 수프사페를 편든다. 그러나 결국 세르발의 다섯 봉우리가 그러하듯 그 둘이 한 산을 이루니, 이 경우에 전승도 적어도 참됨에 매우 가깝다.」
※ 원문 오류: Heb 12:23 → 출애굽기 19:23
※ 판정 근거: 이어받기 숫자 부풀리기. 원문에서 책과 장을 생략한 맨 숫자에 엉뚱한 주소가 붙은 것이다. 앞의 성한 인용을 좇으면 출애굽기 19:23가 되며, 그 절은 「모세가 여호와께 아뢰되 주께서 우리에게 명령하여 이르시기를 산 주위에 경…」이다.
※ 원문 오류: Ex 32:17 다음의 「Acts 1:19」 → 출애굽기 32:19
※ 판정 근거: 이어받기 숫자 부풀리기. 원문은 「Ex. 32:17, 19」로 금송아지를 두르고 춤추는 것을 본 대목이다. 앞의 성한 인용을 좇으면 출애굽기 32:19이며, 그 절은 「진에 가까이 이르러 그 송아지와 그 춤 추는 것들을 보고 크게 노하여 손…」이다.

variants.definition: SI'NAI (burning bush?), a name of a peninsula and of a mountain, or group of mountains. The peninsula of Sinai is a triangular region lying between the two arms of the Red Sea. On the west it extends along the Gulf of Suez for about 190 miles, and on the east along the Gulf of Akabah about 130 miles, while the base of the triangle, on a line from Suez to the north end of Akabah, is 150 miles long. It includes an area of about 11,500 square miles, or a little less than that of Massachusetts and Connecticut. Physical Features. - This district consists largely of sterile ranges of mountains, furrowed by wadies, or valleys with watercourses, which are scantily filled only after a rain. Projecting into it wedgewise from the north is the desert of Tih, or "wilderness of wandering," of limestone formation. South of the hills of the Tih plateau is a broad belt of sandstone, extending nearly from Suez to Akabah. South of this is a great cluster of granite mountains, in such a rugged, tumbled chaos as scarcely to admit of classification, the highest peaks reaching to an elevation of between 8000 and 9000 feet. Between the mountains are deeply-cut valleys, through which a large company might march into the very heart of the mountain-region. The mountain-ranges extend down the east side of Suez and down the west side of Akabah, the two ranges meeting in an angle at the southern portion of the peninsula, where the mountains are the most precipitous and elevated, and where they often assume fantastic shapes and take on gorgeous colors. This huge range is composed of gneiss and granite, or, more exactly, of colorless quartz, felspar, green hornblende, and black slate, with Sinai and the plain of Er Rahah. (After photograph of Ordnance Survey) considerable outcropping of limestone. It is rich in mineral wealth of iron, copper, and turquoise, so that the Egyptians called it the "land of copper." Mines were once extensively worked in this region by the ancient Egyptians and others, but they have been long neglected. The most important were probably the mines of Maghara, situated on the slope of a precipitous mountain, about 145 feet from the bottom of the valley. The opening is broad but low, and the shaft penetrates the rock to a considerable depth, numerous pillars having been left to support the roof. From these a turquoise of a beautiful green color was taken, and copper was found together with a species of malachite. The miners were condemned criminals and prisoners of war. See a striking account of this mining in Ebers' Uarda. History. - This region was known and settled nearly as early as Egypt itself. The first Pharaoh, having conquered the mountain-tribes, claimed to have discovered the mines. The region was dependent on the Pharaohs until the time of the Hyksos kings; after their expulsion the region was again subdued by Egypt, but possesses its chief interest from the journey of the Israelites, who wandered in it for forty years previous to their entrance into Canaan. Christianity was planted here very early, perhaps by Paul; the peninsula was annexed to the Roman empire, a.d. 105. In the fourth century it was peopled by anchorites and various brotherhoods of hermits and monks, their principal settlement being on Mount Serbal and in the Wady Feiran. They suffered terrible massacres from the Saracens, a.d. 373 to a.d. 411. In the reign of Justinian a church of the Virgin was founded on Mount Sinai. Later, the Mohammedans overran the peninsula, and its lonely valleys have been, and are still, traversed by hosts of Mecca pilgrims. Numerous inscriptions have been found in several of the valleys of the peninsula, but chiefly in the Wady Mukatteb, or the "written" valley. Ebers counted more than a hundred inscriptions, chiefly in groups, occurring quite frequently in a few hours' travel. Most of them are on the western side of the valleys. They were once regarded as very mysterious, some supposing them to have been made by the Israelites. The inscriptions are mostly in the Nabataean character, but some are in Greek, and a few in Coptic and Arabic. They are roughly engraved on the rock, which was seldom smoothed for the purpose, and the little figures are often extremely rude and inartistic. They represent armed men, travellers and warriors, camels, horses with and without riders, goats, stars, crosses, and ships; a priest with raised arms and an equestrian performer are also among the figures worthy of notice. They are now believed to be not older than the second century before Christ, while some are not older than the fourth century of the Christian era. Among the highest summits in the peninsula are Jebel (the Arabic word for "mount") Serbal, 6734 feet; Jebel Musa, 7363 feet; Jebel Umm Shomer, 8449 feet; Jebel Katharina, 8536 feet; Jebel Zebir, 8551 feet. "Sinai "is also used to designate the range of mountains from which the Israelites received the Law. The attempt to decide which of the numerous peaks in this extended range is the true Mount of the Law has been a source of protracted and animated discussion. In determining its identity with any existing peak several conditions must be met: (1) The mountain must have before it an open space within sight of the summit, Ex 19:11; Ex 20:18, large enough to contain at least two millions of people; (2) It must rise sharply from the plain, since the people "came near and stood under the mountain," Deut 4:11; it "might be touched," Heb 12:18; and Moses was commanded to "set bounds . . . round about," Ex 19:12; (3) As the Israelites remained in the neighborhood for a year, they must have found a sufficient supply of water and pasturage. At least five mountains have been at different times identified with the Mount of the Law, but two of these, Jebel el-Ejmeh and Jebel Umm Alawi, do not at all fulfil the conditions, and must be set aside. Josephus says that Mount Sinai was the highest of the district, and this led to its identification with Jebel Katharina (8536 feet high), and its twin peak Jebel Zebir (8551 feet). But the mountains surrounding these summits so hem them in that they are not visible from any place in the neighborhood where a large number of people could be assembled. The question was thus narrowed down to Jebel Serbal, Jebel Musa, and Ras Sufsafeh. Jebel Serbal is described by Wilson (Bible Educator, iv. p. 186) as "perhaps the most striking mountain in the peninsula. It rises abruptly to a height of more than 4000 feet above the valley at its base [6734 feet above the sea-level], and its summit, a sharp ridge about 3 Outline Map of Mount Sinai (After the Ordinance Survey.) miles in length, is broken into a series of peaks, varying little in altitude, but rivalling each other in the beauty and grandeur of their outline." There are "some ten or twelve peaks, which vary so little in altitude that when seen from lower ground or from a distance the eye fails to distinguish the highest." Evidently the true Sinai is not to be sought in such a confusion. Nor is there any place in the neighborhood for the encampment of a large host. Holland (Recovery of Jerusalem, p. 410) describes the valleys at its base as "a wilderness of boulders and torrent-beds," and the space between the valleys as "a chaos of rugged mountains." The members of the Ordnance Survey unanimously reached the conclusion that the real Sinai was to be found in Jebel Musa, including its peak Ras Sufsafeh, which is situated a little north-west of the centre of the Sinaitic group, and some 20 miles east by south of Jebel Serbal. "Jebel Musa" is the general name applied to a mountain-mass, 2 miles long and 1 mile broad, which extends north-east and south-west. At its southern extremity is a peak 7363 feet in height, to which the name of "Jebel Musa" ("Mount of Moses") has been for ages applied. This is the traditional mount of legislation. Ras Sufsafeh, which was formerly thought to be a separate mountain, is now known to be only a northern peak of this mass of Jebel Musa. This northern peak, 6937 feet in height, is now regarded as the place of the actual giving of the Law. To avoid confusion arising from this double use of the name "Jebel Musa," Wilson suggests "Musa-Sufsafeh" for the whole mountain, thus limiting the name of "Jebel Musa" to the southern peak. Many writers - Ritter, the great German geographer, among them - supposed that this southern peak was the scene of the giving of the Law, and that there was to the south of it a plain of great extent; but Dean Stanley describes the valley as "rough, uneven, and narrow," and the surveyors found no plain which would accommodate the hosts of Israel. At the northern end of the mountain, however, all the conditions are met in the peak of Ras Sufsafeh. This whole block is isolated from the surrounding mountains by deep valleys, so that boundaries might have been set completely around it. Ex 19:12, Heb 12:23. To the north of Ras Sufsafeh, and extending to its very base is the plain of Er Rahah, 2 miles long and half a mile wide, embracing 400 acres of available standing-ground, directly in front of the mountain. The plain, with its branches, contains 4,293,000 square yards, in full view of the mount, affording more than sufficient standing-ground for the two millions of the Israelites. Here they might stand "at the nether part of the mount," Ex 19:17, which rises so abruptly from the plain as to answer the description of "the mount that might be touched." Heb 12:18. This fulfils all the conditions of the Scripture narrative; and the conclusion is that this stately, awful-looking, isolated mass Ras Sufsafeh is the very mountain where "the Lord came down upon Mount Sinai, on the top of the mount," Ex 19:20, and where "God spake all these words" of the ten commandments. Ex 20:1-17. The southern summit (Jebel Musa) is completely hidden from the plain, and Palmer suggests that it may have been to this secluded spot Moses went when the Lord called him up to the top of the mount. Ex 19:20. There, too, perhaps, he was "with the Lord forty days and forty nights." Ex 34:28. Near the base of Ras Sufsafeh is the Harun, or "hill of the golden calf." On the eastern declivity is the convent of St. Katharine, founded by the emperor Justinian in a.d. 527, where Tischendorf discovered the famous Codex Sinaiticus, one of the oldest and best manuscripts of the N.T. in existence. Four running streams are found in the vicinity, and there is no other spot in the whole peninsula which is nearly as well supplied with water as the neighborhood of Jebel Musa. Besides, there is no other district in the peninsula which affords such excellent pasturage as the neighborhood of Jebel Musa. We add the testimony of modern travellers. Dr. Robinson, on his visit in 1838, first ascended Ras Sufsafeh, and pointed it out as the true locality of legislation. In his account he says (Biblical Res. I. 107): "The extreme difficulty, and even danger, of the ascent was well rewarded by the prospect that now opened before us. The whole plain Er Rahah lay spread beneath our feet, with the adjacent wadys and mountains; while Wady esh-Sheikh on the right, and the recess on the left, both connected with and opening broadly from Er Rahah, presented an area which serves nearly to double that of the plain. Our conviction was strengthened that here, or on some of the adjacent cliffs, was the spot where the Lord 'descended in fire' and proclaimed the Law. Here lay the plain where the whole congregation might be assembled; here was the mount that could be approached and touched, if not forbidden; and here the mountain-brow where alone the lightnings and the thick cloud would be visible, and the thunders and the voice of the trump be heard when the Lord 'came down in the sight of all the people upon Mount Sinai.' We gave ourselves up to the impressions of the awful scene, and read, with a feeling that will never be forgotten, the sublime account of the transaction, and the commandments there promulgated, in the original words as recorded by the great Hebrew legislator. Ex 19:9-25; Ex 20:1-21." Dr. Schaff, who visited Mount Sinai in 1877, gives the following description (Through Bible Lands, p. 177): "Then we climb with difficulty, and some danger, over granite blocks to the giddy height of Ras Sufsafeh. Here, on a projecting rock, we rest an hour, looking down on the vast plain of Er Rahah and the adjoining wadys of esh Sheikh and Lejah, and looking beyond to the amphitheatre of mountains which wall them in and meditating over the past, which here assumes the character of a present overpowering reality, we are lost in amazement at the panorama of terrible sublimity of nature, and the immeasurable significance of that historic event which is felt to this day all over the world as far as the ten commandments are known and read. It is difficult to imagine a more solemn and impressive sight. We then descend a steep ravine (imagining that we follow the track of Moses, Ex 32:17, Acts 1:19), over confused heaps of rocks, to the valley Er Rahah, and return to our camp near the convent. It was the most fatiguing, as well as the most interesting, day's work of mountain-climbing I can remember. I fully satisfied my mind that Ras Sufsafeh is the platform from which the Law was proclaimed. Here all the conditions required by the Scripture narrative are combined. Moses may have received the Law on the higher Jebel Musa, but it must have been proclaimed to the people from Ras Sufsafeh, which can be seen from every part of the plain below. For Er Rahah is a smooth and gigantic camping-ground, protected by surrounding mountains, and contains, as has been ascertained by actual measurement, two millions of square yards; so that the whole people of Israel could find ample room and plainly see and hear the man of God on the rocky pulpit above. Dean Stanley relates that 'from the highest point of Ras Sufsafeh to its lower peak, a distance of about 60 feet, the page of a book, distinctly but not loudly read, was perfectly audible, and every remark of the various groups of travellers rose clearly to those immediately above them.' Descending from that mount through a ravine between two peaks, Moses and Joshua might have first heard the shouts of the people before they saw them dancing round the golden calf. Ex 32:17, Acts 1:19. In one word, there is the most complete adaptation of this locality to all the circumstances of the Sinaitic legislation as described by Moses. Tradition is for Jebel Musa, the Bible for Ras Sufsafeh. But, after all, they form but one mountain (as do the five peaks of Serbal), and tradition in this case is at least very near the truth."
variants.definition_ko: 하나님이 모세에게 율법을 주신 거룩한 산으로(출 19-20장), 아라비아 반도 시내 반도의 화강암 산군 안에 있다. 전통적으로 예벨 무사(해발 7,375피트)와 동일시되며, 4세기 이래 그 기슭에 성 카타리나 수도원이 세워져 있다. 산의 정확한 위치에 대해 예벨 세르발 등 다른 후보도 제시되지만 예벨 무사가 가장 유력한 견해이다.

variants.definition: SI'NAI (burning bush?), a name of a peninsula and of a mountain, or group of mountains. Physical Features. - This district consists largely of sterile ranges of mountains, furrowed by wadies, or valleys with watercourses, which are scantily filled only after a rain. Projecting into it wedgewise from the north is the desert of Tih, or "wilderness of wandering," of limestone formation. South of the hills of the Tih plateau is a broad belt of sandstone, extending nearly from Suez to Akabah. South of this is a great cluster of granite mountains, in such a rugged, tumbled chaos as scarcely to admit of classification, the highest peaks reaching to an elevation of between 8000 and 9000 feet. Between the mountains are deeply-cut valleys, through which a large company might march into the very heart of the mountain-region. The mountain-ranges extend down the east side of Suez and down the west side of Akabah, the two ranges meeting in an angle at the southern portion of the peninsula, where the mountains are the most precipitous and elevated, and where they often assume fantastic shapes and take on gorgeous colors. This huge range is composed of gneiss and granite, or, more exactly, of colorless quartz, felspar, green hornblende, and black slate, with Sinai and the plain of Er Rahah. (After photograph of Ordnance Survey) considerable outcropping of limestone. It is rich in mineral wealth of iron, copper, and turquoise, so that the Egyptians called it the "land of copper." Mines were once extensively worked in this region by the ancient Egyptians and others, but they have been long neglected. The most important were probably the mines of Maghara, situated on the slope of a precipitous mountain, about 145 feet from the bottom of the valley. The opening is broad but low, and the shaft penetrates the rock to a considerable depth, numerous pillars having been left to support the roof. From these a turquoise of a beautiful green color was taken, and copper was found together with a species of malachite. The miners were condemned criminals and prisoners of war. See a striking account of this mining in Ebers' Uarda. History. - This region was known and settled nearly as early as Egypt itself. The first Pharaoh, having conquered the mountain-tribes, claimed to have discovered the mines. The region was dependent on the Pharaohs until the time of the Hyksos kings; after their expulsion the region was again subdued by Egypt, but possesses its chief interest from the journey of the Israelites, who wandered in it for forty years previous to their entrance into Canaan. Christianity was planted here very early, perhaps by Paul; the peninsula was annexed to the Roman empire, a.d. 105. In the fourth century it was peopled by anchorites and various brotherhoods of hermits and monks, their principal settlement being on Mount Serbal and in the Wady Feiran. They suffered terrible massacres from the Saracens, a.d. 373 to a.d. 411. In the reign of Justinian a church of the Virgin was founded on Mount Sinai. Later, the Mohammedans overran the peninsula, and its lonely valleys have been, and are still, traversed by hosts of Mecca pilgrims. Numerous inscriptions have been found in several of the valleys of the peninsula, but chiefly in the Wady Mukatteb, or the "written" valley. Ebers counted more than a hundred inscriptions, chiefly in groups, occurring quite frequently in a few hours' travel. Most of them are on the western side of the valleys. They were once regarded as very mysterious, some supposing them to have been made by the Israelites. The inscriptions are mostly in the Nabataean character, but some are in Greek, and a few in Coptic and Arabic. They are roughly engraved on the rock, which was seldom smoothed for the purpose, and the little figures are often extremely rude and inartistic. They represent armed men, travellers and warriors, camels, horses with and without riders, goats, stars, crosses, and ships; a priest with raised arms and an equestrian performer are also among the figures worthy of notice. They are now believed to be not older than the second century before Christ, while some are not older than the fourth century of the Christian era. Among the highest summits in the peninsula are Jebel (the Arabic word for "mount") Serbal, 6734 feet; Jebel Musa, 7363 feet; Jebel Umm Shomer, 8449 feet; Jebel Katharina, 8536 feet; Jebel Zebir, 8551 feet. At least five mountains have been at different times identified with the Mount of the Law, but two of these, Jebel el-Ejmeh and Jebel Umm Alawi, do not at all fulfil the conditions, and must be set aside. Josephus says that Mount Sinai was the highest of the district, and this led to its identification with Jebel Katharina (8536 feet high), and its twin peak Jebel Zebir (8551 feet). But the mountains surrounding these summits so hem them in that they are not visible from any place in the neighborhood where a large number of people could be assembled. The question was thus narrowed down to Jebel Serbal, Jebel Musa, and Ras Sufsafeh. Jebel Serbal is described by Wilson (Bible Educator, iv. p. 186) as "perhaps the most striking mountain in the peninsula. It rises abruptly to a height of more than 4000 feet above the valley at its base [6734 feet above the sea-level], and its summit, a sharp ridge about 3 Outline Map of Mount Sinai (After the Ordinance Survey.) miles in length, is broken into a series of peaks, varying little in altitude, but rivalling each other in the beauty and grandeur of their outline." There are "some ten or twelve peaks, which vary so little in altitude that when seen from lower ground or from a distance the eye fails to distinguish the highest." Evidently the true Sinai is not to be sought in such a confusion. Nor is there any place in the neighborhood for the encampment of a large host. Holland (Recovery of Jerusalem, p. 410) describes the valleys at its base as "a wilderness of boulders and torrent-beds," and the space between the valleys as "a chaos of rugged mountains." The members of the Ordnance Survey unanimously reached the conclusion that the real Sinai was to be found in Jebel Musa, including its peak Ras Sufsafeh, which is situated a little north-west of the centre of the Sinaitic group, and some 20 miles east by south of Jebel Serbal. "Jebel Musa" is the general name applied to a mountain-mass, 2 miles long and 1 mile broad, which extends north-east and south-west. At its southern extremity is a peak 7363 feet in height, to which the name of "Jebel Musa" ("Mount of Moses") has been for ages applied. This is the traditional mount of legislation. Ras Sufsafeh, which was formerly thought to be a separate mountain, is now known to be only a northern peak of this mass of Jebel Musa. This northern peak, 6937 feet in height, is now regarded as the place of the actual giving of the Law. To avoid confusion arising from this double use of the name "Jebel Musa," Wilson suggests "Musa-Sufsafeh" for the whole mountain, thus limiting the name of "Jebel Musa" to the southern peak. Many writers - Ritter, the great German geographer, among them - supposed that this southern peak was the scene of the giving of the Law, and that there was to the south of it a plain of great extent; but Dean Stanley describes the valley as "rough, uneven, and narrow," and the surveyors found no plain which would accommodate the hosts of Israel. At the northern end of the mountain, however, all the conditions are met in the peak of Ras Sufsafeh. This whole block is isolated from the surrounding mountains by deep valleys, so that boundaries might have been set completely around it. Ex 19:12, Heb 12:23. To the north of Ras Sufsafeh, and extending to its very base is the plain of Er Rahah, 2 miles long and half a mile wide, embracing 400 acres of available standing-ground, directly in front of the mountain. The plain, with its branches, contains 4,293,000 square yards, in full view of the mount, affording more than sufficient standing-ground for the two millions of the Israelites. Here they might stand "at the nether part of the mount," Ex 19:17, which rises so abruptly from the plain as to answer the description of "the mount that might be touched." Heb 12:18. This fulfils all the conditions of the Scripture narrative; and the conclusion is that this stately, awful-looking, isolated mass Ras Sufsafeh is the very mountain where "the Lord came down upon Mount Sinai, on the top of the mount," Ex 19:20, and where "God spake all these words" of the ten commandments. Ex 20:1-17. The southern summit (Jebel Musa) is completely hidden from the plain, and Palmer suggests that it may have been to this secluded spot Moses went when the Lord called him up to the top of the mount. Ex 19:20. There, too, perhaps, he was "with the Lord forty days and forty nights." Ex 34:28. Near the base of Ras Sufsafeh is the Harun, or "hill of the golden calf." On the eastern declivity is the convent of St. Katharine, founded by the emperor Justinian in a.d. 527, where Tischendorf discovered the famous Codex Sinaiticus, one of the oldest and best manuscripts of the N.T. in existence. Four running streams are found in the vicinity, and there is no other spot in the whole peninsula which is nearly as well supplied with water as the neighborhood of Jebel Musa. Besides, there is no other district in the peninsula which affords such excellent pasturage as the neighborhood of Jebel Musa. We add the testimony of modern travellers. Dr. Robinson, on his visit in 1838, first ascended Ras Sufsafeh, and pointed it out as the true locality of legislation. In his account he says (Biblical Res. I. 107): "The extreme difficulty, and even danger, of the ascent was well rewarded by the prospect that now opened before us. The whole plain Er Rahah lay spread beneath our feet, with the adjacent wadys and mountains; while Wady esh-Sheikh on the right, and the recess on the left, both connected with and opening broadly from Er Rahah, presented an area which serves nearly to double that of the plain. Here lay the plain where the whole congregation might be assembled; here was the mount that could be approached and touched, if not forbidden; and here the mountain-brow where alone the lightnings and the thick cloud would be visible, and the thunders and the voice of the trump be heard when the Lord 'came down in the sight of all the people upon Mount Sinai.' entries.definition: SINCERITY stands opposed to dissimulation or hypocrisy, and implies the entire correspondence of the heart with the expressions of the lips. 2 Cor 1:12. The original word refers to the bright and penetrating light of the sun, and denotes such things as, on being examined by the brightest light, are found pure and unadulterated.
entries.definition_ko: 거짓 꾸밈이나 외식과 반대되는 말로, 마음과 입술의 표현이 온전히 일치함을 함축한다(고린도후서 1:12). 원어는 해의 밝고 꿰뚫는 빛을 가리키며, 가장 밝은 빛으로 살펴보아도 순수하고 섞임이 없는 것을 뜻한다.

entries.definition: SI'NIM. This geographical term occurs only once in the Bible, in Isa 49:12. The country meant is generally considered to be China, though some would leave it an open question.
entries.definition_ko: 이 지리 용어는 성경에 한 번만 나온다(이사야 49:12). 가리키는 나라는 대개 중국으로 여겨지나, 열린 문제로 두려는 이들도 있다.

entries.definition: SIN'ITE, a tribe descended from Canaan. Gen 10:17; 1 Chr 1:15.
entries.definition_ko: 아르가 근처 신 땅의 주민을 가리킨다(창세기 10:17).

entries.definition: SIN-MONEY, money sent by persons at a distance, with which to buy the required offerings, 2 Kgs 12:16; and, as there was usually some surplus, it was the perquisite of the priest, and was called "sin-money," or "sin-offering money." Num 18:9.
entries.definition_ko: 멀리 있는 사람들이 필요한 제물을 사도록 보낸 돈이다(열왕기하 12:16). 대개 얼마간 남았으므로 그것이 제사장의 몫이 되어 '속건제 돈' 또는 '속죄제 돈'이라 불렸다(민수기 18:9).

entries.definition: SIN-OF'FERINGS. Num 18:9. See Offering.
entries.definition_ko: 제사 참조(민수기 18:9).

entries.definition: SIN, WILDERNESS OF, a region between Elim and Rephidim. Ex 16:1; Ex 17:1; Num 33:11-12. Here the Israelites were first fed with manna and quails. The wilderness extends 25 miles along the east shore of the Red Sea, from Wady Taiyibeh to Wady Feiran; it is now called the plain of el-Markha. It is barren, but has a little vegetation, and when the rainfall was larger and the drainage from the mountain descended more gradually, instead of sweeping everything before it as now, it may have afforded fair pasturage. Travellers report seeing numerous quails upon this plain in modern times.
entries.definition_ko:
신 광야. 엘림과 르비딤 사이의 지역이다. 출애굽기 16장 1절과 출애굽기 17장 1절과 민수기 33장 11절과 33장 12절이다. 여기에서 이스라엘 사람이 처음으로 만나와 메추라기를 받아먹었다.

이 광야는 홍해 동쪽 기슭을 따라 와디 타이이베에서 와디 페이란까지 이십오 마일에 걸쳐 뻗어 있으며 이제는 엘마르카 평지라 부른다.

메마른 곳이나 풀이 조금 있다. 비가 더 많이 오고 산에서 흘러내리는 물이 오늘처럼 모든 것을 쓸어 가지 않고 더 천천히 내려오던 때에는 꽤 쓸 만한 풀밭이 되었을 수 있다.

오늘날 길손들은 이 벌판에서 메추라기를 숱하게 보았다고 전한다.

entries.definition: SI'ON (lofty), the name of two mountains in Palestine. One of the various names of Mount Hermon. Deut 4:48: See Hermon. The Greek form of the Hebrew name "Zion." Matt 21:5; John 12:15. See Zion.
entries.definition_ko: '높은 곳'이라는 뜻. (1) 헤르몬산을 가리키는 이름(신명기 4:48). (2) 마태복음 21:5 등에 나오는 시온의 헬라어 형태.

entries.definition: SIPH'MOTH (fruitful places), a place in the South of Judah frequented by David when an outlaw. 1 Sam 30:28.
entries.definition_ko: '풍요로운 곳들'이라는 뜻으로 다윗이 사울을 피해 도망칠 때 친구들을 만난 남쪽의 알려지지 않은 장소이다(사무엘상 30:28).

entries.definition: SIP'PAI (threshold?), a Philistine giant, 1 Chr 20:4; called also Saph.
entries.definition_ko: 십브개에게 게셀에서 죽임당한 거인족 중 하나로 삽이라고도 불린다(역대상 20:4).

entries.definition: SI'RAH, THE WELL OF (retreat), the place from which Abner was recalled by Joab, who put him to death at Hebron. 2 Sam 8:26. It is now called 'Ain Sarah, a spring about 1 mile from Hebron, and a little to one side of the main road.
entries.definition_ko:
'물러남'이라는 뜻으로, 요압이 아브넬을 불러들여 헤브론에서 죽인 그 자리다(사무엘하 3:26). 지금은 아인 사라라 불리며 헤브론에서 1마일쯤, 큰길에서 조금 벗어난 곳의 샘이다.
※ 원문 오류: 2 Sam 8:26 → 사무엘하 3:26
※ 판정 근거: 사무엘하 8장은 18절까지뿐이다. 사무엘하 3:26이 시라 우물에서 아브넬을 데리고 돌아온 자리이다.

variants.definition: SI'RAH, THE WELL OF (retreat), the place from which Abner was recalled by Joab, who put him to death at Hebron. 2 Sam 8:26. It is now called 'Ain Sarah, a spring about 1 mile from Hebron, and a little to one side of the main road.
variants.definition_ko: '물러남'이라는 뜻으로, 요압이 아브넬을 불러들여 헤브론에서 죽인 그 자리다(사무엘하 3:26). 지금은 아인 사라라 불리며 헤브론에서 1마일쯤, 큰길에서 조금 벗어난 곳의 샘이다.

entries.definition: SIR'ION (breastplate ?), a Zidonian name of Mount Hermon. Deut 3:9,Ps 29:6. Perhaps this name was applied to a part of Hermon only.
entries.definition_ko: '흉갑'이라는 뜻으로 헤르몬산의 시돈식 이름이다(신명기 3:9, 시편 29:6). 어쩌면 헤르몬의 한 부분에만 이 이름이 쓰였을 것이다.

entries.definition: SISAM'AI (distinguished ?), a descendant of Judah. 1 Chr 2:40.
entries.definition_ko: 여라므엘 계열 세산의 후손이다(역대상 2:40).

entries.definition: SIS'ERA (battle-array). The general of Jabin's army. Judg 4:2. See Barak, Deborah, Jael. The ancestor of some who returned with Zerubbabel. Ezr 2:53; Neh 7:55.
entries.definition_ko: 「싸움 대열」을 뜻한다. 야빈의 군대 장관이다(사사기 4:2). 바락과 드보라와 야엘 항목 참조. 또 하나는 스룹바벨과 함께 돌아온 이들의 조상이다.

entries.definition: SIS'TER'S SON. In Col 4:10 the term should be "cousin." In biblical usage, this word is not limited to our sense, but, like "mother," "father," "son," "daughter," has a far wider application. Thus, in 2 Sam 13:2, it means a step- or half-sister, in Matt 13:56 a cousin, and in Rom 16:1 merely a fellow-believer.
entries.definition_ko: 골로새서 4:10에서 '생질'은 '사촌'으로 옮겨야 한다. 성경에서 이 말은 우리 뜻에 한정되지 않고 '어머니', '아버지', '아들', '딸'처럼 훨씬 넓게 쓰인다. 사무엘하 13:2에서는 이복 누이를, 마태복음 13:56에서는 사촌을, 로마서 16:1에서는 단지 함께 믿는 자를 뜻한다.

entries.definition: SIT'NAH (strife), the name of the second of two wells dug by Isaac in the valley of Gerar, and for which the herdmen disputed. Gen 26:21. It is between Rehoboth and Beer-sheba, in a small valley called Shutnet er-Raheibeh, names in which are doubtless preserved both the Sitnah and Rehoboth of the Scripture.

entries.definition: SLAVE, SLAVERY. Slavery is contrary to the constitution and destination of man and to the spirit of the Bible, which begins and ends with freedom, and represents man as made in the image of God, and places him, as lord, at the head of the whole creation. God gave Adam an equal and only partner in Eve. Slavery, like polygamy and war, was the consequence of sin, and spread with sin among all ancient nations. The Bible tolerates, regulates, moderates, and restrains this abnormal institution, but provides also for its ultimate extinction. "The manner in which Christ and the apostles dealt with an institution so universally prevalent in its worst forms, and so intimately interwoven with the whole public and private life in the Roman empire, is a strong proof of their divine wisdom. Christianity accomplished what no other religion has even attempted before or since. Without interfering with slavery as a political and economical question, without encouraging any revolution or agitation, without denouncing the character or denying the rights of the slave-holder or creating discontent among the slaves, without disturbing the peace of a single family, without any appeal to the passions and prejudices of men on the evils and abuses of slavery, without requiring, or even suggesting, immediate emancipation, in one word, without changing the outward and legal relation between the two parties, but solemnly enforcing the rights and duties arising from it to both, - Christ and the apostles, nevertheless, from within, by purely spiritual and peaceful means, by teaching the common origin and common redemption, the true dignity, equality, and destiny of men, by inculcating the principles of universal justice and love, and by raising the most degraded and unfortunate classes of society to virtue and purity, and to spiritual freedom in Christ, produced a radical moral reformation of the system, and prepared the only effectual way for its gradual, legitimate, and harmless extinction." - Schaff: Slavery and the Bible (1861). A. Hebrew Slavery. - There were only two conditions known among the Jews - independence and servitude. Whenever a man was too poor or otherwise unable to be independent, he became a slave. Slaves, among the Hebrews, were of two general classes: 1. Hebrews; 2. Non-Hebrews. Hebrews. - There were three ways whereby liberty could be taken from a Hebrew: (1) Poverty. He might sell himself in default of payment of debt. Lev 25:39. (2) Theft, when he could not pay the amount required. Ex 22:1, Num 1:3. According to Josephus, he could only be sold to a Hebrew. (3) Parents could sell their daughters as maid-servants, but they were ultimately to be their masters' concubines. Ex 21:7. There were three ways by which the servitude might end:(1) When the debt or other obligation was met: (2) When the year of Jubilee had come. Lev 25:40; (3) At the conclusion of six years of service. Ex 21:2; Deut 15:12, Indeed, no servitude could last longer than six years. In case, however, the slave did not wish to go at the expiration of the time, either because he loved his master or his wife - presumably a foreigner - and children, who must be left behind, as they were the master's property, the master announced this fact to the judges, and then bored his ear through with an awl. Ex 21:6; Deut 15:17. That this was done speaks volumes for the mildness of Hebrew slavery. Indeed, the Law made the condition of a slave very tolerable. The owner was expressly forbidden to "rule over him with rigor." Lev 25:43. Nor was he suffered to go away empty, but must be furnished liberally out of the flock, out of the floor, and out of the wine-press. Deut 15:14. A slave might even marry a daughter of his master. 1 Chr 2:35. In the ease of a female Hebrew slave, there was not the release at the end of six years; but if marriage with the owner or his son did not take place, she was not to be sold to a foreigner, but "he shall cause her to be redeemed" - i.e., he should return her to her father or find her another Hebrew master, or else free her absolutely. Ex 21:7-11. When Hebrews became the slaves of non-Hebrews, they might be redeemed or redeem themselves, or else go free at the year of jubilee. Jewish Hebrew slavery terminated at the Captivity. Non-Hebrews. - These constituted the majority of the slaves among the Hebrews. They were mostly captives made in war from the neighboring tribes, but besides were purchased of dealers. Lev 25:45, foreigners reduced to this condition, or else the children of such slaves. Gen 14:14; Eccl 2:7. This sort of slavery survived the Captivity, but was opposed by the Pharisees. Thirty shekels seems to have been the average price of a slave. Ex 21:32. The slaves' lot was comparatively happy. Their persons were protected against violence; for if they lost an eye or a tooth from rough handling, they got their liberty. Ex 21:26-27. To kill one was murder. Lev 24:17, Josh 11:22. They had full religious privileges, since they were circumcised. Gen 17:12. Slavery at best is bondage, and hence we find the service of these slaves was menial. They ploughed the fields, did the housework, ground the corn, took off and put on their master's sanda1s, washed his feet, and performed all the services expected of those in their condition. But slaves, by their industry and ability, could raise themselves to positions of trust, becoming stewards, as was Eliezer, Gen 15:2, or independent freemen, as was Ziba. 2 Sam 9:2, 2 Sam 9:10. B. Roman Slavery. - The Gospel of Jesus Christ, declaring freedom from the slavery of sin, was preached unto them who were literally bound. The early Christian Church was largely composed of slaves, and around them were thrown none of the protections which rendered a Hebrew slave so safe. On the contrary, the Roman master regarded his slaves as his absolute property. He might treat them kindly - and doubtless many did - but no law compelled him to do so. The Roman proverb, "So many slaves, so many foes," tells a pitiful story of wrong. This was the sort of slavery mentioned incidentally in the N.T. It is remarkable that nothing is said about its abolishment. On the contrary, the slaves were enjoined to be obedient to their masters, and to prove their Christian character by their patience under suffering. The Bible has furnished the defenders of slavery with proof-texts, but yet the study of the Bible has led to the abolishment of the system. The Mosaic legislation on the subject induced such mildness that the very idea could not be tolerated, and so, in Christ's day, Hebrew slavery of both kinds was utterly extirpated. The N.T. directions had a similar result. A Christian could not hold souls in bondage for whom the blood of Christ was shed. And so slavery ended in the empire among Christians. Today it is acknowledged throughout Christendom as a crime; while Mohammedanism holds fast to slavery and polygamy - the two twin-sisters of barbarism. The liberty in Christ Jesus extends to the body as well as to the soul. The gospel, in emancipating from the bondage of sin, breaks the backbone of every other kind of bondage, and substitutes for it the service of God, which is perfect freedom.
entries.definition_ko:
종살이는 사람의 됨됨이와 정해진 뜻에 어긋나고, 자유로 시작하고 끝나며 사람을 하나님의 형상대로 지어진 이로 나타내고 온 창조의 머리에 주인으로 두는 성경의 정신에 어긋난다. 하나님이 아담에게 하와라는 대등하고 오직 하나인 짝을 주셨다. 종살이가 여러 아내를 둠과 싸움처럼 죄의 결과였고 죄와 함께 온 옛 민족에 퍼졌다. 성경이 이 어그러진 제도를 견디고 다스리고 누그러뜨리고 막으면서, 또한 그것이 마침내 없어질 마련도 한다. 「로마 제국의 온 공적이고 사사로운 삶에 그토록 두루 퍼지고 그토록 가까이 얽힌, 더욱이 더없이 나쁜 꼴의 제도를 그리스도와 사도들이 다룬 방식이 그 하나님다운 지혜의 세찬 증거이다. 그리스도교가 다른 어떤 신앙도 앞서도 뒤에도 시도조차 하지 않은 것을 이루었다. 종살이를 정치와 경제의 물음으로 건드리지 않고, 어떤 혁명이나 소요도 북돋우지 않으며, 종 임자의 됨됨이를 나무라거나 그 권리를 부인하지 않고, 종 가운데 불만을 일으키지 않으며, 한 집안의 화평도 어지럽히지 않고, 종살이의 악과 남용에 대하여 사람의 격정과 편견에 호소하지 않으며, 곧바른 놓아줌을 요구하거나 내밀지도 않고, 한마디로 두 편 사이의 바깥과 법의 관계를 바꾸지 않으면서도, 거기서 나오는 양쪽의 권리와 본분을 엄숙히 힘 있게 하며, 그리스도와 사도들이 그런데도 안에서부터, 순전히 영이요 화평한 방편으로, 사람의 함께한 비롯함과 함께한 구속과 참된 존귀함과 대등함과 정해진 뜻을 가르침으로, 두루 미치는 공의와 사랑의 이치를 새김으로, 사회의 더없이 낮추어지고 불행한 계층을 덕과 순수함으로, 그리스도 안의 영의 자유로 일으킴으로, 이 체계의 뿌리로부터의 도덕의 개혁을 낳고 그것이 차츰 마땅하고 해 없이 없어질 유일하게 효험 있는 길을 채비하였다.」—샤프 『종살이와 성경』(1861년). 첫째, 히브리 종살이. 유대인 가운데 알려진 두 처지뿐이었으니 홀로 섬과 종살이이다. 사람이 너무 가난하거나 달리 홀로 설 수 없을 때마다 종이 되었다. 히브리 사람 가운데 종이 두 두루 된 갈래였으니 첫째 히브리 사람이요 둘째 히브리 사람 아닌 이였다. 히브리 사람. 히브리 사람에게서 자유를 빼앗을 수 있는 길이 셋이었다. 첫째 가난이니, 빚을 갚지 못하여 스스로를 팔 수 있었다(레위기 25:39). 둘째 도둑질이니, 요구된 값을 갚을 수 없을 때이다(출애굽기 22:1). 요세푸스에 따르면 오직 히브리 사람에게만 팔릴 수 있었다. 셋째, 부모가 제 딸을 여종으로 팔 수 있었으나 그들이 마침내 그 주인의 첩이 될 것이었다(출애굽기 21:7). 종살이가 끝날 수 있는 길이 셋이었다. 첫째 빚이나 다른 의무가 채워졌을 때요, 둘째 희년이 왔을 때이며(레위기 25:40), 셋째 여섯 해 섬김이 마쳤을 때이다(출애굽기 21:2; 신명기 15:12). 참으로 어떤 종살이도 여섯 해보다 오래 갈 수 없었다. 그러나 그때가 다하여도 종이 가기를 바라지 않으면, 곧 제 주인을 사랑하거나 아마 이방인일 아내와 자녀를 사랑하여 그러하니 그들은 주인의 재산이므로 두고 가야 하기 때문인데, 주인이 이 사실을 재판관에게 알리고 송곳으로 그 귀를 뚫었다(출애굽기 21:6; 신명기 15:17). 이것이 행해졌다는 것이 히브리 종살이의 부드러움을 넉넉히 말해 준다. 참으로 이 법이 종의 형편을 매우 견딜 만하게 하였다. 임자가 「엄하게 부리지」 말라는 뚜렷한 금함을 받았다(레위기 25:43). 또 그를 빈손으로 가게 하지 못하고 양 떼와 타작마당과 포도주 틀에서 넉넉히 주어야 하였다(신명기 15:14). 종이 나아가 제 주인의 딸과 혼인할 수도 있었다(역대상 2:35). 히브리 여종의 경우에는 여섯 해 끝의 놓임이 없었다. 그러나 임자나 그 아들과의 혼인이 이루어지지 않으면 이방인에게 팔 수 없고 「그를 속량하게 할 것이라」 하였으니, 곧 그를 그 아버지에게 돌려보내거나 다른 히브리 주인을 찾아 주거나 아주 놓아주어야 하였다(출애굽기 21:7-11). 히브리 사람이 히브리 사람 아닌 이의 종이 되면, 무름을 받거나 스스로 무르거나 희년에 놓여 날 수 있었다. 유대인의 히브리 종살이가 사로잡힘에서 끝났다. 히브리 사람 아닌 이. 이들이 히브리 사람 가운데 종의 큰 몫을 이루었다. 대개 이웃 지파에게서 싸움으로 사로잡은 이였으나, 그 밖에 장사꾼에게서 사기도 하였고(레위기 25:45) 이 처지로 떨어진 이방인이나 그런 종의 자녀였다(창세기 14:14; 전도서 2:7). 이런 종류의 종살이가 사로잡힘 뒤에도 남았으나 바리새인이 그것을 거스렸다. 서른 세겔이 종의 평균 값이었던 듯하다(출애굽기 21:32). 종의 처지가 견주어 보아 행복하였다. 그 몸이 폭력에서 지켜졌으니, 거칠게 다루어져 눈이나 이를 잃으면 자유를 얻었다(출애굽기 21:26,27). 하나를 죽이는 것이 살인이었다(레위기 24:17). 할례를 받았으므로 신앙의 온전한 특권을 지녔다(창세기 17:12). 종살이가 아무리 나아도 매임이니, 그리하여 이 종의 섬김이 천한 것이었음을 본다. 밭을 갈고 집안일을 하고 곡식을 갈고 주인의 신을 벗기고 신기며 그 발을 씻고, 그 처지의 이에게 바라는 온갖 섬김을 하였다. 그러나 종이 그 부지런함과 능력으로 스스로를 믿음의 자리로 올릴 수 있어, 엘리에셀처럼 청지기가 되거나(창세기 15:2) 시바처럼 홀로 선 자유인이 되었다(사무엘하 9:2,10). 둘째, 로마 종살이. 죄의 종살이에서 벗어남을 밝히는 예수 그리스도의 복음이 글자대로 매인 이들에게 전해졌다. 이른 그리스도인 교회가 크게 종으로 이루어졌고, 히브리 종을 그토록 안전하게 한 그 어떤 지킴도 그들 둘레에 없었다. 도리어 로마 주인이 제 종을 절대의 재산으로 여겼다. 그가 그들을 친절히 대할 수도 있었고 틀림없이 많은 이가 그리하였으나, 어떤 법도 그리하도록 강요하지 않았다. 「종이 많으면 원수가 많다」는 로마 속담이 딱한 부당함의 이야기를 들려준다. 이것이 신약에 곁들여 언급된 종류의 종살이이다. 그 없앰에 대하여 아무 말이 없음이 남다르다. 도리어 종이 그 주인에게 순종하고 고난 아래 참음으로 그리스도인의 됨됨이를 밝히라는 명을 받았다. 성경이 종살이를 지키는 이에게 증거 구절을 주었으나, 그러면서도 성경을 살핌이 이 체계의 없앰으로 이끌었다. 이 주제에 대한 모세의 입법이 그런 부드러움을 낳아 그 생각 자체를 견딜 수 없게 하였고, 그리하여 그리스도 때에 두 종류의 히브리 종살이가 아주 뿌리 뽑혔다. 신약의 지시가 비슷한 결과를 낳았다. 그리스도인이 그리스도의 피가 흘려진 그 영혼을 매어 둘 수 없었다. 그리하여 종살이가 제국 안 그리스도인 가운데 끝났다. 오늘 그것이 온 그리스도교 세계에 죄로 인정된다. 반면에 회교는 종살이와 여러 아내를 둠이라는 야만의 쌍둥이 자매를 굳게 붙든다. 그리스도 예수 안의 자유가 영혼에만이 아니라 몸에도 미친다. 복음이 죄의 매임에서 놓아 주며 온갖 다른 매임의 등뼈를 꺾고, 그 자리에 온전한 자유인 하나님을 섬김을 놓는다.
※ 원문 오류: Josh 11:22 → 레위기 24:22
※ 판정 근거: 이어받기 숫자 부풀리기. 원문에서 책과 장을 생략한 맨 숫자에 엉뚱한 주소가 붙은 것이다. 앞의 성한 인용을 좇으면 레위기 24:22가 되며, 그 절은 「거류민에게든지 본토인에게든지 그 법을 동일하게 할 것은 나는 너희의 하나…」이다.
※ 원문 오류: Num 1:3 → 출애굽기 22:3
※ 판정 근거: 이어받기 숫자 부풀리기. 원문에서 책과 장을 생략한 맨 숫자에 엉뚱한 주소가 붙은 것이다. 앞의 성한 인용을 좇으면 출애굽기 22:3가 되며, 그 절은 「해 돋은 후에는 피 흘린 죄가 있으리라 도둑은 반드시 배상할 것이나 배상…」이다.

Without interfering with slavery as a political and economical question, without encouraging any revolution or agitation, without denouncing the character or denying the rights of the slave-holder or creating discontent among the slaves, without disturbing the peace of a single family, without any appeal to the passions and prejudices of men on the evils and abuses of slavery, without requiring, or even suggesting, immediate emancipation, in one word, without changing the outward and legal relation between the two parties, but solemnly enforcing the rights and duties arising from it to both, - Christ and the apostles, nevertheless, from within, by purely spiritual and peaceful means, by teaching the common origin and common redemption, the true dignity, equality, and destiny of men, by inculcating the principles of universal justice and love, and by raising the most degraded and unfortunate classes of society to virtue and purity, and to spiritual freedom in Christ, produced a radical moral reformation of the system, and prepared the only effectual way for its gradual, legitimate, and harmless extinction." - Schaff: Slavery and the Bible (1861). A. Hebrew Slavery. - There were only two conditions known among the Jews - independence and servitude. Whenever a man was too poor or otherwise unable to be independent, he became a slave. Slaves, among the Hebrews, were of two general classes: 1. Hebrews; 2. Non-Hebrews. could last longer than six years. In case, however, the slave did not wish to go at the expiration of the time, either because he loved his master or his wife - presumably a foreigner - and children, who must be left behind, as they were the master's property, the master announced this fact to the judges, and then bored his ear through with an awl. Ex 21:6; Deut 15:17. That this was done speaks volumes for the mildness of Hebrew slavery. Indeed, the Law made the condition of a slave very tolerable. The owner was expressly forbidden to "rule over him with rigor." Lev 25:43. Nor was he suffered to go away empty, but must be furnished liberally out of the flock, out of the floor, and out of the wine-press. Deut 15:14. A slave might even marry a daughter of his master. 1 Chr 2:35. In the ease of a female Hebrew slave, there was not the release at the end of six years; but if marriage with the owner or his son did not take place, she was not to be sold to a foreigner, but "he shall cause her to be redeemed" - i.e., he should return her to her father or find her another Hebrew master, or else free her absolutely. Ex 21:7-11. When Hebrews became the slaves of non-Hebrews, they might be redeemed or redeem themselves, or else go free at the year of jubilee. Jewish Hebrew slavery terminated at the Captivity. Slavery at best is bondage, and hence we find the service of these slaves was menial. They ploughed the fields, did the housework, ground the corn, took off and put on their master's sanda1s, washed his feet, and performed all the services expected of those in their condition. But slaves, by their industry and ability, could raise themselves to positions of trust, becoming stewards, as was Eliezer, Gen 15:2, or independent freemen, as was Ziba. 2 Sam 9:2, 2 Sam 9:10. B. Roman Slavery. - The Gospel of Jesus Christ, declaring freedom from the slavery of sin, was preached unto them who were literally bound. The early Christian Church was largely composed of slaves, and around them were thrown none of the protections which rendered a Hebrew slave so safe. On the contrary, the Roman master regarded his slaves as his absolute property. He might treat them kindly - and doubtless many did - but no law compelled him to do so. The Roman proverb, "So many slaves, so many foes," tells a pitiful story of wrong. This was the sort of slavery mentioned incidentally in the N.T. It is remarkable that nothing is said about its abolishment. On the contrary, the slaves were enjoined to be obedient to their masters, and to prove their Christian character by their patience under suffering. The Bible has furnished the defenders of slavery with proof-texts, but yet the study of the Bible has led to the abolishment of the system. The Mosaic legislation on the subject induced such mildness that the very idea could not be tolerated, and so, in Christ's day, Hebrew slavery of both kinds was utterly extirpated. The N.T. directions had a similar result. A Christian could not hold souls in bondage for whom the blood of Christ was shed. And so slavery ended in the empire among Christians. Today it is acknowledged throughout Christendom as a crime; while Mohammedanism holds fast to slavery and polygamy - the two twin-sisters of barbarism. The liberty in Christ Jesus extends to the body as well as to the soul. The gospel, in emancipating from the bondage of sin, breaks the backbone of every other kind of bondage, and substitutes for it the service of God, which is perfect freedom.
